verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5

1. ANSWER

| # | Pollutant / averaging time | Primary standard level | Units | Statistical form (40 CFR pt. 50, app. N) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | PM2.5, annual (annual arithmetic mean) | 9.0 | µg/m³ | 3-year average of annual arithmetic mean concentrations | 40 CFR § 50.20(a), (b) |
| 2 | PM2.5, 24-hour | 35 | µg/m³ | 3-year average of annual 98th percentile 24-hour concentrations | 40 CFR § 50.20(a), (c) |

PM2.5 is defined in the same section as particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers, measured in the ambient air by a reference method (appendix L) or an equivalent method (appendix C to part 53). Both standards above are primary (health-based, Clean Air Act § 109) standards; secondary (welfare-based) standards are out of scope per the request and are noted only in § 6 below.

2. REGULATORY BASIS AND 'CURRENT' DETERMINATION

- Controlling provision: 40 CFR § 50.20, 'National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5,' promulgated in 'Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter,' 89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024), signed Feb. 7, 2024, effective May 6, 2024.
- That rule revised the level of the primary annual PM2.5 standard to 9.0 µg/m³ and retained the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m³.
- 'Current' is therefore interpreted as the standards in effect under the most recent finalized NAAQS review for PM2.5 — i.e., the 2024 reconsideration — and not the 2012/2013 review.

3. DISCLOSURE — WHY 12.0 µg/m³ APPEARS IN 40 CFR § 50.18 AND WHY IT IS NOT THE ANSWER TO ASK 1

The frequently cited figures of 12.0 µg/m³ (annual) and 35 µg/m³ (24-hour) come from 40 CFR § 50.18, the provision established by the 2012 PM2.5 NAAQS review (78 FR 3086, Jan. 15, 2013). § 50.18 remains in the Code of Federal Regulations as a transition/implementation provision for the 2012 annual standard while designations and implementation for the 2024 standard proceed; the 2024 rule placed the revised standards in a new § 50.20 rather than amending § 50.18 in place. Consequently:

- § 50.18 still reads 12.0 µg/m³ annual / 35 µg/m³ 24-hour — accurate text, superseded annual level.
- § 50.20 reads 9.0 µg/m³ annual / 35 µg/m³ 24-hour — this is the current primary annual level.
- The 24-hour level is unaffected by this distinction: 35 µg/m³ under both provisions, so ask 2 carries no ambiguity.
- A citation to § 50.18 alone, offered as 'the current standard,' is a provision-level error even though the quoted text is genuine. This determination relies on § 50.20 and discloses the § 50.18 figure explicitly rather than suppressing it.

4. HOW EACH STANDARD IS JUDGED (appendix N to part 50)

- Annual (9.0 µg/m³): an area meets the standard when the 3-year average of the annual arithmetic mean PM2.5 concentrations from eligible monitoring sites is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³. A single year's mean above 9.0 does not by itself constitute a violation.
- 24-hour (35 µg/m³): an area meets the standard when the 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile of 24-hour PM2.5 concentrations is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³.
- Rounding/conventions: concentrations are reported and compared per appendix N (annual means to one decimal place; 98th percentiles computed per the appendix N quantile procedure). Design values are the 3-year statistics above, not single-year statistics.

5. SCOPE AND CAVEATS A REVIEWER SHOULD CONFIRM

- Only primary standards are answered; the request excludes secondary standards.
- Pending or subsequent rulemaking: if a later final rule has revised the PM2.5 NAAQS after the 2024 reconsideration, the levels in § 1 would change. Verification procedure: retrieve https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.20 and confirm the operative text reads '9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration'; cross-check EPA's NAAQS table (https://www.epa.gov/criteria-air-pollutants/naaqs-table). If § 50.20 has been amended, the amended levels control and supersede § 1.
- Transition status of § 50.18: because § 50.18 was to be removed following the effective date of the initial designations for the 2024 annual standard (designations due within two years of promulgation, i.e., February 2026), § 50.18 may be absent from, or annotated in, the current CFR. Its presence or absence does not change the current annual level of 9.0 µg/m³.
- Judicial review of the 2024 rule does not suspend its effective date absent a stay; no stay changed the levels as stated here.

6. OUT-OF-SCOPE CONTEXT (recorded only to prevent conflation)

Secondary PM2.5 standards (welfare-based, 40 CFR § 50.20): 15.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average. These are NOT the primary standards requested and must not be substituted for the values in § 1.

7. BOTTOM LINE FOR DOWNSTREAM USE

Current U.S. national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5: annual = 9.0 µg/m³ (3-year average of annual arithmetic means); 24-hour = 35 µg/m³ (3-year average of annual 98th percentiles). Source of record: 40 CFR § 50.20, as promulgated at 89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024, effective May 6, 2024). The 12.0 µg/m³ annual figure still visible at 40 CFR § 50.18 is the superseded 2012-review level retained for transition and is not the current standard.

(b) The primary annual PM~2.5~ standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m^3^.
(c) The primary 24-hour PM~2.5~ standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m^3^.

verdict.summary:
Answer: 4 feet (1.2 m; 48 inches) or more above a lower level.

Governing federal requirement: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i), OSHA general-industry walking-working surfaces standard, Subpart D. The provision requires that, except as provided elsewhere in the section, the employer ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) guardrail systems; (B) safety net systems; or (C) personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

Scope: This is the general-industry threshold. It is not the construction threshold. Construction fall protection under 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) is triggered at 6 feet (1.8 m); that 6-foot value does not apply to the general-industry walking-working-surface question asked here.

Application procedure:
1. Confirm the work is general industry and governed by 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D, not construction (29 CFR 1926) or another industry-specific standard.
2. Identify the walking-working surface and the unprotected side or edge.
3. Measure the vertical distance from the walking-working surface to the lower level.
4. If the unprotected side or edge is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above the lower level, provide fall protection using one or more of the permitted systems: guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems.
5. Before relying on the 4-foot general threshold alone, check the rest of 29 CFR 1910.28 and any other applicable provision for surface-specific or task-specific exceptions, because the general rule begins with the qualification 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section.' For example, the section contains specific provisions for certain loading rack, loading dock, or teeming platform situations where the employer can demonstrate that fall protection systems are not feasible on the working side; the stated conditions in the regulatory text must be met. Other subparts, such as those for ladders or scaffolds, may carry their own requirements.

Jurisdiction note: This is the federal OSHA answer. OSHA-approved state plans may adopt different or stricter requirements; where a state plan governs, verify the applicable state rule.

Practical compliance statement: For an ordinary general-industry walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge and no applicable exception, the employer must protect the employee at 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above the lower level.

verdict.summary:
# Reserve fuel for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the US

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless the fuel aboard is enough to (a) fly to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, and (b) then fly for **at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed**. The 20 minutes is the reserve; it is *in addition to* the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing.

- Governing rule (Part 91 general operating rules): **14 CFR 91.151(b)**
- Parallel rule for Part 135 helicopter operations: **14 CFR 135.209(b)** — substantively the same 20-minute requirement, so the answer does not change with the operating regime for this question.
- The reserve is expressed in **time**, not in gallons or pounds. A fuel quantity must be derived from the specific helicopter's normal-cruise fuel consumption (§4 below).

## 2. Regulatory text and applicability

**14 CFR 91.151 — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions** (verified against the eCFR text):

> "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Points that follow directly from the text and are the ones that decide compliance:

1. **Rotorcraft paragraph is separate.** Paragraph (a) of 91.151 sets 30 minutes (day) / 45 minutes (night) for *airplanes*. Those figures are **not** the helicopter answer and applying them to a helicopter over-plans by 10–25 minutes; applying the helicopter 20 minutes to an airplane under-plans and is a violation.
2. **No day/night increment for helicopters under Part 91.** The 20-minute figure is the same for day and night VFR. There is no night reserve escalation in 91.151(b).
3. **No destination-weather-reporting condition in the VFR helicopter rule.** 91.151(b) contains no "no weather source at destination ⇒ add an alternate reserve" clause. The only weather element is the "considering wind and forecast weather conditions" qualifier, and it attaches to the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing.
4. **"Begin a flight" = a condition of departure.** The check is made before takeoff. Fuel burned in start, taxi, run-up, or hover before departure is not part of the reserve and must be added on top (§5).
5. **"First point of intended landing"** is wherever the PIC intends to first land — an airport, a heliport, or an off-airport site. It is not necessarily a destination with services.
6. **"Normal cruising speed"** means the speed/consumption from the approved performance data at normal cruise power — not max-range, not best-endurance, and not an idle descent. Use the aircraft flight manual/POH cruise figures.
7. **Usable fuel only.** Fuel that cannot be delivered to the engine does not count toward either the trip fuel or the reserve.

**14 CFR 135.209(b)** (Part 135, on-demand/commuter helicopter VFR) carries the same 20-minute helicopter reserve. Where a Part 135 certificate holder operates helicopters VFR, the planning minimum is therefore identical; any larger figure would come from the certificate holder's OpSpecs or manual, not from the regulation. (Confirm the verbatim wording against the current eCFR text at the cited section before quoting it in a compliance document.)

**Scope limits of this answer:** it is the *regulatory minimum* for VFR under Parts 91 and 135. It is not an IFR reserve (91.167 / 135.223 govern IFR and are outside this question), not a company fuel policy, and not a safety recommendation. The legal minimum and a prudent fuel plan are different things — see §6.

## 3. What the rule requires, stated as a fuel-planning inequality

At brake release / start of the flight:

```
Fuel aboard (usable)  >=  Taxi + run-up + hover fuel
                       +  Trip fuel to first point of intended landing (wind & forecast Wx applied)
                       +  20-minute reserve (normal cruise speed & cruise fuel flow)
```

Equivalently, the reserve alone is:

```
Reserve fuel  =  (20/60) h  x  normal-cruise fuel flow  =  0.3333  x  cruise fuel flow
Reserve distance (for cross-check only)  =  0.3333 h  x  normal cruising speed
```

The reserve is a *quantity in the tanks*, not a distance; the distance form is useful only to sanity-check a plan against the leg length.

## 4. Converting 20 minutes into a fuel quantity (worked examples)

Use the POH normal-cruise fuel flow; the 1/3-hour factor is exact for 20 minutes.

**Example A — piston helicopter, Avgas.** Normal cruise 100 kt, cruise fuel flow 10.0 gal/h.
- Reserve = 10.0 gal/h x 0.3333 h = **3.3 gal** (≈ 20 lb at 6.0 lb/gal).
- Cross-check: 100 kt x 0.3333 h ≈ 33 nm of reserve endurance.
- If the leg to the first landing point is 120 nm at 100 kt ground speed, trip fuel = 1.2 h x 10.0 = 12.0 gal; total before taxi = 12.0 + 3.3 = **15.3 gal**, plus taxi/hover fuel.

**Example B — light turbine helicopter, Jet A.** Normal cruise 120 kt, cruise fuel flow 350 lb/h.
- Reserve = 350 lb/h x 0.3333 h = **116.7 lb**.
- At 6.7 lb/gal: 116.7 / 6.7 = **17.4 gal**.
- Cross-check: 120 kt x 0.3333 h = 40 nm of reserve endurance.
- If the leg to the first landing point is 200 nm at 120 kt no-wind, trip fuel = 1.667 h x 350 = 583.3 lb; total before taxi = 583.3 + 116.7 = **700.0 lb**, plus start/taxi/hover fuel.

Both examples satisfy the inequality in §3 exactly; the reserve term is 1/3 of an hour of cruise flow in each case.

## 5. Common errors that produce a wrong reserve figure

| Error | Consequence | Correct treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Applying the airplane rule (30 min day / 45 min night, 91.151(a)) to a helicopter | Over-plans; masks that the operator is not using the rotorcraft paragraph | Use 91.151(b): 20 min, day or night |
| Treating 20 minutes as a fixed gallon/litre number | Under- or over-fuels aircraft with different burn rates | Multiply the 1/3 hour by *this* aircraft's cruise flow |
| Counting taxi/run-up/hover fuel inside the 20 minutes | Reserve at departure is below the legal minimum | Add ground fuel on top of trip + reserve |
| Using max-range or economy cruise in the plan but flying normal cruise | Actual burn exceeds planned burn; reserve erodes | Use normal-cruise POH figures as the rule specifies |
| Planning the trip leg with no wind/forecast consideration | Trip fuel under-stated on a headwind leg | Apply forecast wind and weather to the leg to first landing; the 20 min is then flown at normal cruising speed |
| Counting unusable fuel | Reserve shortfall in flight | Usable fuel only |
| Assuming the 20 minutes covers a diversion to an alternate | No alternate fuel is planned; the VFR helicopter rule provides none | If an alternate is required by the operation, plan fuel for it separately, on top of the 20 minutes |

## 6. Legal minimum versus operating practice (so the 20 minutes is not misread)

- 20 minutes is a **floor**, not a target. Nothing in 91.151(b) prevents a pilot or operator from planning more, and 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) and 91.3 (PIC authority in an emergency) still apply.
- Operators routinely set higher minima in manuals, OpSpecs, or company fuel policy, particularly for overwater, offshore, night, mountainous, or remote-area helicopter work where en-route alternates are sparse.
- When briefing this answer, state it as: *"Regulatory minimum reserve for VFR in a helicopter: 20 minutes at normal cruising speed, in addition to fuel to the first point of intended landing — 14 CFR 91.151(b); 135.209(b) for Part 135."* Do not present it as a recommended fuel load.

## 7. Verification checklist for a specific flight

1. Confirm the operation is VFR and identify the governing part (91 vs 135). Both give 20 minutes for helicopters; note which one you are citing.
2. Confirm the aircraft is a rotorcraft and that 91.151(b) (not 91.151(a)) is being applied.
3. Pull normal-cruise speed and cruise fuel flow from the approved flight manual/POH.
4. Compute reserve = 1/3 h x cruise fuel flow.
5. Compute trip fuel to the first point of intended landing using forecast wind and weather.
6. Add start/taxi/run-up/hover fuel.
7. Confirm total usable fuel aboard at departure ≥ the sum in step 6; confirm the 20-minute quantity remains in the tanks at departure.
8. If any operator/manual/OpSpec minimum exceeds 20 minutes, plan to the higher figure and cite it as the controlling one.

## 8. What would change the answer

- **IFR instead of VFR:** different rule (91.167 / 135.223); not 20 minutes; outside this question.
- **Airplane instead of helicopter:** 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night under 91.151(a); 135.209(a) for Part 135 airplanes.
- **Non-US registry or operation:** foreign national rules apply; this answer is US 14 CFR only.
- **Operator-imposed minimum:** the higher company/OpSpec figure controls for that flight, though the regulation still sets the 20-minute floor.

verdict.summary:
# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

## 1. Direct answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1? | **RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (IETF, published March 2021; in the BCP series as BCP 195). |
| What status did it give the RFCs that defined them? | **Historic.** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were both moved to Historic status. |

## 2. Evidence — verbatim text from RFC 8996

All three quotations below are from the RFC Editor's canonical HTML rendering, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html> (fetched 2026-11-16T06:07:36Z, sha256 ad8cbc15da5f):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

> "TLS 1.0 MUST NOT be used. Negotiation of TLS 1.0 from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted."

> "TLS 1.1 MUST NOT be used. Negotiation of TLS 1.1 from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted."

The first sentence answers both asks simultaneously and unambiguously: the deprecating document is RFC 8996, and the resulting status of the defining documents is Historic.

## 3. Mapping of affected documents

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Title | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 | **Historic** |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 | **Historic** |

No other RFCs are moved to Historic by RFC 8996. In particular, RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) and RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) are **not** deprecated by this document — RFC 8996's deprecation clause names only RFC 2246 and RFC 4346.

## 4. Reading the answer precisely

Three distinctions matter if this answer is going to be cited in a policy, an audit finding, or a procurement clause:

1. **"Status" here means the RFC Editor's document-status field**, not the IETF stream category of RFC 8996 itself. RFC 8996 is published in the Best Current Practice (BCP) series (BCP 195); Historic is the status *assigned to* RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. The two are different attributes of different documents and should not be conflated in a citation.
2. **Deprecation is normative, not advisory.** RFC 8996 does not merely discourage TLS 1.0/1.1; it states that neither version MUST be used and that negotiation of either version MUST NOT be permitted, from any TLS version. A conforming implementation therefore has to refuse the handshake, not just log a warning.
3. **The mechanism is expressed in the body text.** The status change is stated in the sentence quoted in §2 ("...have been moved to Historic status") and is reflected in the RFC Editor's status field for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. Whether RFC 8996 additionally carries an `Obsoletes: 2246, 4346` line in its header block is a separate bibliographic detail that is *not* covered by the evidence gathered here; do not assert it without opening the RFC header. The substantive claim — Historic status, MUST NOT be used — is fully supported.

## 5. Verification procedure (for anyone re-checking this)

1. Fetch <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html>; search for the string `Historic`. It occurs in the deprecation sentence quoted in §2.
2. Open <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/> and <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346/>; confirm each shows `Status: Historic`.
3. Cross-check <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/> for the publication record (date, stream, BCP number).
4. If machine-readable confirmation is wanted, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.json> carries the same metadata.

A check that would falsify this answer: finding an RFC other than 8996 whose deprecation clause names RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, or finding RFC 2246 / RFC 4346 still listed with a status other than Historic on the RFC Editor index. Neither is the case in the sources consulted.

## 6. One-line citation form

> RFC 8996, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (BCP 195), formally deprecates TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) and moves both documents to Historic status; TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 MUST NOT be used and negotiation of either MUST NOT be permitted.

verdict.summary:
The 2026 US Social Security contribution and benefit base — the maximum amount of annual earnings subject to the OASDI portion of the Social Security payroll tax — is $184,500.

Authority: Social Security Administration 2026 contribution-and-benefit-base notice and the corresponding Federal Register publication. The published language is: 'The OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026.' SSA's 2026 fact-sheet/update page likewise states: 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500.'

Application:
- Wages: covered wages paid in 2026 are subject to the 6.2% employee OASDI rate and the 6.2% employer OASDI rate only up to $184,500.
- Self-employment: covered self-employment income in tax years beginning in 2026 is subject to the 12.4% OASDI portion of self-employment tax only up to $184,500.
- The Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) tax has no equivalent annual wage cap, so $184,500 is not a Medicare threshold.

Cap arithmetic check:
- Employee OASDI at the cap: $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439.00.
- Employer OASDI at the cap: $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439.00.
- Combined employee-plus-employer OASDI at the cap: $184,500 × 12.4% = $22,878.00.
- Self-employed OASDI portion at the cap: $184,500 × 12.4% = $22,878.00.

Separate figure to avoid confusion: the 2026 old-law contribution and benefit base is $137,100. That is not the OASDI payroll-tax wage base and should not be substituted for the $184,500 figure requested here.

Final value: $184,500 (USD).

verdict.summary:
## Answer

**The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan is $24,500** — before any catch-up contribution, and before any employer contribution.

Equivalently: the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation for the year.

### Authority and currency

- IRC §402(g)(1) sets the elective deferral limit; §402(g)(5) indexes it for cost-of-living adjustments. The annual adjusted figure is published in the IRS's year-end cost-of-living notice for retirement plans (for the 2026 plan year, the applicable notice is IRS Notice 2025-67) and mirrored on the IRS retirement-plans contribution-limit pages.
- Directly quoted from the IRS "401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits" page: *"The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."*
- Directly quoted from the IRS contributions page: *"The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."*
- IRS newsroom release for the 2026 limits: *"The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."*

Year-over-year context for payroll and budget modeling: $22,500 (2023) → $23,000 (2024) → $23,500 (2025) → **$24,500 (2026)**, a $1,000 increase.

### Scope of the figure — what it does and does not cover

| Dimension | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Deferral type | Pre-tax (traditional) **and** Roth elective deferrals are aggregated and share this single $24,500 limit. Designated Roth 401(k) accounts do not get a separate allowance. |
| Plan types sharing the limit | The same $24,500 applies to 401(k), 403(b), and governmental 457(b) plans. For an employee who participates in more than one such plan, the limit is applied **per individual across all of them combined**, not per plan (excess-deferral correction under §402(g) is an individual-level exercise). |
| Catch-up contributions | **Excluded from this figure.** Age-50+ catch-up and the SECURE 2.0 ages-60-to-63 enhanced catch-up are separate, additive allowances. Do not add them into the base limit or into a base-limit answer; pull those dollar amounts from the same annual notice and keep them as separate payroll limit codes. |
| Employer contributions | Not covered. Employer match, profit sharing, and forfeiture allocations are governed by the §415(c) annual-additions limit, a separate and much larger figure. |
| SIMPLE 401(k) | **Different limit.** A SIMPLE 401(k) has its own, lower elective deferral limit; do not apply $24,500 to a SIMPLE 401(k). Confirm the SIMPLE figure in the same annual notice before configuring payroll. |
| Compensation condition | The limit is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of compensation. The 100% condition bites only for very low-compensation employees (e.g., a partial-year or newly hired employee with under $24,500 of eligible compensation). |
| Out of scope (named only to prevent confusion) | The 2026 IRA limit is $7,500 per the IRS release title. That is an **IRA** limit, not a 401(k) elective deferral limit, and has no bearing on this answer. |

### HR / plan-administration actions to operationalize the figure

1. **Payroll configuration.** Set the 2026 pre-tax deferral cap and the 2026 Roth deferral cap to a **combined** $24,500 per employee per calendar year. If the payroll system caps pre-tax and Roth separately, replace that with a single shared cap; otherwise a participant can reach $24,500 in each and generate a §402(g) excess. Configure a hard stop, not just an alert.
2. **Catch-up as separate codes.** Keep age-50+ and ages-60-to-63 catch-up as distinct limit buckets with their own election and cap fields, so the base limit is never silently inflated. Confirm the 2026 catch-up dollar amounts against the annual notice before loading them.
3. **Multiple-employer / controlled-group employees.** Where an individual defers into more than one plan of the controlled group (or a prior employer's 401(k)/403(b)/governmental 457(b) during 2026), aggregate their deferrals against the single $24,500 limit and correct any excess under the §402(g) correction procedures (distribute the excess plus attributable earnings by the required deadline, generally April 15 of the following year).
4. **Participant communication.** Issue the 2026 limit notice / open-enrollment update showing $24,500 as the base deferral cap and stating separately that catch-up is additional. Refresh the SPD summary of limits and any benefits-guide tables.
5. **Plan document and testing check.** Confirm the plan's deferral limit language references the §402(g) limit as annually adjusted (so $24,500 applies automatically) rather than a hard-coded dollar amount; if hard-coded, amend. Separately, verify the plan's own lower deferral cap, if any (some plans impose a lower percentage or dollar cap), and confirm ADP/ACP testing assumptions still use the updated compensation and deferral figures.
6. **Compensation-limit dependency.** Deferral elections expressed as a percentage of pay interact with the separate §401(a)(17) annual compensation limit used for testing and match calculations; load the 2026 compensation limit from the same annual notice before running year-end testing.

### Verification note

Every dollar figure asserted above as a 2026 limit is either $24,500 (the answer, sourced to three IRS pages, all consistent) or the $7,500 IRA figure, which is explicitly labeled out-of-scope and non-401(k). No catch-up, §415(c), SIMPLE, or compensation-cap dollar amounts are asserted here, by design — those must be read from the 2026 cost-of-living notice and are not part of this answer. The $24,500 figure does not exceed or conflict with any threshold stated in this deliverable.

verdict.summary:
CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5 — ANNUAL AND 24-HOUR LEVELS

1. HEADLINE ANSWER

| Standard | Level | Averaging time | Statistical form used to determine attainment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary annual PM2.5 | 9.0 µg/m³ | Annual (1-year) arithmetic mean concentration, evaluated as the average of three consecutive annual means | 3-year average of annual arithmetic means ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ |
| Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | 35 µg/m³ | 24 hours | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 consecutive years, ≤ 35 µg/m³ |

Pollutant: PM2.5 means particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers, measured in the ambient air by a reference method under 40 CFR part 50 appendix L or an equivalent method under 40 CFR part 53.

Legal basis: Clean Air Act § 109 (42 U.S.C. 7409); 40 CFR part 50. The operative levels are those of the 2024 PM NAAQS reconsideration rule, "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter," 89 FR 16202 (Feb. 7, 2024), effective May 6, 2024, codified at 40 CFR 50.20. That rule revised the primary annual standard from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³, retained the primary 24-hour standard at 35 µg/m³, retained the secondary PM2.5 standards unchanged, and revised the PM2.5 monitoring network design.

2. FORM AND ROUNDING — HOW EACH LEVEL IS ACTUALLY COMPARED

A NAAQS is a number plus an averagin time plus a statistical form plus a rounding convention. For PM2.5 primary standards under 40 CFR part 50 appendix N:

- 24-hour standard (35 µg/m³): computed as the 98th percentile of the distribution of 24-hour concentrations in a year, then averaged over three consecutive years; the area meets the standard when that 3-year average of 98th percentiles is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³. It is NOT a single-day maximum test, and a single day above 35 µg/m³ does not by itself constitute a violation.
- Annual standard (9.0 µg/m³): computed as the annual arithmetic mean, then averaged over three consecutive years; the area meets the standard when that 3-year average is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³.
- Rounding before comparison: 24-hour concentrations are rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ and annual means to the nearest 0.1 µg/m³ prior to comparison to the level.
- Data completeness: the 3-year statistics must satisfy the minimum data-capture requirements of appendix N (generally 75 percent of scheduled sampling days per year/quarter); otherwise the area is classified as having insufficient data rather than as meeting the standard.

3. EPOCH DISCRIMINATION — DO NOT CONFUSE THE OLD ANNUAL VALUE WITH THE CURRENT ONE

The annual level changed; the 24-hour level did not.

- Current (2024 rule onward, 40 CFR 50.20): annual 9.0 µg/m³; 24-hour 35 µg/m³.
- Superseded (2012 rule, 78 FR 3086, Jan. 15, 2013, as codified in the pre-2024 text of 40 CFR 50.18): annual 12.0 µg/m³; 24-hour 35 µg/m³.

A 12.0 µg/m³ annual figure found in a currently rendered CFR page or in an older permit, SIP, or textbook is the 2012-era level and is not the standard in effect. The 35 µg/m³ 24-hour level has been unchanged since the 2006 PM2.5 rule and is therefore the same in both epochs; only the annual level distinguishes them.

4. SCOPE OF THIS ANSWER

In scope: federal primary (health-based, CAA § 109) PM2.5 standards only. Out of scope and not answered here: the secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards, the PM10 standards, state/local PM2.5 standards, and nonattainment designations or SIP obligations. If a compliance or permitting use is intended, the applicable state implementation plan may impose additional or earlier requirements that are not NAAQS levels.

5. VERIFICATION STEPS FOR THE DOWNSTREAM USER (one minute each)

1) Confirm the codified section: open eCFR current 40 CFR 50.20 and confirm the operative text reads 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour. If a rendering of § 50.18 still shows 12.0, that is the unamended pre-2024 text, not the operative level.
2) Confirm no superseding rulemaking: the 2024 rule has been the subject of reconsideration requests, so before relying on 9.0 µg/m³ in a formal submittal, check the eCFR 'current' date stamp and the EPA PM NAAQS page for any later final rule. If a later rule changed the annual level, substitute that value; the 24-hour 35 µg/m³ level would be unaffected unless the rule expressly addressed it.
3) For attainment work, pull the current appendix N (data handling, percentiles, rounding) and appendix L (reference methods) rather than relying on this summary.

6. CITATIONS

- 40 CFR 50.20 (current PM2.5 primary and secondary standards; 2024 rule).
- 40 CFR 50.18 (pre-2024 primary PM2.5 standards: 12.0 µg/m³ annual, 35 µg/m³ 24-hour).
- 40 CFR part 50, appendix N (interpretation of the NAAQS for PM2.5).
- 40 CFR part 50, appendix L (reference methods for PM2.5).
- 89 FR 16202 (Feb. 7, 2024) — 2024 PM NAAQS reconsideration final rule; effective May 6, 2024.
- 78 FR 3086 (Jan. 15, 2013) — 2012 PM NAAQS rule (annual primary standard of 12.0 µg/m³).

verdict.summary:
ANSWER (ask 1): 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

CONTROLLING PROVISION
29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — OSHA general industry, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces):

  "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:"
    (A) Guardrail systems;
    (B) Safety net systems; or
    (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest systems, travel restraint systems, or positioning systems.

HOW TO APPLY THE FIGURE
1. Measure vertically from the walking-working surface the employee stands on to the lower level below the unprotected side or edge. The trigger is 4 feet or more — the duty attaches at exactly 4.00 ft (it is not "more than 4 feet").
2. If the measured height is 4 ft or more and the side/edge is unprotected, the employer must select at least one of the three methods in (A)-(C). Selection is not free choice in every case: each method must meet its own criteria — guardrails, safety nets and designated areas under 29 CFR 1910.29, and personal fall protection systems under 29 CFR 1910.140.
3. If the height is under 4 ft, 1910.28(b)(1) does not itself require fall protection at that edge. Other provisions or authorities may still apply: other paragraphs of 1910.28 (holes/skylights, hoist areas, ramps and walkways, dangerous equipment, roofs), 29 CFR 1910.23 (ladders), and the general duty clause, OSH Act § 5(a)(1), for a recognized hazard causing or likely to cause death or serious physical harm.
4. Training is separately required: employees exposed to fall hazards must be trained under 29 CFR 1910.30.

CONDITIONS AND EXCEPTIONS THAT TRAVEL WITH THE NUMBER
The provision opens with "Except as provided elsewhere in this section," so the 4 ft figure is the default, not the universal rule. A compliant answer must carry these qualifiers:
- Residential roofs: where the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection systems are not feasible or create a greater hazard, the employer must develop and implement a fall protection plan meeting 29 CFR 1926.502(k) and provide training meeting 29 CFR 1926.503(a) and (c). 1910.28(b)(1)(ii).
- Roofs generally: work on low-slope roofs is governed by distance-from-edge tiers rather than the single 4 ft height trigger. When work is performed less than 6 feet from the roof edge, the employer must ensure protection by guardrail system, safety net system, travel restraint system, or personal fall arrest system; farther-from-edge tiers permit a designated area. Note carefully: these 6 ft / 15 ft figures are horizontal distance from the roof edge, not height above a lower level — do not conflate them with the 4 ft trigger. Steep roofs require protection at 4 ft with a narrower set of options. 1910.28(b)(8)-(9) (verify exact paragraph text in the current CFR).
- Other paragraphs of 1910.28(b) set their own triggers or method limits for hoist areas, holes (including skylights), ramps/inclines/other walkways, excavators, dangerous equipment, overhand bricklaying, and outdoor advertising. Where a specific paragraph applies, it controls over the general (b)(1) rule. Confirm each against the current regulatory text before relying on it.

SCOPE — GENERAL INDUSTRY, NOT CONSTRUCTION
- This answer is 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D. It is not the construction rule. Construction fall protection, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M (e.g., 1926.501(b)(1)), triggers at 6 feet (1.8 m) — a different number for a different industry. Do not import the 6 ft construction figure into general industry work, and do not export the 4 ft figure into construction.
- Industry-specific parts carry their own thresholds and must be checked when the work falls under them: shipyard employment (29 CFR Part 1915), longshoring (29 CFR Part 1918), marine terminals (29 CFR Part 1917), and agriculture (29 CFR Part 1928).
- Regulatory basis/currency: 1910.28 was established by the Walking-Working Surfaces final rule, 81 FR 82494 (Nov. 18, 2016), effective Jan. 17, 2017, with staggered compliance dates for certain provisions. The 4 ft figure is unchanged by that rulemaking in the general (b)(1)(i) rule.
- State Plans: 29 CFR 1910.28 is the federal baseline. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard and may be stricter. Employers in State Plan states must verify the state's adopted text before relying on 4 ft.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE RECORD
A US employer in general industry must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level — by guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system — subject to the more specific provisions elsewhere in 29 CFR 1910.28.

SOURCE BASIS AND LIMITS
Quoted regulatory language above is from the eCFR and the 2025 edition of 29 CFR via GovInfo (the OSHA.gov page itself was not used). The headline 4 ft (1.2 m) figure is directly quoted. Paragraph-level detail for provisions other than 1910.28(b)(1) is summarized and should be confirmed against the current CFR text, including any amendments after the 2025 edition, before being cited in an enforcement or design document.

quotes.question_text: Whether the flight is day or night VFR, since the night requirement adds an alternate-landing fuel calculation
quotes.text: (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

quotes.question_text: Whether general Part 91 rules apply or whether an operating certificate's rules (e.g., Part 135) impose a higher reserve
quotes.text: (b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

verdict.summary:
Answer: 20 minutes at normal cruising speed, in addition to the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing.

Governing rule for a civil helicopter under VFR in the US: 14 CFR § 91.151(b): "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

For commercial helicopter operations under Part 135, 14 CFR § 135.209(b) imposes the same VFR helicopter reserve: enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then at least 20 minutes at normal cruising fuel consumption. Thus the regulatory minimum reserve is 20 minutes for helicopter VFR operations under both Part 91 and Part 135. Day and night VFR helicopter reserves are the same; the day/night split in § 91.151(a) applies to airplanes, not rotorcraft.

Interpretation:
- "Beyond the fuel to reach the first point of intended landing" means the reserve is separate from trip fuel. Minimum fuel at the start is trip fuel to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather, plus the 20-minute reserve.
- The 20 minutes is a time, not a fixed gallon or pound quantity. It must be converted using the helicopter's normal cruise fuel flow and usable fuel.
- The first point of intended landing may be an intermediate stop or the destination; the 20-minute reserve is required after that point.

Conversion procedure:
1. Establish normal cruise fuel flow FF in the units used for fuel planning, such as lb/h or gal/h, using the helicopter's performance data at the planned normal cruise power setting.
2. Reserve time t = 20 min = 20/60 h = 0.3333 h.
3. Reserve quantity Q_res = FF × 0.3333.
4. Minimum fuel to begin = Q_trip_to_first_landing + Q_res, plus any additional operational fuel the operator chooses to carry, such as taxi and run-up fuel. Use usable fuel and account for unusable fuel separately.

Worked examples:
- If normal cruise fuel flow is 300 lb/h, Q_res = 300 × 20/60 = 100 lb.
- If normal cruise fuel flow is 50 gal/h, Q_res = 50 × 20/60 = 16.7 gal.
These examples illustrate conversion only; the legal minimum remains 20 minutes at normal cruising speed.

Operational note: company policy, operations specifications, insurance requirements, or flight-planning practice may require more than the regulatory minimum. Those are not the regulatory minimum stated here. The pilot must also ensure the trip fuel to the first point of intended landing is sufficient considering wind and forecast weather conditions.

Answer

1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (IETF Best Current Practice, BCP 195).

2. It gave the RFCs that defined those protocol versions Historic status:

   - RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) -> Historic

Exact basis from RFC 8996:

   "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Terminology note: Historic is the RFC status category assigned by the RFC Editor. It is distinct from the 'Obsoletes' relationship: RFC 4346 obsoleted RFC 2246, and RFC 5246 obsoleted RFC 4346, but RFC 8996's action on the TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 defining documents was to move them to Historic status.

verdict.summary:
# 2026 US Social Security Contribution and Benefit Base

## 1. Answer

**The 2026 OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500.**

This is the maximum amount of annual earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax for 2026. It applies to:

- **remuneration paid in 2026** (wages, including bonuses, commissions, and nonqualified deferred compensation actually paid during the year), and
- **self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026**.

This is an **officially established figure, not a projection.** It was set by the Social Security Administration's annual determination and published in the *Federal Register* on 2025-11-03 (document 2025-19763), and is carried on SSA's Contribution and Benefit Base page. No further rulemaking or revision is pending; the amount is fixed for the year.

## 2. Governing authority and primary citation

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Statutory basis | Section 230 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. § 430), which governs the annual determination of the contribution and benefit base |
| Annual determination published in | *Federal Register*, document 2025-19763, published 2025-11-03 |
| SSA reference page | https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/cola/cbbdet.html (also https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html) |
| Controlling text | "(1) The Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) contribution and benefit base will be $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026." |

For a procurement, audit, or compliance file, cite the *Federal Register* notice as the controlling instrument and the SSA COLA page as the operative public reference.

## 3. How the figure is derived (for auditability)

SSA sets the base each autumn for the following calendar year using the statutory formula in § 230:

1. Take the national average wage index (NAWI) for the year **two years prior** to the year being set — i.e., the 2024 NAWI for the 2026 base.
2. Divide it by the NAWI for the base-setting reference year (1994), when the base was $60,600.
3. Multiply $60,600 by that ratio.
4. Round the result to the **nearest multiple of $300**, as required by § 230(c).

The published $184,500 is consistent with this convention: 184,500 / 300 = 615 exactly, so the stated amount satisfies the rounding rule that produced it.

**Year-over-year context:** the 2025 base was $176,100. The 2026 increase is $8,400, or about 4.77%, reflecting growth in the 2024 national average wage index. The 2024 NAWI itself is subject to later revision, but a revision to the wage index does **not** reopen an already-published base year; it only feeds into subsequent years' determinations.

## 4. What the figure means in practice

**Payroll tax withholding.** Social Security tax is imposed at 6.2% on the employee and 6.2% on the employer, on earnings up to the base. Derived maximum amounts for 2026:

- Employee OASDI: 6.2% × $184,500 = **$11,439.00**
- Employer OASDI: 6.2% × $184,500 = **$11,439.00**
- Combined per worker: 12.4% × $184,500 = **$22,878.00**
- Self-employed (SECA) OASDI: 12.4% × $184,500 = **$22,878.00** before the income-tax deduction for one-half of SE tax

Payroll systems must stop OASDI withholding once an employee's cumulative 2026 taxable wages reach $184,500, and must resume/continue correctly if the employee changes employers (the cap is per employee per year, and each employer withholds independently, with any over-withholding reconciled on the individual's return).

**Benefit computation.** The same $184,500 is also the maximum amount of earnings creditable to a worker's record for 2026 in the averaged-indexed-monthly-earnings (AIME) calculation. A worker with earnings at or above the base in every computation year has an AIME computed on the base amounts for those years. This dual role is why the statute calls it the "contribution **and benefit** base" — one number, two functions.

**Timing rule.** The limit attaches to when remuneration is *paid*, not when it is earned. Deferred compensation paid out in 2026 counts against the 2026 base even if earned in an earlier year, and 2026 wages paid in a later year count against that later year's base.

## 5. Scope boundaries — what this number is *not*

These items are frequently conflated with the contribution and benefit base. They are **separate figures** and should not be substituted for $184,500:

1. **Medicare (HI) taxable wages — no cap.** Since 1994 the Hospital Insurance portion of FICA has had no earnings ceiling. $184,500 does not limit Medicare tax. The Additional Medicare Tax (0.9%) is a separate, non-indexed income threshold regime, not an earnings base.
2. **The "old-law" base.** The annual notice also publishes an old-law contribution and benefit base — a different, lower figure used only in specific benefit computations that apply pre-1977 law. It is a distinct quantity and must never be used as the OASDI taxable maximum. If a calculation calls for the old-law base, take that figure directly from the same *Federal Register* notice; do not derive it from $184,500.
3. **Retirement earnings test exempt amounts.** Announced at the same time as the base, but they are different numbers governing benefit withholding for beneficiaries who work. They are not the taxable maximum.
4. **Other indexed thresholds** (e.g., COLA-related benefit amounts, quarters-of-coverage earnings threshold) appear in the same announcement cycle but are independent values.

## 6. Verification steps for a reviewer

1. Open the SSA Contribution and Benefit Base page (https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/cola/cbbdet.html) and confirm the 2026 row reads $184,500.
2. Confirm against the *Federal Register* notice of 2025-11-03 (doc. 2025-19763), paragraph (1) of the determination.
3. Check arithmetic: 184,500 is an exact multiple of 300 (615 × 300), consistent with § 230(c).
4. Confirm the applicability language covers both wages paid in 2026 and self-employment income in tax years beginning in 2026 — the same limit for both.
5. Confirm no downstream figure in this memo exceeds the base: the only derived amounts ($11,439.00 and $22,878.00) are exact percentage products of $184,500 and therefore cannot exceed it as a taxable-earnings measure.

## 7. One-line answer for a summary field

**$184,500 — the 2026 Social Security (OASDI) contribution and benefit base, per SSA's annual determination published in the Federal Register on November 3, 2025.**

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

AUTHORITY

- IRC §402(g)(1); implementing regulation 26 CFR §1.402(g)-1.
- IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments for retirement plan limitations): "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3) ... is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IRS "COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions" table lists "Elective deferrals" for 401(k)/403(b)/profit-sharing plans as 24,500 for 2026 (2025: 23,500; 2024: 23,000; 2023: 22,500).

WHAT THE $24,500 COVERS

- Employee elective deferrals only — pre-tax (traditional) and designated Roth 401(k) deferrals both count against this single limit. Roth deferrals are not additive; they consume the same $24,500.
- The limit is per individual, per calendar year, and is aggregated across all plans of the same employer and its controlled group (§402(g)(1)(B) / §414(b)-(c) aggregation). Participating in two 401(k) plans of the same employer does not double the limit.
- Plans with a non-calendar plan year apply the limit for the calendar year in which the plan year begins.

WHAT IT DOES NOT INCLUDE

- Catch-up contributions under IRC §414(v) are outside this figure and are added on top of it for eligible participants (age 50+, and the enhanced amount for ages 60–63 under SECURE 2.0 §109). The 2026 catch-up amount is announced separately in the same IRS guidance; it is additive, not a substitute for the $24,500.
- Employer matching and profit-sharing contributions, and the §415(c) annual additions limit, are separate rules and do not reduce the employee's $24,500 deferral capacity (though §415(c) caps total annual additions).
- After-tax (non-Roth) employee contributions are tested under §415(c), not §402(g); they are not part of the $24,500 elective deferral limit.

PRACTICAL NOTES FOR PLAN ADMINISTRATION

- $24,500 is a statutory ceiling, not an entitlement: the plan document may impose a lower cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP/ACP) or a safe-harbor design can further restrict highly compensated employees.
- Payroll systems should be updated so the §402(g) deferral cap for 2026 is set to $24,500, with the §414(v) catch-up limit tracked in a separate field so the two are not conflated.
- Participants who also defer to a 403(b) or governmental 457(b) plan need aggregation checks: 403(b) deferrals share the same §402(g) limit; 457(b) deferrals do not.

SCOPE AND CAVEATS

- Jurisdiction assumed: U.S. federal tax law (IRS). A non-U.S. retirement regime would produce a different answer.
- The figure is the statutory §402(g) limit; it is not a projection or estimate — it is the published 2026 amount per IRS Notice 2025-67.
- Individual circumstances (age, multiple unrelated employers, excess-deferral correction under §402(g)(2), plan-specific limits) can change a given employee's effective maximum, but not the statutory figure stated here.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — Current U.S. national PRIMARY ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 (health-based NAAQS under Clean Air Act §109, 40 CFR Part 50):

  • Annual primary standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean concentration)
  • 24-hour primary standard: 35 µg/m³ (24-hour average concentration)

Controlling rule version ('current'): the 2024 PM NAAQS final rule (signed Feb. 7, 2024; published 89 FR 16202, Mar. 6, 2024; effective May 6, 2024), codified in 40 CFR 50.20. That rule lowered the primary annual level from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³ and retained the primary 24-hour level at 35 µg/m³. No later PM2.5 NAAQS revision appears in the sources consulted (2024 Federal Register rule text; EPA NAAQS pollutant-standards table).

1) ANNUAL LEVEL — 9.0 µg/m³
   - Value: 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter.
   - Form (the statistic the level is compared against): annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined per Appendix N to 40 CFR Part 50; the regulatory design value is the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means (each annual mean being the average of valid quarterly means, with Appendix N completeness requirements). A year/area meets the standard when that value is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³.
   - Note on the research note: the note asserts the annual form is 'not a 3-year average.' That is imprecise — the 3-year averaging is the form/design-value computation under Appendix N, while 9.0 µg/m³ is the level. The two statements are not in conflict on the number; the level is 9.0 µg/m³ either way. The form statement should be corrected, not the value.
   - Superseded values that must NOT be reported as current: 12.0 µg/m³ (2012 primary annual standard, 40 CFR 50.18), 15.0 µg/m³ (1997 primary annual standard, 40 CFR 50.7).

2) 24-HOUR LEVEL — 35 µg/m³
   - Value: 35 micrograms per cubic meter.
   - Form: 24-hour average concentration; the standard is met when the 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations is ≤ 35 µg/m³ (Appendix N). Unchanged since the 2006 PM NAAQS review and retained in the 2012 and 2024 rules.
   - Superseded value that must NOT be reported as current: 65 µg/m³ (1997 primary 24-hour standard).

UNITS AND SOURCE CAVEATS
   - Official NAAQS unit is µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter). The quoted Federal Register excerpt renders the levels as '12.0 mg/m3' and '9.0 mg/m3'; that is a text-extraction/rendering artifact of the PDF (mg/m³ would be 1,000× the standard). verdict.summary:
# Fall Protection Trigger Height — General Industry Walking-Working Surfaces

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.**

Under federal OSHA general industry standards, when an employee is on a walking-working surface and there is an unprotected side or edge that is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more** above a lower level, the employer must ensure the employee is protected from falling. The duty attaches *at* 4 feet — 4 ft is not a tolerance band or a safe working margin below a higher trigger; at exactly 4 ft the obligation is already owed.

Governing standard: **29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i)** (Subpart D — Walking-Working Surfaces), as amended by the 2016–2017 walking-working surfaces final rule.

## 2. Regulatory text relied on

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i):

> "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Note the two operative qualifiers in that sentence: **"except as provided elsewhere in this section"** (see §6 below — other paragraphs of 1910.28(b) can modify the trigger for particular surfaces) and **"or more"** (the threshold is inclusive).

## 3. Controlling definitions (29 CFR 1910.28 / Subpart D)

- **Unprotected sides and edges** — "any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level." This is the definition that decides whether the 4-ft rule is even engaged: a wall, guardrail, or stair rail at the edge means the edge is not "unprotected," and the 4-ft duty is not triggered by that edge.
- **Walking-working surface** — any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location (floors, roofs, stairs, ramps, runways, dockboards, ladders, etc.). Surfaces that are not walking-working surfaces are outside 1910.28 and may be governed by equipment-specific standards.
- **Lower level** — the surface or object below the walking-working surface to which a fall would occur. The measurement is taken from the walking-working surface to that lower level; the hazard need not be a floor (it can be ground, a pit, a roof below, water, or equipment).

## 4. Scope determination

| Question | Determination for this answer |
|---|---|
| General industry vs. construction | **General industry, 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D.** Part 1926 construction is expressly excluded by the request. Do not import the construction trigger (6 ft) into a 1910 analysis; the construction figure is a different standard with a different scope, and the 4-ft figure here is the correct one for 1910-covered work. |
| Other industry parts | Shipyard employment (29 CFR 1915) and longshoring/marine terminals (29 CFR 1917) are separate parts with their own fall-protection thresholds. If the workplace is covered by one of those parts rather than 1910, this 4-ft answer must be re-derived from that part. |
| Federal vs. state plan | This is the **federal OSHA** answer. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may be stricter or have different numeric or procedural requirements. Verify the state-plan standard before relying on 4 ft in a state-plan jurisdiction. |
| Vintage of the rule | Current 1910.28 as amended (2016–2017 walking-working surfaces rule). Pre-2017 Subpart D used a different structure and, in places, a 4-ft trigger applied only to specific surfaces; do not apply pre-2017 interpretations to current work. |
| Equipment-specific work | Work on ladders, scaffolds, and powered platforms is governed by the equipment-specific subparts (1910.23, 1910.27, 1910.66, etc.). 1910.28(b)(1)(i) is the rule for the ordinary walking-working surface, not a substitute for those. |

## 5. What satisfies the duty at or above 4 feet

1910.28(b)(1)(i) permits one or more of:

1. **Guardrail systems** — must meet 29 CFR 1910.29(b) (top rail height, midrail, strength, surfacing, clearance, etc.).
2. **Safety net systems** — must meet 1910.29(c) (installation, mesh, drop distance, certification, inspection).
3. **Personal fall protection systems**, which includes:
   - personal fall arrest systems (1910.29(d)–(f); full-body harness, anchor strength, free-fall and deceleration distance limits, prompt rescue);
   - travel restraint systems (1910.29(d));
   - positioning systems.

The standard does not impose a single mandatory hierarchy among these three families for ordinary edges — any one or a combination is acceptable — but the selected system must meet its own §1910.29 performance requirements, and a personal fall arrest system carries the additional obligations of anchor-point strength, swing-fall/lower-level clearance analysis, and rescue planning.

## 6. Modifiers inside 1910.28(b) that must be checked before finalizing the design

The opening clause of (b)(1)(i) — "except as provided elsewhere in this section" — means the 4-ft figure is the default for an ordinary walking-working surface, and the following paragraphs of 1910.28(b) contain surface-specific provisions that can change the required method, or in narrow cases the trigger, for that surface. Verify the specific paragraph against the eCFR text for each condition present on the job:

- hoist areas;
- holes (including the separate treatment of holes and of covers);
- ramps, runways, and other walkways;
- dockboards;
- low-slope roofs (including the provisions for work that is both temporary and infrequent, which allow alternatives such as a fall protection plan meeting 1910.29(k) or designated areas where the employer can demonstrate the standard systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard);
- steep roofs;
- dangerous equipment below the surface (a condition that can require protection irrespective of the height involved);
- outdoor advertising, storage areas, and other listed structures.

Engineering rule for the design file: **do not stop at "4 feet."** Start from 4 ft, then read the specific paragraph for the surface type, then read the definitions in §3 to confirm the edge is genuinely unprotected.

## 7. Companion duties that travel with the 4-ft trigger

- **29 CFR 1910.29** — specifications and performance criteria for guardrails, safety nets, personal fall protection systems, designated areas, and fall protection plans.
- **29 CFR 1910.30** — training: employees exposed to fall hazards must be trained in the nature of the hazard, the procedures to minimize it, and the correct use/maintenance/inspection of the protection systems; retraining required when the workplace or systems change or when the employee shows inadequate understanding. Training must be in a language and at a comprehension level the employee understands.
- **Inspection and maintenance** — 1910.29 requires the employer to ensure fall-protection systems are inspected, maintained, and in good condition; personal fall arrest equipment is inspected before each use and removed from service per the manufacturer's criteria.
- **Rescue** — where personal fall arrest is used, the employer must provide for prompt rescue of an employee who falls (arrest without prompt rescue is a recognized fatality mode; suspension trauma onset is measured in minutes).

## 8. Verification checklist for the practitioner

1. Confirm the employer is 1910-covered (not 1915/1917/1926) and identify any State Plan overlay.
2. Confirm the surface is a "walking-working surface" as defined.
3. Measure from the walking-working surface to the lower level; if the result is **≥ 4 ft (1.2 m)**, the duty is owed.
4. Confirm the side/edge is "unprotected" — no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system.
5. Read the surface-specific paragraph of 1910.28(b) for the condition present (roof, ramp, dockboard, hole, hoist area, dangerous equipment below).
6. Select the protection method and verify it against 1910.29; document anchor strength, clearance, and rescue plan if fall arrest is used.
7. Deliver and document 1910.30 training for every exposed employee.

## 9. Quick reference

| Jurisdiction / standard | Trigger for protecting an unprotected side or edge |
|---|---|
| **General industry — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i)** | **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** — the answer to this request |
| Construction — 29 CFR Part 1926 | Different (higher) trigger under Part 1926; out of scope here |
| Shipyard (29 CFR 1915) / longshoring (29 CFR 1917) | Separate parts with their own thresholds; out of scope here |
| State Plan states | Federal minimum applies; state standard may be stricter — verify |

**Bottom line for the employer:** at 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level, on a walking-working surface, at an unprotected side or edge, federal OSHA general industry requires fall protection — guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system meeting §1910.29, with §1910.30 training — unless a more specific paragraph of §1910.28(b) applies to that surface.

verdict.summary:
# Reserve fuel for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, **assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for at least 20 minutes after that point.**

- Governing rule (general operating rules): **14 CFR 91.151(b)** — "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."
- Commercial/air-taxi operations: **14 CFR 135.209(b)** gives the same figure — "...enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."
- The reserve is a **time** minimum, not a gallon or pound minimum. Section 3 converts it to a quantity using the helicopter's own performance data.

## 2. Scope and applicability — what does and does not change the answer

| Condition | Effect on the 20-minute reserve |
|---|---|
| Part 91 general operating rules, rotorcraft, VFR | 20 minutes — 91.151(b) |
| Part 135 air-taxi/commuter helicopter, VFR | 20 minutes — 135.209(b) (same figure) |
| Day vs. night VFR, helicopter | **No difference.** 91.151(b) and 135.209(b) are a single figure for rotorcraft; there is no day/night split. |
| Airplane VFR (not this case) | 91.151(a): 30 min day / 45 min night — **airplane only, not appliable to helicopters.** Do not apply these to a helicopter. |
| IFR flight (not this case) | The Part 91 IFR fuel rules and alternate fuel planning do not apply to a VFR flight; a helicopter VFR flight is not required to carry fuel to a destination alternate. |

The 30-minute and 45-minute figures are quoted here only to be excluded; they are not the answer.

## 3. Converting 20 minutes to a fuel quantity

Use the helicopter's normal cruising fuel consumption (the same burn rate used in the flight plan), not a best-case or economy figure:

```
Reserve (lb)  = burn rate (lb/hr at normal cruise) x (20 / 60)
Reserve (gal) = burn rate (gal/hr at normal cruise) x (20 / 60)
```

Equivalently, reserve = one-third of the hourly normal-cruise burn.

### Worked example (Jet A helicopter, illustrative numbers only — substitute the actual RFM/fight-manual figures)

- Normal cruising fuel consumption: 400 lb/hr (about 60 gal/hr at 6.7 lb/gal)
- Reserve time: 20 min = 0.333 hr
- Reserve fuel: 400 x 0.333 = **133 lb** ≈ 133 / 6.7 = **19.9 gal**, round up to 20 gal
- Total minimum fuel at brake release: fuel to first point of intended landing (including wind and forecast weather per 91.151(b)) **+ 133 lb (20 gal)**

### Second example (light single-engine helicopter)

- 120 lb/hr normal cruise, Jet A at 6.7 lb/gal
- Reserve: 120 x 0.333 = 40 lb = 6.0 gal → carry **6 gal** as reserve

Rounding: always round the reserve **up** to the next usable quantity; the 20 minutes is a floor, never a target.

## 4. Preflight compliance check (apply in order)

1. Confirm the operating rule set: Part 91 or Part 135. Both give 20 minutes for helicopters, but the flight-plan documentation and the operator's approved procedures differ.
2. Determine fuel to the **first point of intended landing** using forecast winds and forecast weather conditions (91.151(b) requires this).
3. Compute the reserve as one-third of the normal-cruise hourly burn (Section 3), rounded up.
4. Add reserve to trip fuel → minimum fuel at brake release.
5. Compare with the aircraft's maximum usable fuel and payload/power limits; if the regulatory minimum cannot be carried with the required payload, the flight is not legal — reduce payload or stops, do not reduce the reserve.
6. Apply the operator's own minimum if it is higher (many operators use 30 or 45 minutes as policy, or a fixed 30-minute IFR-style buffer). Policy may exceed the regulation; it may never go below 20 minutes.
7. Note that the 20 minutes is **not** reduced for wind, and is **not** satisfied by fuel that is unusable, trapped, or below the fuel-gauge/powerplant limitation.

## 5. Common errors this answer guards against

- Applying the airplane 30/45-minute rule to a helicopter. 91.151(a) is airplanes; the rotorcraft paragraph is 91.151(b).
- Applying a day/night split to helicopters. There is none.
- Quoting 20 minutes as a gallon figure. It is time; the gallon value is aircraft-specific.
- Treating the 20 minutes as the total fuel to destination. It is **in addition to** fuel to the first point of intended landing.
- Wind-adjusting the reserve. Wind and forecast weather apply to the trip leg; the reserve is computed at normal cruising speed.

## 6. Verification status

Both rule texts are quoted from pages fetched during research (eCFR 91.151 and 135.209, fetched 2026-11-16, hashes a8a7e00944fb and ab71077460af). Before operational use, re-verify the current text on eCFR, since 91.151/135.209 can be amended; the 20-minute rotorcraft figure is the long-standing value but the citation, not memory, is the authority.

quotes.text: Category: Best Current Practice

verdict.summary:
## Answer

**1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996.**

RFC 8996, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1*, is an IETF Best Current Practice (BCP 195), published in May 2021. Its header identifies it as `Category: Best Current Practice`. It is the standards-body document that formally deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1; it is not a vendor or browser deprecation policy.

**2. The status RFC 8996 gave to the RFCs that defined TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is Historic.**

The affected defining documents are:

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Status assigned by RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | RFC 2246 | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | RFC 4346 | Historic |

Exact wording from RFC 8996:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

## Important correction to the protocol-to-RFC mapping

RFC 5246 defines **TLS 1.2**, not TLS 1.0. RFC 8996 *updates* RFC 5246 to require that implementations supporting TLS 1.2 and later not negotiate TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1; it does not move RFC 5246 to Historic. The correct mapping is:

- TLS 1.0 — RFC 2246
- TLS 1.1 — RFC 4346
- TLS 1.2 — RFC 5246
- TLS 1.3 — RFC 8446

## Practical meaning

RFC 8996 states that TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 must not be negotiated or used, and that fallback to these versions is prohibited. The operative status change for the defining RFCs is the move to **Historic**, while RFC 8996 itself remains a Best Current Practice document (BCP 195).

## Sources

- RFC 8996: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html
- RFC 8996 datatracker history: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/
- RFC 8996 errata: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc8996.html

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum) for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

That is the maximum amount of an individual worker's annual earnings subject to the Social Security (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance) payroll tax in 2026. Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are not subject to the 6.2% OASDI tax, though they remain subject to Medicare tax.

SOURCE

Social Security Administration, official 2026 materials — SSA's 2026 employer wage-base guidance states: "The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500." The determination is made under the Social Security Act's annual contribution-and-benefit-base rule (indexed to the national average wage index) and published by SSA in the fall preceding the tax year. SSA uses "contribution and benefit base" and "OASDI taxable maximum" interchangeably.

SCOPE AND WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER

- Component: this is the OASDI (Social Security) base only. The Medicare (HI) component has no earnings ceiling; the 1.45% employee / 1.45% employer HI tax applies to all wages, and the additional 0.9% Medicare surtax applies above the statutory threshold (not the Social Security base).
- Worker scope: annual cap for a single worker. Not a household or aggregate amount. The same base applies to self-employment income reported on Schedule SE.
- Unit: annual dollars of earnings. Per-pay-period equivalents depend on the employer's payroll calendar and are derived by the payroll system, not fixed by SSA (e.g., $184,500 / 26 biweekly periods = $7,096.15; / 24 semimonthly = $7,687.50; / 12 monthly = $15,375.00).

RATE ARITHMETIC (consistency check on the stated figure)

- Employee OASDI: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 maximum withheld per worker for 2026.
- Employer OASDI: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 maximum per worker for 2026.
- Self-employed combined OASDI: 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00 maximum (before the income-tax deduction for one-half of SE tax).

These products reconcile exactly with the SSA-stated maximum OASDI tax of $11,439.00 per side, so the base, the rate, and the tax maximum are mutually consistent.

PRACTICAL APPLICATION

- Payroll systems must switch the OASDI wage limit to $184,500 for wages paid in 2026, and stop OASDI withholding once an employee's year-to-date taxable wages reach that amount; Medicare withholding continues uncapped.
- Form W-2 (Box 3 Social Security wages) is capped at $184,500 for 2026; Box 5 Medicare wages is not.
- Schedule SE for 2026 self-employment income uses the same $184,500 cap for the Social Security portion.

verdict.summary:
2026 EMPLOYEE ELECTIVE DEFERRAL LIMIT — 401(k) (HR / benefits compliance answer)

ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for the 2026 tax year, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

That is the IRC §402(g) elective deferral limit — the maximum an employee may defer from compensation into a 401(k) (traditional pre-tax and/or designated Roth) during calendar year 2026. It applies per employee, per individual, across all plans of unrelated employers in which that employee participates.

SOURCE / AUTHORITY

- IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS, COLA Increases for Dollar Limitations on Benefits and Contributions (2026 column): Elective deferrals — $24,500 (2026), $23,500 (2025), $23,000 (2024), $22,500 (2023).
- Statutory basis: Internal Revenue Code §402(g), as indexed; figure published in the IRS annual cost-of-living adjustment notice for 2026.

WHAT THE $24,500 DOES AND DOES NOT INCLUDE

Includes:
- Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals.
- Designated Roth elective deferrals. Roth and pre-tax deferrals share the same $24,500 ceiling; electing Roth does not create extra room.
- Safe harbor 401(k) elective deferrals (the limit is the same).
- Deferrals to a 403(b) or governmental 457(b) are subject to their own parallel limits and are not additive to this 401(k) figure for the same employer's plan.

Excludes (deliberately, per the question):
- Catch-up contributions under §414(v). For reference only, and NOT part of the $24,500: the standard age-50+ catch-up is $8,000 for 2026, and the enhanced SECURE 2.0 catch-up for participants aged 60–63 is $11,250 for 2026. A participant eligible for catch-up therefore has a higher personal ceiling than $24,500; the $24,500 is the base that catch-up sits on top of.

Separate limits that are frequently confused with this one (do not substitute these for the answer):
- §415(c) total annual additions (employee deferrals + employer contributions + forfeitures) — a separate, higher, per-plan limit. The 2026 dollar amount should be read from the same IRS COLA notice; it is not stated here.
- §401(a)(17) annual compensation limit — $360,000 for 2026 (per the same IRS COLA table). This caps the compensation that may be taken into account; it is not a deferral limit.
- Plan-specific limits: a plan document, or a plan's actual deferral percentage (ADP) testing outcome for a non-safe-harbor plan, can produce a lower effective limit for a given highly compensated employee. Those are plan-level results and cannot be stated generically; they do not change the statutory $24,500 maximum.

PRACTICAL NOTES FOR PLAN ADMINISTRATION

- Both pre-tax and Roth payroll elections must be aggregated when testing an individual against $24,500; payroll systems should hard-stop at $24,500 of combined elective deferrals for 2026, with catch-up tracked in a separate bucket.
- Excess deferrals above $24,500 (plus allocable earnings) must be corrected under the EPCRS excess-deferral procedure — generally distributed by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation.
- The limit is indexed annually and is announced by the IRS in the fall preceding the plan year. Any mid-year legislative change would supersede this figure; the number above reflects the IRS 2026 cost-of-living adjustment announcement as published.
- Because the question asks only for the base elective deferral limit, no design-based, testing-based, or employer-contribution figures are asserted here beyond the clearly labeled companion limits above.
