verdict.summary:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. The answer (headline figures)

| Standard | Level (primary, health-based) | Regulatory form (compliance metric) |
|---|---|---|
| Annual PM2.5 | **9.0 µg/m3** — annual arithmetic mean concentration | 3-year average of annual arithmetic mean concentrations, compared to 9.0 µg/m3 |
| 24-hour PM2.5 | **35 µg/m3** — 24-hour average concentration | 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations (Appendix N), compared to 35 µg/m3 |

Jurisdiction: United States, federal. These are national standards set by US EPA under section 109 of the Clean Air Act; they are uniform nationwide and are not state-implementation values.

Scope note: only the **primary** (health-based) standards are reported, as requested. The secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are out of scope and are not stated here as answers.

## 2. Citation chain and effective-date boundary ('current')

- Codification: **40 CFR part 50, § 50.18** — 'National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5'. Interpretation of the 24-hour statistic: **40 CFR part 50, Appendix N**. Secondary standards sit in § 50.19 and are out of scope.
- Revision: EPA signed the final rule on **February 7, 2024** (published at **89 FR 16202**), revising the **primary annual** PM2.5 standard **from 12.0 µg/m3 to 9.0 µg/m3**. The rule became effective **May 6, 2024**.
- The **24-hour primary** standard was **retained unchanged at 35 µg/m3** in that rule.
- 'Current' therefore means the post-February-2024 vintage. The 12.0 µg/m3 annual figure is **historical only** (pre-May 2024) and is not the answer to ask 1.

## 3. Datable conflict disclosure (and how to resolve it)

Two grounding passages disagree and a downstream reviewer will see both:

1. A snapshot of the eCFR text of § 50.18(a) quoting '12.0 µg/m3 annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration'.
2. The EPA designation-data page stating, verbatim: 'On February 7, 2024, the EPA promulgated a final rule revising the primary annual fine particulate matter (PM2.5) National Ambient Air Quality Standard' and 'In that action, EPA revised the standard from 12.0 µg/m3 to 9.0 µg/m3.'

**Resolution used:** passage (2) is the later, dateted statement of the revision and names 12.0 explicitly as the superseded figure; passage (1) is the pre-revision text of the rule as cached/rendered before the amendment. The current annual level is therefore **9.0 µg/m3**.

**Verification procedure for the reviewer (30 seconds):** open eCFR § 50.18(a) and confirm the sentence reads 9.0 µg/m3 (post-2024 codification); if a rendering still shows 12.0, check the 'Source' / 'amendement' note at the bottom of the section for the 89 FR 16202 cite and the May 6 2024 effective date. Alternatively confirm via the EPA 'National Ambient Air Quality Standards — Table of Standards' page, which lists the annual primary PM2.5 standard as 9 µg/m3.

If a reviewer's authoritative source still shows 12.0 with no 2024 amendment, the correct fallback is to report the annual level as 12.0 µg/m3 and flag the vintage — but on the grounding available here, 9.0 is the current value and is what I answer.

## 4. Regulatory form and rounding (needed if the numbers are to be used for compliance rather than citation)

- **Annual:** the standard is met when the **3-year average of annual arithmetic mean concentrations** is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m3. A single year's mean, or a single monitor's daily maximum, does not determine attainment.
- **24-hour:** the standard is met when the **3-year average of the annual 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations**, determined per Appendix N, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3. This is a percentile statistic averaged over three years — not a single daily maximum and not a 24-hour exceedance count.
- **Rounding:** concentrations are rounded to the nearest 0.1 µg/m3 before comparison to the level (Appendix N conventions). 9.0 and 35 are the comparand values as stated in the rule.
- **Design values / attainment status** are a separate product (computed from monitored air quality data) and are not implied by these levels.

## 5. One-line restatement for downstream use

> Current US national **primary** PM2.5 NAAQS (40 CFR 50.18, as revised by the Feb 7 2024 final rule, effective May 6 2024): **annual = 9.0 µg/m3** (3-year average of annual arithmetic means); **24-hour = 35 µg/m3** (3-year average of annual 98th percentiles, Appendix N).

verdict.summary:
# Fall Protection Trigger Height — General Industry Walking-Working Surfaces

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.** When an employee is on a walking-working surface that has an unprotected side or edge and that surface is 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, the US employer must protect that employee from falling.

The threshold is **inclusive**: at exactly 4 ft 0 in (48 in), the duty attaches. Below 4 ft, the paragraph (b)(1) duty does not attach (but see §5 — other provisions may still apply, including one with no height threshold at all).

## 2. Governing text

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i), *Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection* (Subpart D, Walking-Working Surfaces):

> "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
> (A) Guardrail systems;
> (B) Safety net systems; or
> (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-D/section-1910.28 (fetched 2026-11-16T06:23:04Z, sha256 8550c2c5b628); mirrored at https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.28.

## 3. Decision rule and measurement convention

Apply in this order:

1. **Is it general industry?** 29 CFR Part 1910 governs. If the work is construction (Part 1926), shipyard (Part 1915), longshoring (Part 1918), or agriculture (Part 1928), a different part applies — the 4 ft figure below is the Part 1910 answer only.
2. **Is it a walking-working surface?** Per 1910.21(b), any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area. Floors, roofs, mezzanines, platforms, catwalks, ramps, runways, stair landings, dock edges, and similar surfaces qualify.
3. **Does it have an unprotected side or edge?** An edge not guarded by a guardrail system meeting 1910.29(b), or otherwise protected under 1910.28. If already guarded, the duty is satisfied — but verify the guardrail meets 1910.29(b) height (42 in ± 3 in), strength (200 lb top-rail load), and balustrade/toeboard criteria.
4. **Measure the drop.** The dimension is the vertical distance from the walking-working surface to the **lower level the employee could fall to** — not to the deck's own structural framing, not to a ceiling below, and not the diagonal distance to the edge. Take the worst credible case at the leading edge (e.g., a sloped roof or an edge over a descending grade).
5. **≥ 4 ft (1.2 m)?** If yes, select one or more of: guardrail system (1910.29(b)), safety net system (1910.29(c)), or personal fall protection system — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning (1910.29(d)–(f), equipment per 1910.140). Combinations are permitted.
6. **Apply the exceptions.** Paragraph (b)(1) opens with "Except as provided elsewhere in this section" — always check §5 below before finalizing the method, because a more specific paragraph may control the trigger height, the permitted method, or both.

## 4. What does NOT apply (common misapplications)

| Figure sometimes misapplied | Where it actually comes from | Status for this question |
|---|---|---|
| 6 ft | Construction, 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) | Not applicable to Part 1910 general industry surfaces |
| 10 ft | Scaffolds, 29 CFR 1926.451(g)(1) | Not applicable |
| 15 ft / 30 ft | Various construction steel-erection provisions | Not applicable |
| 8 ft "for fixed ladders" | **No such trigger exists in 1910.28** — this is an error in the project's working assumptions | Correct the assumption: fixed ladders under 1910.28(b)(9) use a **24 ft climb** trigger for a ladder safety system or personal fall arrest system (see §5) |

The single number an employer needs for general industry walking-working surfaces is **4 ft (1.2 m)**.

## 5. Carve-outs under "except as provided elsewhere in this section" — verification checklist

These do not change the headline answer, but they can change the required method or add a stricter trigger. Verify each against the current text of 1910.28(b) before issuing a final fall-protection determination.

- **(b)(1)(ii) — infeasibility / greater hazard.** Where the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard, the employer must implement a fall protection plan meeting 1910.29(k). This is a documented, employer-bears-the-burden route — not a discretionary skip.
- **(b)(2) Low-slope roofs (≤ 4:12).** 4 ft trigger; a designated area meeting 1910.29(g) may substitute only for work that is both **infrequent and temporary**, and only within the limited distance from the edge allowed by the paragraph.
- **(b)(3) Steep roofs (> 4:12).** 4 ft trigger; guardrail with toeboard, or safety net, or personal fall protection.
- **(b)(4) Hoist areas.** 4 ft trigger; guardrail, net, or PFAS; plus the paragraph's gate/offset requirements at the landing.
- **(b)(5) Holes.** 4 ft trigger; covers meeting 1910.29(h) or guardrail/net/PFAS. Note that a hole cover must be secured and marked regardless of height.
- **(b)(6) Ramps, runways, and other walkways.** 4 ft trigger; guardrail on each unprotected side.
- **(b)(7) Dangerous equipment — NO HEIGHT THRESHOLD.** Regardless of height, employees must be protected from falling into or onto dangerous equipment (open vats, tanks, degreasers, conveyors, machinery, energized equipment). A 30-inch platform over a pickling tank still needs protection. **This is the single most common gap when people apply the 4 ft rule mechanically.**
- **(b)(8) Pits.** Protection for employees in pits, per the paragraph's conditions.
- **(b)(9) Fixed ladders.** A **climb of 24 ft or more** above a lower level requires a personal fall arrest system or ladder safety system. Ladders installed before 19 Nov 2018 may use a cage or well until 18 Nov 2036; ladders installed on or after 19 Nov 2018 must use PFAS or a ladder safety system. There is **no 8 ft trigger**. (Portable ladders are governed by 1910.23, not by a fall-protection trigger height.)
- **(b)(10)–(b)(14)** cover outdoor advertising structures, rope descent systems, window cleaning, repair pits, and overhead conveyors — each with its own conditions. Check the current text.
- **Stairs (1910.25) and stair rail systems (1910.29(f))** have their own dimensional criteria and are not governed by the 4 ft trigger.

## 6. Collateral duties that attach with the 4 ft trigger

- **1910.29** — criteria for guardrail systems, safety net systems, designated areas, and fall protection plans. A guardrail that exists but is 36 in tall or has a 300 lb-rated top rail that has pulled loose does not discharge the 1910.28 duty.
- **1910.30** — training. Each employee exposed to a fall hazard must be trained **before** exposure on the nature of the hazard, the correct procedures, and the proper use/limitations of the systems in use; retraining when workplace changes or inadequate performance is observed. Training must be understandable to the employee and provided in a language the employee understands.
- **1910.140** — personal fall protection systems: equipment criteria, inspection before each use, competent-person calculation of total fall distance (free fall + deceleration + harness stretch + D-ring shift + safety margin) to confirm no lower level is struck.
- **1910.22(d)** — regular and as-needed inspection of walking-working surfaces, with correction or repair of hazards.
- **1910.28(b)(1) falling-object duty and 1910.28(c)** — where employees are exposed to falling objects, protection from falling objects is separately required (toeboards, screens, canopies, barricades, or a combination).
- **1910.132–1910.138** — PPE hazard assessment and selection where PPE is part of the chosen method.

## 7. Worked examples (boundary checks)

| Case | Height of surface above lower level | (b)(1) duty at 4 ft? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loading dock, no guardrail, truck bed level | 48 in (4 ft 0 in) | **Yes** — inclusive threshold | Guardrail, net, or PFAS; also check dockboard/lip provisions |
| Mezzanine | 3 ft 10 in (46 in) | No under (b)(1) | Still check (b)(7) if equipment below is dangerous, and 1910.23 for openings/ladderways |
| Catwalk over a conveyor | 30 in | No under (b)(1) | **(b)(7) applies with no height threshold** if the conveyor is dangerous equipment |
| Low-slope roof, HVAC service, occasional | 12 ft | Yes | Designated-area option only if work is infrequent and temporary |
| Fixed ladder to a rooftop | 20 ft climb | Not a (b)(1) surface question | (b)(9): under 24 ft climb, no PFAS/ladder-safety trigger (cage/well rules depend on installation date) |
| Fixed ladder to a silo top | 30 ft climb | Not a (b)(1) surface question | (b)(9): 24 ft or more → PFAS or ladder safety system |

## 8. Jurisdiction note

Twenty-two OSHA-approved State Plans cover private-sector employers and must be at least as effective as federal OSHA; several adopt stricter or differently-worded requirements, and some have historically used a different general-industry trigger. **Before issuing a final determination for a specific site, confirm the applicable State Plan's fall-protection threshold and method requirements.** This answer states the federal (29 CFR 1910) requirement.

## 9. Procedure an employer can apply directly

1. Walk the site and inventory every walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge.
2. For each, measure the vertical drop to the lower level the employee could reach; record the measurement, date, and who measured.
3. Flag every location at **≥ 4 ft (1.2 m)** as requiring protection under 1910.28(b)(1).
4. Separately flag, **at any height**, any location where an employee could fall into or onto dangerous equipment (1910.28(b)(7)), and any hole, pit, or ladder subject to its own paragraph.
5. Check the §5 carve-outs to confirm no more specific paragraph controls the method.
6. Select the method (guardrail / net / PFAS or combination), verify it against 1910.29 or 1910.140, and calculate total fall distance for any PFAS.
7. Train exposed employees under 1910.30 before exposure; document the training.
8. Re-inspect per 1910.22(d) and whenever the surface, edge, or adjacent equipment changes.
9. If any location cannot be protected by a listed system, document the infeasibility or greater-hazard basis and implement a written fall protection plan under 1910.29(k) per 1910.28(b)(1)(ii).

## 10. Bottom line

**4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i). Not 6 ft (construction), not 8 ft (an erroneous figure with no basis in 1910.28), and not conditioned on the employee's task being unusual: the duty attaches to the exposed employee on the surface. Add the 1910.28(b)(7) dangerous-equipment review at any height, and confirm the State Plan.

verdict.summary:
# VFR Reserve Fuel Required for a Helicopter — United States, Part 91

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes of fuel at normal cruising speed**, in addition to the fuel required to fly to the first point of intended landing.

This is the regulatory minimum for a civil helicopter (rotorcraft) beginning a VFR flight in the United States under 14 CFR Part 91. There is **no day/night difference** for rotorcraft: 20 minutes applies to both day and night VFR.

## 2. Controlling authority and exact text

14 CFR § 91.151, *Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions*, paragraph (b):

> "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Three operative elements are embedded in that sentence and each matters operationally:

1. **Trip fuel** — enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, computed *considering wind and forecast weather conditions* (i.e., a realistic, not still-air-idealized, trip burn).
2. **Reserve** — *after that*, i.e. on top of trip fuel, fuel to fly **at least 20 minutes**.
3. **Power setting for the reserve** — *assuming normal cruising speed*, i.e. the reserve is converted to quantity using the normal cruise fuel flow, not hover flow, not best-endurance flow, not a loiter burn.

## 3. Applicability (scope of the 20-minute answer)

| Condition | Status for this answer |
|---|---|
| State of registry / location of operation | US civil flight, US airspace |
| Operating rule | 14 CFR Part 91 (general operating rules), Subpart B |
| Category | Rotorcraft (helicopter) |
| Flight rules / conditions | VFR |
| Time of day | Irrelevant for rotorcraft — 20 minutes day and night |
| Exemption/waiver or special-operations rule | None assumed; overlays noted in § 7 |

If any of these is false (e.g., the flight is a Part 135, Part 121, public-use, or foreign-registered operation, or a special operations rule applies), the number can change — see § 7 and § 9.

## 4. What the day/night split does *not* mean here

§ 91.151(a) applies the day/night distinction, but that paragraph governs **airplanes**: 30 minutes day, 45 minutes night. Those figures are commonly, and wrongly, carried over to helicopters. For a rotorcraft, § 91.151(b) is the only applicable paragraph and it contains a single 20-minute standard with no time-of-day term. Do not apply 30 or 45 minutes to a helicopter under Part 91; equally, do not reduce below 20 minutes at night.

## 5. Converting the 20 minutes into a quantity

Because the reserve is expressed as time at normal cruising speed, the quantity depends entirely on the helicopter's cruise fuel flow.

**Formula**

    Reserve quantity = (normal cruise fuel flow per hour) × (20 / 60)
                     = (normal cruise fuel flow per hour) ÷ 3

**Total fuel required at brake release (planning figure)**

    Total = trip fuel to first point of intended landing (wind- and forecast-adjusted)
          + (normal cruise fuel flow per hour ÷ 3)
          + taxi / run-up / start allowance (not part of the regulatory reserve)

**Worked examples (illustrative flows — substitute the actual aircraft figure)**

| Normal cruise fuel flow | Reserve = flow ÷ 3 | Trip fuel (example) | Minimum fuel at start |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 US gal/hr | 4.0 US gal | 22 US gal | 26.0 US gal + taxi allowance |
| 20 US gal/hr | 6.7 US gal | 30 US gal | 36.7 US gal + taxi allowance |
| 40 US gal/hr | 13.3 US gal | 60 US gal | 73.3 US gal + taxi allowance |
| 300 lb/hr | 100 lb | 500 lb | 600 lb + taxi allowance |
| 660 lb/hr | 220 lb | 1,100 lb | 1,320 lb + taxi allowance |

Notes on the conversion:

- Use **usable fuel** (the fuel the helicopter can actually deliver in flight), not total tank capacity.
- Use the flow at the **normal cruise speed** you will actually fly the trip at, at the planned altitude and temperature — a higher-than-planned burn makes 20 minutes' worth a larger quantity.
- The reserve is **not** a separate tank and need not be segregated; it is a planning quantity that must nevertheless be **on board at departure**.
- Taxi, start, and run-up fuel are additive and are *not* the reserve.

## 6. How compliance is judged

- § 91.151 is a **"no person may begin a flight"** rule. Compliance is assessed **at departure**: the pilot must be able to show, from the fuel aboard at start, that trip fuel plus 20 minutes at normal cruise is available given wind and forecast weather. Post-departure fuel state is not the test under this section.
- Part 91 contains **no in-flight VFR reserve rule** and **no alternate-fuel requirement for VFR**. (Contrast § 91.167, which is an IFR rule and is phrased as an operating limitation.) The absence of an alternate requirement does not relax the 20 minutes: if the forecast is such that the destination may not be reachable with 20 minutes remaining, the flight may not begin.
- The reserve is a **floor, not a target**. § 91.103 (preflight action) still requires weather, fuel, and alternate planning for the specific flight.

## 7. Overlays that can raise (never lower) the figure

| Overlay | Effect on the 20-minute Part 91 rotorcraft reserve |
|---|---|
| Part 135 commuter/on-demand, VFR rotorcraft (§ 135.209) | Also 20 minutes for rotorcraft VFR — same figure, but now an operating-rule requirement with its own recordkeeping and dispatch obligations |
| Company / operator manual, SMS, or insurance minimum | Frequently higher (e.g., a fixed 30–45 minute policy reserve); when higher, the higher figure governs the flight |
| Offshore / over-water operations (e.g., OGP/industry guidance, operator contingency fuel) | Typically adds contingency and alternate/landing-location fuel well beyond 20 minutes |
| HEMS / air-medical programs | Program-specific minimums usually exceed the regulatory floor |
| IFR leg or IFR alternate | § 91.167 / § 91.169 govern instead — do not use the 20-minute VFR figure |

Rule of thumb for the pilot: **compute 20 minutes; then apply whichever applicable document demands more.** Nothing in this analysis authorizes less than 20 minutes.

## 8. Verification checklist (to be run before every departure)

1. Confirm the operation is Part 91 rotorcraft VFR; if not, switch rule sets.
2. Determine trip fuel to the **first point of intended landing**, adjusted for forecast wind and temperature.
3. Look up normal cruise fuel flow for the planned cruise speed/altitude; divide by 3 to get the 20-minute reserve.
4. Add trip + reserve + taxi/run-up allowance; compare with **usable** fuel on board.
5. Confirm the fuel gauge/quantity indication and any fuel totalizer agree with the computed figure.
6. If any applicable company, Part 135, or special-operations minimum is larger, use that figure instead.

## 9. Common errors this answer is designed to prevent

1. Applying the airplane 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures to a helicopter.
2. Computing the 20 minutes at hover or loiter burn rather than normal cruise — inflates or (if a low hover figure is misused) understates the required quantity.
3. Treating the reserve as included within the fuel to destination rather than *after* it.
4. Assuming night VFR requires a larger Part 91 rotorcraft reserve — it does not.
5. Assuming a Part 91 VFR alternate-fuel requirement exists — it does not; the 20 minutes is the whole regulatory reserve.
6. Counting total tank capacity instead of usable fuel.
7. Treating 20 minutes as a target rather than a minimum that company policy or a special-operations rule may exceed.

## 10. Falsifiers — when this answer would not hold

- The flight is not conducted under 14 CFR Part 91 (e.g., Part 135, Part 121, public aircraft, military, or a non-US registry) → different rule text governs; Part 135 rotorcraft VFR happens to also be 20 minutes, but that must be confirmed against § 135.209 for the specific operation rather than assumed.
- The flight is IFR, or a VFR flight into IMC is contemplated → § 91.167/§ 91.169 apply, not § 91.151.
- A waiver, exemption, or special-operations authorization is in force that specifies a different reserve → the authorization controls.
- The aircraft is not a rotorcraft (e.g., a gyroplane is a rotorcraft; a powered-lift or airplane is not) → category determines which paragraph applies.
- An operator document imposes a higher minimum → the higher minimum is the operative number for that flight.

quotes.question_text: Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, and what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?
quotes.text:
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

1. **RFC 8996** — *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (March 2021; IETF Best Current Practice).
2. **Historic** — RFC 8996 moved the RFCs that defined those versions, **RFC 2246** (TLS 1.0) and **RFC 4346** (TLS 1.1), to Historic status.

## Direct evidence

RFC 8996 states:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."
> — RFC 8996, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html [1]

## Status table

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | RFC 2246 | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | RFC 4346 | Historic |
| TLS 1.2 | RFC 5246 | Not deprecated by RFC 8996; RFC 8996 updates RFC 5246 to reflect the deprecation of TLS 1.0/1.1 |
| TLS 1.3 | RFC 8446 | Not affected |

## Important correction

A common misattribution — also present in the project context — is to call **RFC 5246** the TLS 1.1 RFC. That is incorrect: **RFC 5246 is TLS 1.2**. The TLS 1.1 defining document is **RFC 4346**. The two documents moved to Historic by RFC 8996 are RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1).

## Interpretation

- "Historic" here is an **RFC document status** assigned through the IETF process; it is not a runtime protocol flag or cipher-suite status. It means the defining documents are no longer current standards and are deprecated for use.
- The RFC header field "Obsoletes:" is not the mechanism to read for this answer; the authoritative statement is the quoted text moving RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 to Historic.
- RFC 8996 does not define a replacement protocol. TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) and TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) remain the current protocol versions; RFC 8996 also updates RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) and RFC 6347 (DTLS 1.2) to reflect the deprecation.

## Verification against the asks

- Ask 1: final identifier = **RFC 8996**; unit empty (identifier, not a number).
- Ask 2: final identifier/status = **Historic**; unit empty (identifier, not a number).
- No numeric values, thresholds, or bounds are stated in this deliverable, so there is no threshold-consistency conflict to check.
- Both asks are supported by the quoted source passage; nothing is blocked.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for 2026 is $184,500.

SCOPE AND DEFINITION
- Applies to: remuneration paid in calendar year 2026, and self-employment income for tax years beginning in 2026.
- Tax covered: Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) only. The 6.2% employee / 6.2% employer OASDI rates apply only up to this amount; earnings above $184,500 are not subject to OASDI tax.
- Not covered: Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI). HI has no earnings limit — the 1.45%/1.45% HI tax (and the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above the statutory threshold) applies to all wages with no cap. Do not attach a dollar cap to HI.
- The cap is per worker, applied to wages and self-employment income combined; an employer's matching obligation is capped at the same per-worker amount.

AUTHORITY AND STATUS
- Determined annually by statute (Social Security Act, Title II; formula indexed to the national average wage index), published by the Social Security Administration as the OASDI contribution and benefit base, with the determination also published in the Federal Register.
- The 2026 figure has been officially published by SSA; it is a final determination, not a projection or a payroll-vendor estimate.
- Primary references: SSA Contribution and Benefit Base pages (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html and cbbdet.html) and SSA's 2026 Fast Facts, which lists OASDI = 184,500 and HI = No limit.

DERIVED FIGURES (for payroll-system configuration and verification)
- 2025 base: $176,100. 2026 base: $184,500. Year-over-year change: +$8,400 (+4.77%).
- Maximum employee OASDI tax for 2026: $184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00.
- Maximum employer OASDI tax per worker for 2026: $184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00.
- Maximum combined OASDI tax per worker for 2026: $22,878.00.
- Maximum self-employed OASDI (SECA) contribution for 2026: $184,500 x 12.4% = $22,878.00 (before the deduction for one-half of SE tax and any above-the-cap wage offset).
- Related but distinct figure: the old-law contribution and benefit base for 2026 is $137,100. It is used only for certain benefit-computation purposes (e.g., pre-1977-law benchmarks) and is NOT the payroll-tax wage base; do not use it for withholding.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTES
- Set the 2026 OASDI wage base parameter to 184500 (USD). Reset the year-to-date OASDI taxable-wage accumulator at the start of 2026 (or at the employee's mid-year hire date) so withholding stops exactly when cumulative OASDI wages reach $184,500.
- Do not change the HI taxable-wage logic; HI remains uncapped.
- Verify after configuration: an employee with $200,000 of 2026 OASDI wages should show employee OASDI withholding of exactly $11,439.00, with $15,500 of wages above the cap exempt.

CONSISTENCY CHECKS PASSED
- 176,100 < 184,500 (2026 base exceeds 2025 base, as an indexed increase requires).
- 11,439.00 = 6.2% x 184,500 and does not exceed that bound; 22,878.00 = 12.4% x 184,500.
- 137,100 (old-law) < 184,500 (current-law), consistent with the statutory relationship between the two series.
- No numeric limit is stated for Medicare HI, consistent with its uncapped status.

verdict.summary:
2026 ELECTIVE DEFERRAL LIMIT (IRC §402(g)) — HR/BENEFITS ANSWER

ANSWER
=====
The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is a per-employee, per-calendar-year dollar limit. It applies to taxable years beginning in 2026 (i.e., the 2026 plan/payroll year for a calendar-year plan).

AUTHORITY
=========
- Governing rule: IRC §402(g)(1) — the annual limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in §402(g)(3) — as adjusted for cost-of-living under §402(g)(4).
- Annual adjustment notice: IRS Notice 2025-67 (released November 13, 2025; published in IRB 2025-49). The notice states the §402(g)(1) limitation 'is increased from $23,500 to $24,500' for taxable years beginning in 2026.
- Corroborating IRS guidance: IRS 'Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits' page, which lists the employee elective deferral limit (traditional and safe harbor plans) as '$24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
- Prior-year comparison for context: the 2025 limit was $23,500; the 2026 increase is $1,000.

WHAT THE $24,500 COVERS
=======================
1. Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals to a 401(k) are aggregated and counted against the SAME single $24,500 limit. An employee cannot defer $24,500 pre-tax plus another $24,500 Roth. Answer is identical whether the employee elects pre-tax, Roth, or a mix.
2. The limit applies per individual employee, per calendar year, and is aggregated across all 401(k) plans of the same employer — including plans of employers treated as a single employer under §414(b), (c), or (m) (controlled group / affiliated service group). Two plans of the same employer do not each get $24,500.
3. The §402(g) limit is an individual limit that also aggregates the employee's elective deferrals under other §402(g)(3) arrangements (e.g., 403(b) and governmental 457(b) elective deferrals, and the Thrift Savings Plan, which Notice 2025-67 expressly notes is covered). Where an employee defers under two unrelated employers in the same year and exceeds $24,500 in total, the excess is generally corrected by the individual on the tax return; a plan's own excess-deferral distribution process addresses amounts exceeding the limit within that plan/employer. HR should flag multi-employer situations at onboarding and at year-end.

WHAT IT EXCLUDES / DOES NOT CHANGE
==================================
- Catch-up contributions under §414(v) (age 50+, and the SECURE 2.0 age 60–63 enhanced catch-up) are ADDED ON TOP of the $24,500 and are a separate, separately announced figure. The request excludes them, so they are not part of this answer.
- Employer contributions — matching and nonelective — are not elective deferrals and do not count against $24,500.
- The §415(c) total annual additions limit (employee deferrals + employer contributions + forfeitures, per participant per limitation year) is a separate and larger figure announced in the same annual notice. $24,500 is NOT the total plan contribution limit; do not use it as such in plan communications.
- A SIMPLE 401(k) is subject to a different (lower) deferral limit and is not governed by this figure.
- SECURE 2.0's 2026 catch-up-related provisions (e.g., the wage-indexed threshold that affects catch-up eligibility/design and the Roth catch-up requirement for higher earners) are separate compliance items. They do not alter the $24,500 base limit and are out of scope here.
- A plan document may impose a LOWER cap (e.g., a percentage-of-pay deferral cap, a per-payroll cap, or an HCE-specific administrative limit). A plan-level restriction does not change the statutory 2026 limit of $24,500; it only means a given employee may be permitted to defer less. Confirm against the plan document/SPD before communicating a lower number to employees.

PAYROLL / ADMINISTRATION PROCEDURE
==================================
1. Configure the 2026 plan-year deferral cap at $24,500 per employee for pre-tax + Roth combined, with catch-up tracked in a separate bucket so the base cap is not prematurely stopped for age-50+ participants.
2. Run a year-to-date aggregation check across all plans of the employer/controlled group before each payroll so a mid-year transfer or plan merger does not produce a second $24,500 allowance.
3. On termination or at year-end, run the §402(g) excess-deferral test. Excess deferrals (plus allocable earnings) must be distributed to the participant by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation; coordinate with the recordkeeper and issue the required reporting.
4. At open enrollment, state the figure precisely: '$24,500 for 2026 (pre-tax and Roth combined), excluding catch-up contributions.' Do not label it the 'total 401(k) limit.'
5. Re-verify the figure against the IRS's annual COLA notice each fourth quarter; the number is indexed and changes most years.

verdict.summary:
CURRENT US NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5
As of the most recent completed PM NAAQS rulemaking (2024 revision, effective May 6, 2024).

=====================================================================
1. THE ANSWER
=====================================================================

ASK 1 — Annual primary PM2.5 standard:  9.0 µg/m³
ASK 2 — 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³

Both expressed as micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) of ambient PM2.5
(particles with an aerodynamic diameter ≤ a nominal 2.5 micrometers),
measured by an FRM based on 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix L and designated
under Part 53, or by an FEM designated under Part 53.

Governing text: 40 CFR § 50.18 (National primary ambient air quality
standards for PM2.5). Data handling and attainment determination:
Appendix N to 40 CFR Part 50.

=====================================================================
2. THE STANDARDS STATED IN FULL — LEVEL *AND* FORM
=====================================================================

The numeric level is only half of a NAAQS. Each standard is a level plus a
statistical form plus an averaging/compliance basis. Stated completely:

  ┌──────────────┬───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Standard     │ Level     │ Statistical form (part of the standard)  │
  ├──────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Primary      │ 9.0 µg/m³ │ Annual arithmetic mean concentration,    │
  │ annual       │           │ computed as the 3-year average of the    │
  │ PM2.5        │           │ annual arithmetic mean concentrations    │
  │              │           │ at each monitor.                         │
  ├──────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Primary      │ 35 µg/m³  │ 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations│
  │ 24-hour      │           │ at each monitor, computed as the 3-year  │
  │ PM2.5        │           │ average of the annual 98th percentile    │
  │              │           │ 24-hour values.                          │
  └──────────────┴───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘

Attainment test, stated the way § 50.18 and Appendix N state it:
  - Annual: the standard is met when the 3-year average of annual
    arithmetic mean concentrations is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³.
  - 24-hour: "The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th
    percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with
    appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³."
    (quoted from § 50.18; the 98th percentile is itself taken as the
    3-year average of annual 98th percentiles per Appendix N.)

Rounding / comparison conventions (Appendix N data handling):
  - Annual mean values are rounded to the nearest 0.1 µg/m³ before
    comparison with 9.0 µg/m³ — hence the level is written 9.0, not 9.
  - 24-hour values are rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ before comparison
    with 35 µg/m³ — hence the level is written 35, not 35.0.
  These are comparison conventions; they do not change the levels.

What is NOT included: this answer addresses the PRIMARY (health-based)
standards only, as asked. The secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are
tabulated separately in § 50.18 and should be read directly from the
current CFR text if needed — do not assume they are numerically identical
to the primary values without checking the section.

=====================================================================
3. DISCREPANCY IN THE SOURCE PACKET — DISCLOSED AND RESOLVED
=====================================================================

The source packet contains one quoted passage from § 50.18 that reads:

  "The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0
   micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) annual arithmetic mean concentration
   and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration ..."

That 12.0 is NOT the current annual level. It is the level that stood from
the 2012 PM NAAQS rulemaking until the 2024 revision. Two independent
indicators confirm this is a pre-2024 rendering of the section rather than
the current codification:

  (a) The packet's own source list includes the CFR-2016 title-40
      compilation of § 50.18 — a document that, by construction, reads
      12.0. A snippet retrieved from a stale snapshot, cache, or older
      compilation will carry 12.0.
  (b) The packet's researched answer states the 2024 action changed the
      primary annual level from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³, which is only coherent
      if 12.0 is the superseded value.

The 24-hour figure of 35 µg/m³ is unaffected: it is identical before and
after the 2024 revision, which is why the conflicting snippet is safe on
that half of the sentence and unsafe only on the annual half.

Reported position: annual = 9.0 µg/m³ (current), with 12.0 recorded here
as the superseded pre-2024 value so that no reader mistakes the stale
snippet for the answer.

=====================================================================
4. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (run this before relying on the numbers)
=====================================================================

Step 1 — Open 40 CFR § 50.18 on eCFR and read the currency banner
         ("up to date as of ..."). It must be a date on or after
         May 6, 2024. If it is earlier, you are on a stale snapshot.
Step 2 — Read the first sentence of paragraph (a). It must read
         "9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) annual arithmetic mean
         concentration and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration."
         If it reads 12.0, you have the pre-2024 text — do not use it.
Step 3 — Check the CFR source note / authority citation at the end of
         § 50.18. It must cite the 2024 PM NAAQS final rule (published
         in the Federal Register in early 2024; confirm the volume/page
         from the source note itself rather than from memory). A source
         note ending with the 2012 rulemaking confirms a stale copy.
Step 4 — Cross-check the EPA NAAQS table page, which lists the primary
         PM2.5 standards as 9 µg/m³ annual (annual mean, 3-year average)
         and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour (98th percentile, 3-year average).
Step 5 — Confirm Appendix N is the version in force; the attainment
         computations above are Appendix N computations, and a rule that
         amended Appendix N would change how the levels are applied even
         if the levels themselves did not move.

=====================================================================
5. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS ANSWER
=====================================================================

- A later final PM NAAQS rulemaking that revises § 50.18. A signed or
  proposed action does not change the standard; only a final rule that
  has taken effect does.
- Pending reconsideration or judicial review. A standard under
  reconsideration or on review remains the codified standard and remains
  in effect unless and until a final agency action or court order lifts
  or vacates it. If you need a legally operative answer for a specific
  compliance date, confirm the status of any such proceeding as of that
  date; the levels above are the codified current standards, not a
  prediction of future ones.
- A request that turns out to mean secondary standards, PM10, or a
  state/local standard — different numbers, different section.

=====================================================================
6. ONE-LINE ANSWER
=====================================================================

Current US national primary PM2.5 NAAQS: 9.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean
(3-year average) and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour (98th percentile, 3-year average),
per 40 CFR § 50.18 as revised by the 2024 PM NAAQS final rule.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

In general industry (not construction), a US employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface that has an unprotected side or edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level from falling. The 4-foot trigger is the default rule; it can be tightened, never loosened, by the surface- and activity-specific paragraphs of the same section and by other subparts (see 'Conditions that change or override the number' below).

1. REGULATORY BASIS

Standard: 29 CFR 1910.28, 'Fall protection,' in Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces) of Part 1910 (Occupational Safety and Health Standards), federal OSHA general industry. Promulgated in the 2016 Walking-Working Surfaces final rule (81 FR 82494).

Controling text — § 1910.28(b)(1)(i):

  '(i) Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
   (A) Guardrail systems;
   (B) Safety net systems; or
   (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

Catch-all text — § 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) uses the same 4-foot (1.2 m) figure: 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems...'

2. WHAT THE NUMBER MEANS IN PRACTICE

- Measurement convention: the 4 feet is the vertical distance from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level. It is not a measurement to the employee's body part, and not a horizontal distance to the edge.
- Trigger is '4 feet or more': exactly 4'0" (1.2 m) is covered. 3'11" is not covered by this default paragraph (but may be covered by another provision — see below).
- 'Walking-working surface' is used in the regulatory sense (29 CFR 1910.21(b)): any surface, whether permanent or temporary, on which an employee walks or works, including floors, roofs, ramps, bridges, runways, and similar surfaces.
- 'Unprotected side or edge' means no guardrail, and no equivalent barrier, at the edge. An employee who is already behind a compliant guardrail, or who is under a compliant travel-restraint system, is not an unprotected exposure and needs no further protection for that edge.
- Compliant means are the three listed: guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems (fall arrest, travel restraint, positioning). The employer chooses; the standard does not require guardrail specifically.

3. CONDITIONS THAT CHANGE OR OVERRIDE THE NUMBER (must be checked on the actual condition)

The 4-foot default is expressly qualified by 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part.' A safety professional applying this must verify, before relying on 4 ft:

(a) Surface/activity-specific paragraphs within § 1910.28(b). The section contains separate paragraphs for docks, hoist areas, holes, and ramps/runways/other walkways, and a paragraph addressing falls onto or into dangerous equipment. Some of these require protection at the same 4 feet; the dangerous-equipment provision requires protection regardless of height where an employee can fall onto or into hazardous equipment (for example, open vats, molten metal, or machinery that can cause injury). Locate and apply the paragraph matching the actual surface rather than the general rule.
(b) Other subparts of Part 1910 with their own rules for particular equipment — for example, laders (§ 1910.23) and stairways (§ 1910.25), plus scaffolds and other equipment-specific standards. Where one of those applies, it governs instead of the general 4-foot rule.
(c) State-plan jurisdictions. Federal OSHA standards are a floor. States and territories with OSHA-approved plans must be at least as effective as federal, and some are more stringent. If the workplace is in a state-plan state, check the state rule before relying on 4 ft.
(d) Regime boundaries. This answer holds for general industry. It does not hold for: construction (29 CFR 1926 — conventionally 6 ft for unprotected sides and edges under § 1926.501(b)(1)); shipyard employment (5 ft); longshoring (8 ft); or agricultural operations. If the work is construction-adjacent (alteration/repair versus maintenance), the construction threshold, not this one, may govern.

None of (a)–(d) raises the 4-foot figure in the answer; they can only require protection at a lower height or regardless of height.

4. THE MOST COMMON ERRER TO AVOID

Quoting 6 feet. Six feet is the construction-industry threshold (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)), not the general-industry threshold. The request expressly excludes construction; for general industry the answer is 4 feet (1.2 m). Shipyard (5 ft) and longshoring (8 ft) figures are similarly not applicable.

5. ONE-LINE RESULT FOR THE EMPLOYER'S WRITTEN FALL-PROTECTION POLICY

'Where an employee is exposed to an unprotected side or edge of a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, the employer will provide guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall protection systems (fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning), except where a more specific provision of 29 CFR 1910.28(b), another subpart of Part 1910, or an applicable OSHA-approved state plan requires protection at a lower height or regardless of height.'

(A) Guardrail systems;
(B) Safety net systems; or
(C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

verdict.summary:
Under 14 CFR 91.151(b), the minimum VFR reserve fuel for a helicopter in the United States is 20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed, after reaching the first point of intended landing. The rule states: 'No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

Answer: at least 20 minutes of fuel beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing.

Computation:
- Reserve time = 20 minutes = 1/3 hour.
- Reserve fuel quantity = normal cruising fuel flow x (20/60).
- Example only: if the helicopter burns 30 gal/hr at normal cruising speed, the minimum reserve is 30 x (20/60) = 10 gal. If it burns 120 lb/hr, the minimum reserve is 120 x (20/60) = 40 lb.
- The 20-minute reserve is a time-based minimum, not a fixed volume; the usable fuel quantity must be at least the amount the aircraft will burn in 20 minutes at normal cruising speed.

Applicability and planning notes:
- This is the Part 91 general-operating VFR rotorcraft requirement. It applies to helicopters; the 30-minute day and 45-minute night VFR reserve figures in the same regulation are airplane requirements and do not apply to rotorcraft.
- The rule contains no separate day/night reserve for helicopters; 20 minutes applies to both day and night VFR under Part 91.
- Wind and forecast weather must be considered in determining that there is enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing. The reserve segment itself is calculated assuming normal cruising speed.
- The reserve is after the first point of intended landing, so the pre-takeoff fuel load must cover: fuel to the first landing point + 20 minutes at normal cruising speed + any additional fuel required by the specific flight conditions or operating rules.
- If the flight is conducted under an operating rule other than Part 91, such as Part 135, verify the applicable rule; the Part 91 answer above is the general VFR rotorcraft minimum.

verdict.summary:
# Answers

**1. Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1?**

**RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (IETF, March 2021), published in the Best Current Practice category as **BCP 195**.

**2. What status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?**

**Historic.** RFC 8996 moves **RFC 2246** (which defined TLS 1.0) and **RFC 4346** (which defined TLS 1.1) to Historic status.

## Primary-source statement

The determining sentence, quoted verbatim from the RFC Editor copy of RFC 8996:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."
> — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html

That single sentence answers both asks: the deprecating document is RFC 8996; the assigned status is Historic; the recipients of that status are RFC 2246 and RFC 4346.

## Scope table (what changed, and what did not)

| RFC | Protocol it defined | Status after RFC 8996 | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFC 2246 | TLS 1.0 | **Historic** | Named explicitly in RFC 8996 |
| RFC 4346 | TLS 1.1 | **Historic** | Named explicitly in RFC 8996 |
| RFC 5246 | TLS 1.2 | **Unchanged by RFC 8996** | *Not* deprecated and *not* moved to Historic by this document |

**Correction to a working assumption.** A common shorthand is that RFC 8996 "retired the old TLS RFCs" and that this includes RFC 5246. It does not. The document's own scope sentence names exactly two defining RFCs — 2246 and 4346 — and the deprecation is of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 only. TLS 1.2 remained a Standards Track specification after RFC 8996; only TLS 1.0 and 1.1 lost standing. Any answer that lists RFC 5246 among the RFCs moved to Historic by RFC 8996 is contradicted by the quoted passage.

## What the status change means operationally

"Historic" is an RFC 2026 non-Standards-Track maturity level (§4.2.3, *Historic*), applied to a specification the community no longer recommends for new use. Paired with the deprecation, RFC 8996 carries normative force as a BCP:

- TLS 1.0 **MUST NOT** be used.
- TLS 1.1 **MUST NOT** be used.
- Negotiation of either version is prohibited; a peer offering only TLS 1.0/1.1 has no compliant path to proceed.
- The rationale given is that both versions had already been superseded by TLS 1.2 and, subsequently, TLS 1.3.

For an implementer or policy author, the practical reading is: "Historic" is not merely a label on a shelf — it is the RFC-status expression of a MUST NOT.

## Verification procedure

Because status changes are metadata edits made by the RFC Editor, verify against the RFC Editor rather than a secondary summary:

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246` and `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346`. The `Status:` field on each info page should read **Historic**.
2. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996`. Confirm `Category: Best Current Practice` and `BCP: 195`.
3. Cross-check the Datatracker history page (`https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/`) if an audit trail of the status transition is required.
4. Check the inline errata page (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc8996.html`) before quoting the deprecation sentence in a compliance artifact; if an erratum touches that sentence, quote the corrected text and cite the erratum ID.
5. Note the BCP 195 lineage: RFC 8996 sits in a document series that has since been revised (RFC 9325, *Recommendations for Secure Use of TLS and DTLS*, is the later BCP 195 document and obsoletes RFC 8996). Confirm the current BCP 195 pointer on the RFC Editor before citing "current guidance" — but the act of deprecating TLS 1.0/1.1, and the Historic reclassification of RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, was performed by **RFC 8996** and is the correct answer to the question as asked.

## Ready-to-use citation forms

- Narrative: "TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 were deprecated by RFC 8996 (BCP 195), which moved their defining specifications, RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, to Historic status."
- Tabular: `Deprecated by: RFC 8996 (BCP 195) | Resulting status of RFC 2246, RFC 4346: Historic`
- Change-log line: "TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) — status: Historic per RFC 8996; MUST NOT be used or negotiated."

## Pitfalls to avoid in downstream copies

- Do not say RFC 8996 "obsoletes" RFC 2246/RFC 4346. The status change is a reclassification to Historic; obsoletion is a separate relationship and the document's wording is "moved to Historic status."
- Do not extend the Historic status to RFC 5246 in this citation.
- Do not attribute the deprecation to vendor policy, to the TLS 1.3 work in RFC 8446, or to an IANA registry action; the formal IETF deprecation is RFC 8996.

## Contribution and Benefit Base

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The U.S. Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

It applies to remuneration paid in 2026 and to self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026.

1. AUTHORITY AND EXACT LANGUAGE

Governing source class: the Social Security Administration's annual cost-of-living / automatic-adjustment determination published in the Federal Register, issued under Section 230 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. §430). This notice, not a news summary or a projection, is the controlling specification of the base. SSA's own published pages and forms are supporting official references and should agree with it; if they ever disagree, the Federal Register notice governs.

Primary citation: SSA, "Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2026," Federal Register document 2025-19763, published November 3, 2025 — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/html/2025/11/03/2025-19763.html

Operative sentences:
  • "Because $184,500 exceeds the current base amount of $176,100, the OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for 2026."
  • "The OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026."

Corroborating official sources:
  • SSA Publication No. 05-10003 (2026 factsheet), "Social Security taxes" table: employee/employer (each) "6.2% on earnings up to $184,500"; self-employed "12.4% on earnings up to $184,500" (2025 column: $176,100).
  • SSA contribution-and-benefit-base summary table (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html), row "2026 ... 184,500."

2. HOW THE FIGURE IS PRODUCED (statutory mechanism, for context only)

Section 230 of the Social Security Act requires the base to be redetermined each year by indexing the 1994 base ($60,600) to the growth in the SSA national average wage index (AWI), then rounding the result to the nearest multiple of $300. The base is not discretionary and is not set by Congress annually; it moves automatically with the AWI. The 2026 figure therefore reflects wage growth from the 1994 indexing year through the AWI for 2024, and is mechanically distinct from the cost-of-living adjustment applied to benefit amounts.

Internal consistency check on the rounding rule: $184,500 / 300 = 615 exactly, so the published figure is a valid multiple of $300. The adjacent bases quoted below also satisfy this test ($176,100 / 300 = 587; $137,100 / 300 = 457), which is a useful sanity check when verifying any year's figure.

3. COMPANION FIGURES FOR 2026 (state these alongside the base so it is not misapplied)

  | Item | 2025 | 2026 |
  |---|---|---|
  | OASDI contribution and benefit base (taxable maximum) | $176,100 | $184,500 |
  | Employee rate on earnings up to the base | 6.2% | 6.2% |
  | Employer rate on earnings up to the base (matches employee) | 6.2% | 6.2% |
  | Self-employed OASDI rate on net earnings up to the base | 12.4% | 12.4% |
  | Old-law contribution and benefit base (separate statutory concept) | — | $137,100 |
  | Medicare (HI) wage cap | No limit | No limit |

  • Maximum employee OASDI tax for 2026: $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439.00 (employer owes the same, so $22,878.00 per worker across both shares).
  • Maximum self-employed OASDI tax for 2026: $184,500 × 12.4% = $22,878.00, before the income-tax deduction for the employer-equivalent half.
  • Year-over-year increase in the ceiling: $184,500 − $176,100 = $8,400; at 6.2% this raises the maximum employee contribution by $520.80, from $10,918.20 (2025) to $11,439.00 (2026).

4. DISTINCTIONS THAT PREVENT THE MOST COMMON ERRORS

  • Not the old-law base. The same Federal Register notice states: "The old-law contribution and benefit base for 2026 is $137,100." The old-law base is used only for certain statutory computations; it is not the payroll-tax ceiling and must never be reported as the answer to this question.
  • Not a Medicare figure. The Hospital Insurance (HI) component has no earnings cap; the 1.45%/2.9% HI rates apply to all wages, and the additional 0.9% HI surtax above the statutory threshold amounts (which are fixed in statute, not indexed, and are separate from this base) is likewise unaffected by the $184,500 figure. The $184,500 applies to OASDI only.
  • Not the 2025 figure. $176,100 remains the base for 2025 only; it is superseded for 2026.
  • Not a projection. Third-party calculators published before the October announcement produced estimates in roughly the $183,000–$185,000 range; those were estimates, not the base. The $184,500 figure is the officially announced amount and should be preferred over any conflicting secondary or preliminary number.
  • Not the earnings-test thresholds. The retirement earnings test exempt amounts and the taxable-maximum benefit computation points are separate determinations announced in the same notice; do not conflate them with the contribution and benefit base.
  • Not an aggregate. $184,500 is per individual worker per year; it is not an employer-level, household-level, or economy-wide figure.

5. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (if the figure must be re-confirmed before use)

  1. Open the Federal Register notice for the applicable determination year (search Federal Register for SSA "Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations" plus the year) and read the paragraph expressly headed as the OASDI contribution and benefit base.
  2. Confirm the sentence pattern: "The OASDI contribution and benefit base is $[X] for remuneration paid in [year] and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in [year]."
  3. Cross-check against SSA's contribution-and-benefit-base table (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) and the current SSA factsheet (Publication 05-10003) tax table; all three must show the same dollar amount.
  4. Confirm the amount is a multiple of $300 (rounding rule) and that it exceeds the immediately preceding year's base.
  5. Confirm you are reading the OASDI base, not the old-law base line in the same notice.
  6. For downstream tax software, forms, and instructions, the same $184,500 must appear in IRS guidance for tax year 2026 and on Form W-2 wage reporting; a mismatch at that stage indicates a stale table, not a different base.

BOTTOM LINE

For 2026, the maximum amount of an individual's earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax is $184,500, per SSA's Federal Register determination for 2026. Medicare taxes have no such cap, and the old-law base of $137,100 is a separate figure that does not answer this question.

verdict.summary:
# 2026 401(k) Employee Elective Deferral Limit (Before Catch-Up)

## 1. Answer

**$24,500.**

That is the maximum amount an employee may elect to defer to a 401(k) plan for calendar year 2026 under IRC §402(g), **before** any age-based catch-up contribution under IRC §414(v). It is up from $23,500 for 2025.

## 2. Authority

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Statutory provision | IRC §402(g)(1); inflation adjustment under §402(g)(4) |
| IRS guidance | IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments) |
| Corroborating IRS publications | IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits; IRS 2026 newsroom release on contribution limits |
| Quoted language (Retirement Topics page) | "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments" |
| Quoted language (newsroom release) | "The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025." |

This is the published, final figure — not a projection. It does not require estimation or inflation modeling; the §402(g)(4) indexing (adjustments in $500 increments) has already been applied by the IRS.

## 3. Scope — what this number does and does not include

**Included in the $24,500:**
- Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals.
- Designated Roth elective deferrals — Roth 401(k) contributions are elective deferrals and share the same §402(g) dollar cap. There is no separate Roth bucket.
- Safe harbor nonelective and safe harbor match **employer** contributions do **not** count against it (they are employer contributions), but an employee's own deferrals made to satisfy a safe harbor plan do.

**Excluded from the $24,500 (do not add these to reach the answer):**
- The §414(v) age-50 catch-up amount — a separate, additional limit published in the same IRS notice.
- The §414(v) "super catch-up" for participants aged 60–63 — a separate, higher catch-up figure in the same notice.
- The §415(c) total annual additions limit (employee deferrals + employer contributions + forfeitures) — a separate, larger limit.
- The §401(a)(17) compensation limit and the §414(q) HCE threshold — separate figures.

Because the request is specifically "before any catch-up contribution," the answer is the base figure only. **$24,500 is the ceiling on the employee's own pre-tax plus Roth elections for 2026.**

## 4. How the limit applies (operating rules)

1. **Per individual, not per plan.** The §402(g) limit applies to the individual employee and aggregates elective deferrals across all §401(k) plans (and §403(b) and governmental §457(b) plans) in which that employee participates during the calendar year — including plans of unrelated employers. Two jobs with two 401(k) plans do not produce two $24,500 allowances; excess deferrals must be corrected.
2. **Calendar-year measurement.** The §402(g) limit is measured on the individual's calendar-year deferrals, even where the plan's limitation year is a non-calendar plan year.
3. **Plans may set a lower limit.** The statutory figure is a ceiling, not an entitlement. A plan document may cap deferrals lower (e.g., a percentage-of-compensation cap, a cap tied to the match formula, or a lower dollar cap). The operative payroll limit is:

   `effective_limit = min(plan_document_limit, 24,500)`

   For a participant with no plan-specific cap, `effective_limit = 24,500`.
4. **Per-participant proration for partial years.** If a participant becomes eligible mid-year, the $24,500 is **not** prorated — it remains the full calendar-year ceiling, though the plan may separately limit the percentage of pay deferrable.
5. **Excess deferral correction.** Deferrals above $24,500 (net of any valid catch-up, which is not part of this answer) are excess deferrals under §402(g). They must be distributed, with allocable earnings, by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation; if corrected timely, they are taxable in the year deferred and the earnings in the year distributed.
6. **Payroll translation.** For an employee paid semi-monthly (24 pay periods), the level per-paycheck deferral that exactly reaches the limit is 24,500 / 24 = $1,020.83; for biweekly (26 periods), 24,500 / 26 = $942.31. Because plans typically deduct in whole cents and stop at the cap, use a front-loaded or true-up approach rather than rounding up, which would produce excess deferrals.

## 5. Common failure modes this answer guards against

- **Confusing the answer with the catch-up limit.** The catch-up amount is additive and age-conditional; it is not part of the $24,500.
- **Confusing the answer with the §415(c) annual additions limit.** That limit covers employer money plus employee money and is materially higher; it is a different test.
- **Importing a different plan year's figure.** $23,500 is the 2025 limit; $25,500 is the announced 2027 limit. Neither is the 2026 answer.
- **Assuming Roth deferrals sit outside the cap.** They do not.
- **Treating the figure as per-employer.** It is per-employee, aggregated across plans.

## 6. Verification checklist for the reviewer

- [ ] Figure matches IRS Notice 2025-67 / IRS Retirement Topics page: **$24,500 for 2026**.
- [ ] Figure is the base elective deferral limit, not the catch-up amount.
- [ ] Figure is not the §415(c) annual additions limit.
- [ ] Figure is stated for calendar year 2026, not 2025 ($23,500) or 2027 ($25,500).
- [ ] Figure applies to pre-tax and Roth deferrals combined.

**Bottom line: $24,500 for 2026, before any catch-up contribution.**

verdict.summary:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## Answer

| Standard | Primary (health-based) level | Regulatory form (statistical metric) |
|---|---|---|
| **Annual PM2.5** | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 consecutive years |
| **24-hour PM2.5** | **35 µg/m³** | 24-hour average concentration — the 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 consecutive years |

Both are primary (health-based) standards under the Clean Air Act NAAQS program, codified at 40 CFR 50.18, with the statistical form defined in 40 CFR part 50 Appendix N. Units are micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³); the annual level is expressed to one decimal place, the 24-hour level as a whole number.

**These are the values in force as of the verification date of the cited sources (2026-11-16).**

## How these values were established

1. **Annual standard = 9.0 µg/m³.** EPA's NAAQS for PM page states: *"EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection..."* EPA's 2024 designations page confirms the direction and magnitude of the change: *"On February 7, 2024, the EPA promulgated a revised primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS, strengthening the standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3..."* The December 2024 administrative correction document repeats it: *"The final rule revised the primary annual PM2.5 standard by lowering the level from 12.0 µg/m3 to 9.0 µg/m3..."*

2. **24-hour standard = 35 µg/m³, unchanged.** The same designations page: *"...retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m3."* The 2024 final rule overview presentation: *"The primary (health-based) and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards stay at the level of 35 µg/m3."* The rule overview document: *"The EPA Administrator concluded that the revised annual standard together with the current 24-hour standard will protect public health with an adequate margin of safety."* Four independent EPA documents agree on 35 µg/m³, so this value is not in contention.

## Governing rulemaking and effective date

- The operative rulemaking is EPA's **2024 reconsideration of the particulate matter NAAQS**, signed **February 7, 2024**, published in the Federal Register on **March 6, 2024** at **89 FR 16202** (FR Doc. 2024-02637, "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter").
- It lowered the primary annual PM2.5 level from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³, **retained** the primary 24-hour PM2.5 level at 35 µg/m³, retained the primary 24-hour PM10 level at 150 µg/m³, and retained the existing suite of secondary PM standards.
- A subsequent EPA administrative correction document (December 5, 2024, OAR PM NAAQS reconsideration correction) restates the same levels and does not alter them.
- **Verification item:** the effective date is 60 days after Federal Register publication (i.e., early May 2024); confirm the exact date on the FR document before relying on it in a legal or permitting filing. The levels themselves are not sensitive to this date.

## Do not use the 12.0 µg/m³ figure

One commonly retrieved source — EPA's 2018 "Chapter 2: Ambient Standards" document — quotes the pre-2024 regulatory text: *"(i) 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration..."* That is a verbatim restatement of 40 CFR 50.18 **as it stood before the 2024 revision**. It is superseded for the annual standard. Any answer that reports 12.0 µg/m³ as the current annual level is out of date by one rulemaking. (The 35 µg/m³ figure in that same quote remains correct, which is a common source of confusion.)

## Scope notes

- **Primary vs. secondary.** The request asks for primary standards only. For completeness and to prevent conflation: the secondary (welfare-based) standards are **15.0 µg/m³ annual** and **35 µg/m³ 24-hour**. Do not substitute the 15.0 figure for the 9.0 primary annual level.
- **PM10 is out of scope.** The primary 24-hour PM10 standard remains 150 µg/m³; it is a different pollutant and is not part of this answer.
- **"Current" depends on purpose.** The 2024 rule did not change PM NAAQS implementation programs. For most implementation contexts (designations, permitting, SIP planning), an older value may still be the operative reference until the applicable compliance or designations provisions take effect for a given area. The **standards themselves** are 9.0 and 35 µg/m³; the **implementation value** applicable to a specific action must be checked against that action's Federal Register notice.
- **Litigation status.** No court-ordered stay or contrary operative standard appeared in any source reviewed. Litigation status was not independently verified and should be confirmed before the values are relied on in an enforcement or litigation posture.

## Sources

1. EPA, National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for PM — https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/national-ambient-air-quality-standards-naaqs-pm
2. EPA, Particle Pollution Designations — 2024 Revised Annual PM2.5 NAAQS — https://www.epa.gov/particle-pollution-designations/particle-pollution-designations-2024-revised-annual-pm25-naaqs
3. 89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024), Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/03/06/2024-02637/reconsideration-of-the-national-ambient-air-quality-standards-for-particulate-matter
4. EPA, 2024 PM NAAQS Final Rule Overview presentation — https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-02/2024-pm-naaqs-final-overview-presentation.pdf
5. EPA, PM NAAQS Overview — https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-02/pm-naaqs-overview.pdf
6. EPA, PM NAAQS Reconsideration administrative correction (Dec. 5, 2024) — https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-12/8635.1-02-oar_pm-naaqs-reconsideration_correction_20241205_admin.pdf
7. 40 CFR 50.18 and 40 CFR part 50 Appendix N (regulatory text defining levels and statistical form).
