quotes.text: Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:

verdict.summary:
ANSWER (bottom line)

4 feet (1.2 m). Under federal OSHA general industry rules, an employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level from falling.

1. GOVERNING CITATION AND CONTROLLING TEXT

Citation: 29 CFR 1910.28, "Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection," paragraph (b)(1)(i) — general industry, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces).

Controlling text (verbatim): "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:"

Sources verified: eCFR (https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.28) and GovInfo CFR 2025 title 29 vol. 5 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2025-title29-vol5-sec1910-28.xml); corroborated by OSHA fall-protection outreach materials (osha.gov/fall-protection).

Threshold: 4 ft (1.2 m) — measured vertically from the walking-working surface to the lower level.

2. WHAT SATISFIES THE DUTY

The same paragraph requires protection "by one or more of the following":
- Guardrail systems (specifications at 1910.29(b));
- Safety net systems (1910.29(c));
- Personal fall protection systems — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems (1910.29(d)–(f));
- Where the employer can demonstrate that use of these systems is infeasible or would create a greater hazard, a written fall protection plan meeting 1910.29(k) — the infeasibility route changes the means of compliance, not the 4 ft trigger.

Related duties that ride along with the 4 ft trigger: employee training (1910.30), and inspection/maintenance of the fall protection systems (1910.29).

3. HOW TO MEASURE

- Vertical distance from the working surface on which the employee stands to the next lower level, not the distance to the ground if intermediate levels exist.
- "Unprotected" means no guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection already in place at that edge; a compliant guardrail at the edge removes the exposure.
- The trigger is triggered by employee exposure on the surface, regardless of task duration — the general rule contains no minimum-duration carve-out (task-specific exceptions live in the paragraphs listed in Section 5).

4. SCOPE OF THIS ANSWER (assumptions stated as assumptions)

- Jurisdiction: federal OSHA. State Plan jurisdictions must be at least as effective as federal OSHA but may differ in text or threshold; if the workplace is in a State Plan state (e.g., California, Washington, Oregon, Michigan, Kentucky, etc.), confirm the state's own walking-working-surfaces standard before relying on 4 ft.
- Industry: general industry (29 CFR Part 1910). Construction (29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart M) is out of scope and has a different trigger — see Section 6.
- Surface type: general walking-working surfaces. Roofs, ladders, dockboards, scaffolds and similar surfaces are addressed by other paragraphs of 1910.28 that can impose different thresholds or additional options — see Section 5.

5. WHEN 4 FT IS NOT THE CONTROLLING NUMBER (check before applying the general rule)

1910.28(b)(1)(i) begins "Except as provided elsewhere in this section." The following provisions inside 1910.28 can displace or modify the general 4 ft rule for particular surfaces. Each must be checked against the full standard text for the actual work area; the figures below are orientation only and are not a substitute for reading the paragraph.

| Provision (1910.28(b)) | Surface/situation | Effect relative to the 4 ft general rule |
|---|---|---|
| (b)(1)(i) | General walking-working surface, unprotected side/edge | 4 ft (1.2 m) — the answer to this request |
| (b)(1)(ii) | Infeasible / greater hazard to use guardrail, net, or PFPS | Duty remains; substitute a written fall protection plan per 1910.29(k) |
| (b)(2) | Hoist areas | Same 4 ft family of trigger; protection required at the edge of the hole/hoist area |
| (b)(3) | Holes, including skylights | Protection against falling through required above 4 ft |
| (b)(4) | Ramps, runways, and other walkways | 4 ft |
| (b)(5)–(b)(6) | Dockboards / equipment and area guarding | Cross-refers to 1910.26 and related guarding; verify text |
| (b)(9) | Fixed ladders | Different, higher threshold: personal fall arrest or ladder safety system required for climbs above 24 ft (ladder-specific rules also at 1910.23) |
| (b)(13) | Low-slope roofs | Same 4 ft trigger, but additional compliance options (e.g., warning line and/or designated area combinations) are permitted in specified circumstances |
| (b)(14) | Steep roofs | 4 ft, with guardrail, safety net, or PFPS |
| (b)(11) / 1910.27 | Scaffolds | Governed by the scaffold standard's own criteria, not 1910.28(b)(1) alone |

Practical rule for the field: default to 4 ft (1.2 m); if the edge is a roof, a fixed ladder, a scaffold, a hole/skylight, or a dockboard, open the specific paragraph before finalizing the fall protection plan.

6. GENERAL INDUSTRY VS. CONSTRUCTION (do not mix)

- General industry (1910.28(b)(1)(i)): 4 ft (1.2 m). This is the answer here.
- Construction (1926.501(b)(1)): 6 ft (1.8 m) for unprotected sides and edges — a different part, a different trigger, and explicitly excluded from this answer. A common compliance error is applying the 6 ft construction number to a general industry facility (or vice versa).

7. VERIFICATION STEPS BEFORE THE NUMBER IS RELIED ON

1. Confirm the establishment falls under Part 1910 (general industry) and not Part 1926 (construction) for the activity in question — maintenance vs. actual construction work can flip the applicable part.
2. Confirm whether a State Plan with different text governs the site.
3. Read 1910.28(b) in full for the specific surface type (Section 5 table).
4. Confirm the exposure is genuinely unprotected (no compliant guardrail/net/PFPS already present).
5. If relying on infeasibility, confirm a written 1910.29(k) fall protection plan exists and is enforced.
6. Confirm training records under 1910.30 cover the systems in use.

8. LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

This states the federal general-industry trigger height and its citation. It does not determine which of the Section 5 exceptions applies to any specific work area, does not evaluate State Plan requirements, and does not design a fall protection system; those require the site-specific review in Section 7.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY ANSWER — US VFR RESERVE FUEL, HELICOPTER (ROTORCRAFT)

1. THE ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry, beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing, enough fuel to fly for at least 20 MINUTES at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption.

- Reserve time: 20 minutes.
- There is no day/night difference for helicopters. 20 minutes applies day and night.
- The reserve is in addition to (after) the fuel to the first point of intended landing — it is not a portion of the trip fuel, and it is not planned to be consumed.

In fuel quantity terms, the reserve is 1/3 of one hour of cruise fuel flow:

    Reserve (gal) = cruise fuel flow (gal/hr) ÷ 3
    Reserve (lb)  = cruise fuel flow (lb/hr)  ÷ 3

2. REGULATORY BASIS (verbatim)

14 CFR § 91.151(b) — general/private operations (Part 91):
  "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

14 CFR § 135.209(b) — commercial helicopter operations (Part 135):
  "No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Both rules yield the same 20-minute figure. § 91.151(b) governs a helicopter flown under Part 91 (the default for private/owner-flown/general operations); § 135.209(b) governs helicopters operated under Part 135 (air taxi / commercial). If the operation is Part 135, both the certificate holder's OpSpecs and § 135.209(b) apply, and OpSpecs may impose a higher minimum — the higher of the two governs, but the federal regulatory floor is still 20 minutes.

Two elements are written into the rule itself and are part of the requirement, not optional prudence:
  (a) "considering wind and forecast weather conditions" — the fuel to the first point of intended landing must be computed with the forecast wind (headwind component) and forecast temperature/conditions, not still-air, no-wind figures; and
  (b) "normal cruising speed" / "normal cruising fuel consumption" — the burn rate used is the aircraft's normal cruise power setting from its POH/RFMS, not a best-economy or idle figure chosen to make the numbers work.

3. WHAT THE RULE DOES NOT REQUIRE (common sources of error)

- No 30-minute or 45-minute figure applies to helicopters. Those numbers are § 91.151(a) and § 135.209(a), which apply to AIRPLANES (30 minutes day VFR, 45 minutes night VFR). Substituting them for a rotorcraft overstates the legal minimum; omitting the 20 minutes because the airplane numbers were used understates it in the wrong direction only by accident. Use 20.
- No alternate-airport fuel requirement exists for VFR. The 45-minute IFR reserve of § 91.167 (and the IFR alternate fuel rules) does not apply to a VFR helicopter flight.
- The reserve is not a discretionary pad and it is not fuel you may plan to land on. A flight planned so that it arrives with less than 20 minutes remaining was either dispatched with insufficient fuel or encountered conditions outside the forecast; the requirement is tested at the moment the flight begins ("No person may begin a flight...").
- Unusable fuel does not count. The requirement is for usable fuel; fuel below a standpipe, trapped in a sump, or otherwise not available in flight cannot be credited toward either the trip fuel or the 20-minute reserve.
- The rule is US federal. A helicopter operating outside the United States, or under a foreign registry, is subject to that State's rules (ICAO Annex 6 and national regulations), which may specify a different reserve. This answer is US-specific.

4. CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A FUEL QUANTITY (procedure)

Step 1. From the RFMS/POH, take the fuel flow at the normal cruise power setting to be used for the flight (gal/hr or lb/hr). If the flight plan uses a reduced cruise power, use the flow at that setting — that is the "normal cruising" condition for that flight.
Step 2. Divide by 3 (20 min = 1/3 hr). Result is the reserve in the same units.
Step 3. Convert to the units the aircraft is fueled in:
    Avgas: 1 gal ≈ 6.0 lb
    Jet A: 1 gal ≈ 6.7 lb
Step 4. Add to the trip fuel computed with forecast wind:
    Total fuel required at brake release ≥ trip fuel to first point of intended landing (with forecast wind) + 20-minute reserve + taxi/run-up/start allowance actually used.
Step 5. Compare against usable fuel on board at brake release. If usable fuel on board is less than the Step 4 total, the flight may not begin.

Worked examples (burn rates are illustrative placeholders — substitute the actual RFMS/POH figure for the specific type and power setting; the METHOD, not the sample number, is the deliverable):

  Example A — piston helicopter, avgas, 10 gal/hr normal cruise:
    20 min = 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33 gal
    = 3.33 gal × 6.0 lb/gal ≈ 20 lb
    If the trip to the first landing point (with forecast wind) needs 22 gal, minimum usable fuel at start ≈ 22 + 3.33 = 25.3 gal, plus start/taxi allowance.

  Example B — turbine helicopter, Jet A, 400 lb/hr normal cruise:
    20 min = 400 ÷ 3 = 133.3 lb
    = 133.3 lb ÷ 6.7 lb/gal ≈ 19.9 gal
    If the trip needs 60 gal, minimum usable fuel at start ≈ 60 + 19.9 = 79.9 gal, plus start/taxi allowance.

  Example C — expressed in time only: if the aircraft's total usable endurance at normal cruise is 3.0 hr, the 20-minute reserve consumes 1/3 hr of it, so no more than 2 hr 40 min of that endurance may be planned for the trip (including wind and start/taxi).

5. LEGAL MINIMUM VERSUS PRUDENT PLANNING

The 20 minutes is the legal floor, not a recommended plan. Standard practice adds a personal/operational margin on top (commonly 10-20 minutes additional, or a fixed extra quantity) to cover unforecast winds, ATC routing, and the fact that the 20-minute figure leaves no allowance for a single unexpected delay. Any such margin is policy, not regulation, and must not be presented as the legal requirement. Likewise, a Part 135 certificate holder's OpSpecs, an operator's fuel policy, or a rental agreement may require more than 20 minutes — comply with the most restrictive applicable requirement, but the federal VFR helicopter minimum remains 20 minutes.

6. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE RECORD

20 minutes at normal cruising fuel consumption, after the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather conditions — 14 CFR § 91.151(b) (Part 91) and § 135.209(b) (Part 135 helicopters); no day/night difference for rotorcraft.

not_answering.passage: (b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

| RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 | **RFC 8996** |
| Status it assigned to the RFCs that defined them (RFC 2246, RFC 4346) | **Historic** |

Governing quotation (abstract of RFC 8996):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

## 2. Document details for RFC 8996

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| RFC number | 8996 |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 |
| Also published as | BCP 195 (Best Current Practice) |
| Publication date | March 2021 |
| Stream | IETF |
| RFC 2026 category / maturity | Best Current Practice (not Standards Track) |
| Authors | Kathleen Moriarty (Center for Internet Security); Stephen Farrell (Trinity College Dublin) |
| Working group | TLS (IETF) |
| Source draft | draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate (revisions 00 through 12) |
| Updates | RFC 7525 (the earlier BCP 195, "Recommendations for Secure Use of TLS and DTLS") |
| Obsoletes | none |
| DOI | 10.17487/RFC8996 |

RFC 8996 shares BCP 195 with the document it updates: BCP numbers are series identifiers, so more than one RFC can carry the same BCP number. RFC 7525 was the original BCP 195; RFC 8996 was added to BCP 195 to record the deprecation. (RFC 9325 later obsoleted RFC 7525 and also sits in BCP 195; it does not reverse the deprecation.)

## 3. Which RFC defined which TLS version

The two documents reclassified by RFC 8996 are distinct, which is why the question asks about "the RFCs" (plural):

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Title | Original publication | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | **RFC 2246** | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 | January 1999 | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | **RFC 4346** | The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 | April 2006 | Historic |

Note the pre-existing obsoletion chain, which is separate from the Historic reclassification:

- RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) was obsoleted by RFC 4346.
- RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) was obsoleted by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2).
- RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) was obsoleted by RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3).

So RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 were already *Obsoleted* documents before 2021. "Obsoleted by" and "Historic" are two different fields in the RFC Editor's records: obsoletion says a newer specification supersedes the text; Historic says the protocol the document describes is no longer recommended for use. RFC 8996 added the second, and the RFC Editor's info pages for RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 now show `Status: Historic` alongside their obsoletion notes.

## 4. "Deprecated" versus "Historic" — why both words are in the answer

These are related but not interchangeable, and the question touches both:

- **Deprecation** is a protocol-level statement made *inside* RFC 8996: TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are no longer acceptable for use, and implementations are told not to negotiate them. This is a normative requirement, not merely advice.
- **Historic** is an RFC Editor / IETF status label (maturity level defined in RFC 2026) applied to a *document*. It is the administrative consequence of the deprecation: because the protocols are deprecated, the specifications that define them no longer represent recommended practice.

So RFC 8996 does two things at once, and the second question is specifically about the second thing: it deprecates the *protocol versions* and, "accordingly", moves the *defining documents* to Historic.

## 5. Normative content a practitioner should carry forward

RFC 8996 does not merely label the versions old; it sets requirements. The operative rules, in substance:

- TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 **MUST NOT** be used.
- Negotiation of TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 **MUST NOT** be permitted (i.e. do not offer them, do not accept them, do not fall back to them).
- Because RFC 8996 is a BCP, these are IETF-wide operational requirements for IETF protocols that use TLS, not a per-implementation suggestion.

Practical consequences that follow directly from the MUST NOTs:

- Remove TLS 1.0/1.1 from cipher-suite and protocol-version configuration; set minimum protocol version to TLS 1.2 (or 1.3 where supported).
- Disable downgrade/fallback paths that could re-enable 1.0/1.1; a client that offers 1.0/1.1 and a server that accepts it are both non-conformant with BCP 195.
- Expect interoperability failures with legacy peers to be resolved by upgrading the peer, not by re-enabling the deprecated versions.
- Audit for the specific version constants in libraries (e.g. `TLSv1`, `TLSv1_1` in OpenSSL-family APIs, `SslProtocols.Tls`/`Tls11` in .NET, `PROTOCOL_TLSv1` in Python's `ssl` module) since defaults in older library versions may still permit them.

## 6. Process note (how the status change happened)

RFC 8996 is an IETF-stream document. It went through the TLS working group, IETF Last Call, and IESG review, and was approved as a Best Current Practice. The reclassification of RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 to Historic was approved as part of that same IESG action and recorded by the RFC Editor; it was not a separate RFC and there is no separate "move to Historic" document to cite. This is the standard route for retiring a protocol version: a new document states the deprecation and requests the status change, and the RFC Editor's metadata is updated accordingly.

The closest precedent in the same area is RFC 7568, "Deprecating Secure Sockets Layer Version 3.0", which performed the same function for SSLv3. RFC 8996 is the TLS 1.0/1.1 analogue.

## 7. Caveats and things this answer deliberately does not claim

- The answer is about **IETF** action. Browser vendors and other organizations independently removed TLS 1.0/1.1 support on their own schedules; those announcements are not the RFC and are not what the question asks for.
- Earlier SSL specifications (SSLv2, SSLv3) are out of scope; they were deprecated by other documents.
- RFC 8996 deprecates the protocol versions, not the *implementations*; a library may still contain TLS 1.0 code while being configured to refuse it.
- Later IETF work (notably RFC 9325, BCP 195, November 2022, which obsoletes RFC 7525) restates TLS usage recommendations but does not un-deprecate TLS 1.0 or 1.1. Nothing in the authoritative record contradicts RFC 8996 on this point.

## 8. One-line answer for a changelog or ticket

> TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 were deprecated by **RFC 8996** (BCP 195, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", March 2021), which moved the defining documents **RFC 2246** (TLS 1.0) and **RFC 4346** (TLS 1.1) to **Historic** status and requires that neither version be used or negotiated.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

KEY ATTRIBUTES
- Figure: $184,500 per worker, per year.
- Tax year: wages paid / self-employment income earned in calendar year 2026 (Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2026).
- Scope: OASDI only (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance). It is simultaneously the contribution base (taxable-max side) and the benefit base (the level up to which earnings count toward a benefit computation).
- Prior year: $176,100 for 2025. Change: +$8,400, i.e. +4.77% (8,400 / 176,100 = 0.04770).
- Authority: Social Security Act automatic-adjustment mechanism (annual determination of the contribution and benefit base, tied to the national average wage index and rounded per statute), as published by the Social Security Administration in its contribution-and-benefit-base determination and 2026 COLA materials, and mirrored in IRS 2026 Schedule SE instructions.

WHAT IT IS NOT (common confusions to rule out)
- Not the Medicare (HI) wage base: hospital insurance tax applies to all wages with no cap; there is no 2026 Medicare maximum. The $184,500 ceiling applies to the 6.2% OASDI tax only. Additional Medicare Tax (0.9%) on wages over $200,000 (single) / $250,000 (MFJ) is a separate, uncapped-base surtax and does not change the OASDI base.
- Not a household, employer-aggregate, or lifetime limit: it is a per-individual, per-year cap applied by each employer to that individual's wages; multiple employers each apply the cap, with the excess recovered on the individual's return (Form 1040 excess Social Security withholding credit).
- Not the earnings-test exempt amounts, the taxable-maximum-related pension limits, or the Supplemental Security Income resource limits; those are separate 2026 thresholds that are announced alongside the base but are not the base.

DERIVED TAX FIGURES AT THE MAXIMUM (context only; the base itself is the answer)
- Employee OASDI: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00.
- Employer OASDI: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00.
- Combined OASDI: 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00.
- Self-employed (Schedule SE): 12.4% OASDI on self-employment income up to $184,500 = $22,878.00, plus 2.9% Medicare on all net self-employment earnings (no cap), plus any Additional Medicare Tax. The 6.2%/6.2%/12.4% rates are statutory and were assumed unchanged; only the base is adjusted annually.

SOURCES
1. SSA, 2026 COLA Fact Sheet — table row "Social Security (OASDI only) | $176,100 | $184,500" (2025 vs. 2026 maximum taxable earnings). https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html
2. IRS, 2026 Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040): "For 2026, the maximum amount of self-employment income subject to social security tax is $184,500." https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1040sse--2026.pdf
3. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base determination and table: https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/cola/cbbdet.html and https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/COLA/cbb.html

USAGE NOTE FOR PAYROLL/ENGINEERING IMPLEMENTATION
Set the 2026 OASDI wage-base parameter to 184500.00 (USD). Apply it as a year-to-date cumulative cap on OASDI-taxable wages per employee per calendar year; do not apply it to Medicare wages. Reset the accumulator at the start of the 2026 tax year and at any mid-year rehire only if the employee's YTD OASDI wages for 2026 have not already been exhausted by a prior employer (standard practice: carry YTD where known, otherwise let the employee claim the excess-withholding credit).

verdict.summary:
## Answer

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for tax year 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is **$24,500**.

This is the statutory cap under IRC §402(g)(1), as adjusted for cost of living. It is the maximum amount an employee may elect to defer for 2026 across all 401(k) plans in which the employee participates, and it is subject to the statutory override that the limit cannot exceed 100% of the employee's compensation — i.e., the operative limit is **the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of compensation**.

## Authority

- IRC §402(g)(1) — the annual elective deferral limitation, indexed for cost-of-living adjustments under §402(g)(4).
- IRS, *Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits*: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS, *Retirement topics — Contributions*: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."
- IRS, *COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions*: for 2026, the detailed guidance is **Notice 2025-67**, published in IRB 2025-49, page 761. Notice 2025-67 is the controlling annual COLA notice and should be cited as the primary source in any plan communication, SPD, or payroll configuration record.

## Scope — what this figure is and is not

| Attribute | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Tax year | Calendar year 2026 |
| Character of limit | Employee elective deferrals only (§402(g)) |
| Pre- or post-catch-up | **Pre-catch-up**; the age-based catch-up is a separate, additive limit |
| Roth vs. traditional | Both count against the same $24,500; designated Roth deferrals are not a separate bucket |
| Per plan or per person | Per individual, aggregated across all plans of all employers for the year; not per plan, per employer, or per payroll provider |
| Employer contributions | Not counted here; match, profit sharing, and forfeitures are governed by the separate §415(c) annual additions limit |
| Plan-level caps | A plan document may impose a lower cap or a percentage-of-pay cap; the statutory figure is a ceiling, not a floor |

Explicitly **out of scope** for this answer, and deliberately not quantified here: the age-50-plus catch-up amount, the enhanced catch-up for ages 60–63 under SECURE 2.0 §109, the §415(c) total annual additions limit, the §401(a)(17) compensation cap, and the highly compensated employee thresholds. Each has its own 2026 figure in Notice 2025-67 and must be read from that notice directly rather than inferred from the $24,500 figure above.

## How to apply it

1. **Payroll configuration.** Set the 2026 pre-tax plus Roth deferral cap at $24,500 per employee for the plan year, applied to the employee's aggregate deferrals, not per pay cycle or per plan code. Where an employee participates in more than one plan (e.g., a prior employer earlier in the year), the employee is responsible for monitoring the aggregate; the plan's own system cap is not a safe harbor for the §402(g) aggregation rule.
2. **Compensation test.** Before treating $24,500 as available in full, confirm the employee's §402(g)-eligible compensation for 2026 will reach $24,500. Below that level, the limit is 100% of compensation.
3. **Excess deferrals.** Amounts deferred above the limit are excess deferrals under §402(g)(2) and must be distributed, with allocable income, no later than April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation; this is an operational obligation that follows from the figure, not a separate limit.
4. **Documentation.** Cite Notice 2025-67 (IRB 2025-49, p. 761) as the source of record in the plan's 2026 limits documentation and in any participant-facing communication of the figure.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

In US general industry, the employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

Controlling provision: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (OSHA Walking-Working Surfaces, Subpart D).

This is the general-industry trigger. It is NOT the construction trigger (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1), 6 feet / 1.8 m). Using 6 ft in a general-industry setting, or 4 ft in construction, is a specification error.

1. REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim)

§1910.28(b)(1)(i): "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

§1910.28(b)(15) (Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed): "Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

2. WHAT THE TRIGGER ACTUALLY REQUIRES

Three elements must all be present before the duty attaches:
  a. An employee is on a walking-working surface — any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location (§1910.21(b)).
  b. That surface has an unprotected side or edge — no guardrail, no equivalent barrier.
  c. The surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

The threshold is INCLUSIVE. At exactly 4 ft 0 in (1.2 m) measured to the lower level, the duty attaches; it does not begin somewhere above 4 ft. Design and audit to the threshold, not to a rounded-up value.

3. HOW THE HEIGHT IS MEASURED

Measure the vertical distance from the walking-working surface itself to the lower level, taken at the unprotected side or edge. It is not measured from the employee's feet, from the employee's center of gravity, or from the top of a tool or load. Where the lower level is sloped or uneven, use the point directly below the edge that yields the greatest drop, because that is the fall exposure the employee actually has.

4. HOW THE EMPLOYER DISCHARGES THE DUTY

One or more of the following, per §1910.28(b)(1)(i)(A)–(C):
  - Guardrail system meeting §1910.29(b) (top rail 42 in ± 3 in / 1.1 m ± 0.08 m, midrail 21 in / 53 cm, 200 lb load criteria, etc.).
  - Safety net system meeting §1910.29(c).
  - Personal fall protection system meeting §1910.29(d) and §1910.140 — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning.

Supporting duties that travel with the trigger: §1910.30 (fall protection training before exposure, and retraining), §1910.29 (system specifications and inspection), and §1910.140 (personal fall protection equipment criteria).

5. EXCEPTIONS AND SURFACE-SPECIFIC PARAGRAPHS — CHECK BEFORE APPLYING THE 4 FT FIGURE

The 4 ft figure is the general rule and is expressly subject to "except as provided elsewhere in this section." The following must be checked for the specific surface:

  - Infeasibility / greater hazard. Where the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection is not feasible or would create a greater hazard, the employer must develop and implement a fall protection plan meeting §1910.29(k). This is a documented, plan-based exception — not a self-declared waiver.
  - Working side of a platform at a loading rack, loading dock, or teeming platform. Where the employer can demonstrate fall protection is not feasible, work may proceed without a fall protection system if the stated conditions of the provision are met (employee training, and the other conditions in the paragraph). Confirm the exact subparagraph lettering in the current eCFR text of §1910.28(b)(1) before citing it in an enforcement-facing document.
  - Low-slope roofs. Between 4 ft and less than 15 ft (4.6 m), a designated area combined with a fall protection plan is permitted as an alternative to guardrail/net/personal fall protection for certain roof work; other roof-work situations (e.g., within a specified distance of the edge) carry stricter requirements. Confirm current paragraph text.
  - Fixed ladders. §1910.28(b)(9) imposes a separate trigger: personal fall arrest system or ladder safety system (cage/well permitted on older ladders) at 24 ft (7.3 m) or more above a lower level, with phase-in dates for existing ladders.
  - Portable ladders. Climbing a portable ladder is not, by itself, a 4 ft walking-working-surface trigger; ladder condition and use requirements sit in §1910.23.
  - Dangerous equipment. Where an employee can fall into or onto dangerous equipment (e.g., vats, tanks, conveyors, machinery), protection is required regardless of height — the 4 ft threshold does not apply. Confirm the current paragraph.
  - Holes, ramps, runways, dockboards, hoist areas, pits, and similar enumerated surfaces each have their own paragraph in §1910.28(b); several carry the same 4 ft figure, but read the specific paragraph rather than assuming.

Where a surface-specific paragraph applies, it controls over the general 4 ft rule. Where none applies, §1910.28(b)(15) supplies the same 4 ft (1.2 m) figure.

6. SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

  - Federal OSHA general industry (29 CFR 1910, Subpart D) only.
  - State-plan states must be at least as effective as the federal standard; the federal 4 ft figure is the floor. Confirm the applicable state plan's adopted text before relying on 4 ft in a state-plan jurisdiction.
  - Other industry categories are governed by different subparts and different triggers: construction 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M — 6 ft (1.8 m) for the general case under §1926.501(b)(1); maritime (29 CFR 1915 shipyard, 1918 longshoring) and agriculture (29 CFR 1928) have their own fall-protection provisions. Do not carry the 4 ft figure into those settings without checking.

7. COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE (WHAT A SAFETY ENGINEER APPLIES)

  Step 1. Classify the work as general industry (1910), not construction (1926) or maritime/agriculture. Record the basis for the classification.
  Step 2. Identify each walking-working surface and each unprotected side or edge on it.
  Step 3. Measure the vertical drop from the surface to the lower level at each unprotected edge.
  Step 4. If any measurement is 4 ft (1.2 m) or greater, the duty attaches — select guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection, or document an infeasibility/greater-hazard determination and implement a §1910.29(k) fall protection plan.
  Step 5. Check the surface-specific paragraphs in §1910.28(b) (fixed ladders, low-slope roofs, dock/loading rack, holes, dangerous equipment) and apply the stricter or more specific requirement where it governs.
  Step 6. Train exposed employees under §1910.30 before exposure; inspect and maintain systems under §1910.29 and §1910.140.
  Step 7. Re-measure whenever the surface, the edge protection, or the lower level changes (new equipment, excavation, mezzanine modification, removed guardrail section).

8. COMMON APPLICATION ERRORS TO AVOID

  - Applying the 6 ft (1.8 m) construction trigger in a general-industry plant.
  - Treating 4 ft as "more than 4 ft" and leaving 4 ft 0 in to 4 ft 11 in edges unprotected.
  - Measuring from the employee's feet or from a platform's handrail instead of from the walking-working surface to the lower level.
  - Relying on an infeasibility exception without the written §1910.29(k) fall protection plan.
  - Assuming one paragraph of §1910.28(b) covers every surface on the site; the enumerated surfaces each have their own paragraph.

9. SOURCE AND VERIFICATION NOTE

The 4 ft (1.2 m) figure and the three protection options are quoted verbatim from the current eCFR text of 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) and §1910.28(b)(15). Subparagraph lettering for the infeasibility, loading-dock/teeming-platform, low-slope-roof, fixed-ladder, and dangerous-equipment provisions should be re-confirmed against the current eCFR text of §1910.28 before being pinned into an enforcement-facing document; the underlying requirements described above are stable, but letter designations in Subpart D have been revised since the 2017 rulemaking.

(i) Guardrail systems;
(ii) Safety net systems; or
(iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

2. Whether it is Part 91 or Part 135 operations, since the reserve requirement differs

quotes.question_text: Whether the question concerns VFR specifically (which it states) or could include IFR planning
quotes.text: No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry, beyond the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing, reserve fuel sufficient to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed (Part 91) / normal cruising fuel consumption (Part 135), considering wind and forecast weather conditions.

Answer value: 20 minutes of flight time. There is no day/night split and no separate higher figure for helicopters.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

14 CFR 91.151(b) (Part 91, rotorcraft):
"No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Part 135 (commercial helicopter VFR):
"No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

FAA guidance confirms the same number for rotorcraft: "During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes" and AC 91-88 describes 91.151 as first point of intended landing "plus 20 minutes reserve fuel."

Citation note to verify before publication: the retrieved govinfo PDF for the Part 135 text is labeled sec135-203, whereas the Part 135 "VFR: Fuel supply" provision is conventionally numbered 135.209. The 20-minute requirement itself is not in doubt (both the Part 91 text and the FAA guidance independently establish it), but the Part 135 section number should be confirmed against the current eCFR before it is quoted in an operator document.

2. SCOPE — WHY THE ANSWER DOES NOT DEPEND ON THE OPEN VARIABLES

- Part 91 vs. Part 135: both rules set 20 minutes. The difference is wording only ("normal cruising speed" vs. "normal cruising fuel consumption") and the applicable part. So the unresolved operating-rule question does not change the value; it changes only which citation is primary.
- Day vs. night: 91.151(b) contains no day/night distinction for rotorcraft. The 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures in 91.151(a) apply to airplanes only. Night VFR in a helicopter therefore still requires 20 minutes.
- Passengers/cargo for hire: does not change the 20-minute figure; it may change whether Part 135 applies, and Part 135 imposes additional operational requirements (OpSpecs, manual, fuel policy), but not a different VFR reserve number for helicopters.
- VFR vs. IFR: the 20 minutes is the VFR figure. IFR fuel planning is a different provision (e.g., 91.167's 45 minutes for IFR) and is outside this answer. The question is expressly VFR.
- Remote/overwater: no additional federal fuel increment attaches to Part 91 helicopter VFR flight merely because the route is remote or overwater. Additional fuel may be required by an operator's manual/OpSpecs or prudent practice, but that is not the regulatory minimum asked for.
- Units: the regulation is time-based. Gallons/pounds are a derived quantity, computed below.

3. CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A QUANTITY

Reserve is defined in time, so the tank quantity is aircraft- and power-setting-specific:

  Reserve (gal) = FF_cruise (gal/hr) x (20 min / 60 min/hr) = FF_cruise / 3
  Reserve (lb)  = FF_cruise (lb/hr) / 3

Total fuel at start = fuel to first point of intended landing (taxi, start, climb, cruise with forecast wind, descent, approach) + Reserve.

Illustrative values (approximate published cruise fuel flows; use the specific aircraft's POH/RFMS and the planned cruise power setting):

  Helicopter (example)      Cruise FF (gal/hr)   Reserve (gal, 20 min)
  Robinson R22              8-9                 2.7-3.0
  Robinson R44              13-15               4.3-5.0
  Bell 206B JetRanger       25-27               8.3-9.0
  Bell 407                  28-30               9.3-10.0
  Airbus H125 (AS350)       35-40               11.7-13.3

Worked example: R44 planned at 14 gal/hr cruise. Reserve = 14 / 3 = 4.7 gal. If the leg to the first point of intended landing is planned at 1.6 hr, that leg consumes 1.6 x 14 = 22.4 gal, so the aircraft must begin the flight with at least 22.4 + 4.7 = 27.1 gal of usable fuel.

4. PLANNING PROCEDURE

Step 1. Identify the operating rule (Part 91 or Part 135) to select the citation; the reserve value is 20 minutes either way.
Step 2. Determine the first point of intended landing. Note that the rule keys to the FIRST point of intended landing, not the final destination: on a multi-leg flight, each departure must independently satisfy the rule, and a planned refueling stop does not let you arrive at that stop inside the reserve.
Step 3. Compute leg fuel to that first point using forecast wind and forecast temperature/weather (the rule requires considering wind and forecast weather).
Step 4. Compute the reserve as 20 minutes at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption — not hover flow, not maximum-range flow, not idle flow.
Step 5. Sum leg fuel + reserve; add taxi/start/climb and any ATC/approach allowance the operator's policy requires; compare to usable fuel (confirm unusable fuel is excluded from the usable figure).
Step 6. If total required exceeds usable fuel, shorten the leg or add a fuel stop — do not reduce the 20-minute reserve.
Step 7. For Part 135, confirm the operator's manual/OpSpecs fuel policy; where it exceeds 20 minutes, the higher figure governs the operation.

5. COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST

- Applying the airplane 30-minute day / 45-minute night reserve to a helicopter.
- Applying the 45-minute IFR reserve to a VFR helicopter flight.
- Treating the reserve as a fixed gallon quantity independent of power setting or aircraft type.
- Planning to land at the first intended landing point with the reserve already consumed.
- Reading "20 minutes" as an operational target rather than a minimum; the regulatory floor is not a planning goal, and operators commonly plan more.

verdict.summary:
# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

## Short answers

1. **Deprecating RFC:** **RFC 8996**, *"Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1"* (IETF, published as **BCP 195**).
2. **Status given to the defining RFCs:** **Historic**. RFC 2246 (which defined TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (which defined TLS 1.1) were both moved to Historic status.

## The deprecating document

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| RFC number | 8996 |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 |
| Document stream / class | IETF, Best Current Practice (**BCP 195**) |
| Action taken | Formally deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 |
| Protocols deprecated | TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 |
| Defining documents affected | RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0), RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) |
| Status assigned to those documents | **Historic** |

## The status change, stated precisely

RFC 8996's abstract states, verbatim:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Two things are worth separating, because they are easy to conflate:

- **The protocol versions** (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) are what get deprecated.
- **The documents that define them** (RFC 2246, RFC 4346) are what get the status change: each is now an **Historic** RFC rather than a Standards-Track (Proposed Standard) RFC.

So the answer to "what status did it give them" is the RFC status category **Historic**, applied to both RFC 2246 and RFC 4346.

## Mapping of defining documents

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Title | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | RFC 2246 | The TLS Protocol Version 1.0 | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | RFC 4346 | The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1 | Historic |

## What the deprecation does and does not mean

- **It is a normative prohibition, not just advice.** RFC 8996 states that TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 **MUST NOT** be used, and that negotiation of those protocol versions **MUST NOT** be permitted. This operational requirement is a separate statement from the status change applied to the defining documents; both appear in RFC 8996, but they answer different questions.
- **Historic does not mean deleted.** RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 remain published and retrievable from the RFC Editor for reference and historical accuracy; the status label signals they are not the current specification and should not be implemented for new work.
- **Scope is limited.** Only TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are deprecated. TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) and TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) are outside the scope of RFC 8996 and are unaffected by it.
- **Practical consequence for implementers and operators:** disable TLS 1.0/1.1 in server and client configuration, remove them from cipher-suite/version negotiation ranges, and treat any peer that requires them as non-compliant with current best practice (BCP 195).

## Sources

- RFC Editor information page for RFC 8996 — https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ (abstract quoted above; fetched 2026-11-16T06:43:34Z, sha256 2f3c7e0ff7cb)
- IETF Datatracker record for RFC 8996 — https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/
- Datatracker draft history (draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate) — https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate/12/
- RFC 8996 document history — https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/

## Confidence and limits

Both answers rest on a direct quotation of the RFC Editor's own abstract for RFC 8996, i.e., the authoritative record for the document's status action. No inference or reconstruction was needed, and no aspect of either ask is blocked.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

This is the maximum amount of an individual's earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax for remuneration paid in 2026 and for self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026.

AUTHORITY AND VERIFICATION

- Federal Register notice establishing the 2026 figure: "The OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026." (Federal Register, document 2025-19763, published 2025-11-03.)
- SSA Publication 05-10003 (Social Security taxes), 2026 column: employee/employer each "6.2% on earnings up to $184,500"; self-employed "12.4% on earnings up to $184,500." Prior-year column shows $176,100 for 2025.
- SSA Contribution and Benefit Base table: https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html and determination detail at https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html.

The two sources agree exactly on the amount and on the year it applies to, so no reconciliation is required.

SCOPE NOTES (what the figure is and is not)

1. The base is the OASDI taxable maximum only. The Medicare (HI) tax has no earnings cap; the additional Medicare tax of 0.9% on wages above $200,000 (single) / $250,000 (joint) is a separate provision and is not part of this base.
2. The base is a per-individual annual limit, not per employer and not per household. An individual with multiple employers in 2026 can have excess OASDI withheld across employers and claim it as a credit on Form 1040.
3. The same figure is the maximum amount of 2026 earnings creditable toward Social Security benefit computation (it is simultaneously the contribution base and the benefit base).
4. Self-employed individuals apply the base to net earnings from self-employment computed on Schedule SE; the 12.4% OASDI rate applies only up to $184,500 of that net amount, with the HI portion (2.9%, plus 0.9% additional Medicare tax where applicable) continuing above it.

COMPANION FIGURES (derived directly from the base, shown for completeness)

- Employee maximum annual OASDI tax: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00
- Employer maximum annual OASDI tax: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00
- Combined employee + employer maximum: $22,878.00
- Self-employed maximum annual OASDI tax: 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00
- Increase over the 2025 base of $176,100: $8,400 (4.77%)

USAGE NOTE

The figure is set annually by SSA under the automatic adjustment provisions of the Social Security Act and is announced in the fall preceding the tax year. The $184,500 amount above is the published determination for 2026; re-verify against https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html before relying on it in a filing, since the agency periodically reissues corrected notices.

results.unit: USD per year (maximum earnings per individual subject to OASDI)

verdict.summary:
# 2026 401(k) Elective Deferral Limit (Pre-Catch-Up)

## Answer

**$24,500.**

For the 2026 calendar year, an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan are capped at **$24,500**, before any catch-up contribution is added. This is the standard participant limit under Internal Revenue Code §402(g), as adjusted annually for cost of living and as published by the IRS for 2026.

## Authority and source language

The figure is the IRS's own published 2026 number, not an estimate derived from indexing methodology. Three IRS sources state it:

1. **IRS Publication 560 (Retirement Plans for Small Business):** "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $23,500 for 2025 and increases to $24,500 for 2026."
2. **IRS Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits:** "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: - $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
3. **IRS Retirement Topics — Catch-Up Contributions:** "Elective deferrals are not treated as catch-up contributions until they exceed the limit of $24,500 in 2026 or the ADP test limit of section 401(k)(3) or the plan limit (if any)."

The annual adjustment is issued in IRS cost-of-living guidance for the year (the 2026 figures appear in IRS Notice 2025-67) and is reflected on the IRS retirement-plan limits pages and in Publication 560. Because the official 2026 figure has been published, no indexing calculation is required or appropriate here.

## What the $24,500 does and does not include

- **Traditional and Roth deferrals combined.** The §402(g) limit is a single employee-level cap that applies to the employee's elective deferrals in the aggregate across traditional (pre-tax) and designated Roth deferrals in 401(k) plans of the same employer. Designating a deferral as Roth does not create additional room.
- **Excludes catch-up contributions.** Amounts treated as catch-up contributions under IRC §414(v) are not counted against the §402(g) limit. Catch-up eligibility and the catch-up dollar limit are set separately by the IRS for 2026 and are outside the scope of this question. Note that the catch-up limit is a separate, additional amount — it does not change the $24,500 base figure.
- **Aggregated across plans of the same employer.** If an employee participates in more than one 401(k) plan of the same employer (or, in the case of a controlled group, plans of related employers), the $24,500 applies once to the employee in total, not once per plan.
- **Not the same as other limits.** The $24,500 is distinct from: the §415(c) limit on total annual additions (employee deferrals plus employer contributions plus forfeitures); the §401(a)(17) compensation limit used to measure contributions; the ADP/ACP nondiscrimination test limits; and the separate elective deferral limit that applies to SIMPLE 401(k) plans. Those are governed by different Code sections and are published as separate figures. Do not substitute any of them for the §402(g) amount.
- **Subject to further cost-of-living adjustment.** The IRS describes the figure as "subject to cost-of-living adjustments," meaning it is fixed at $24,500 for 2026 only and may change in later years.

## Practical notes for plan administration

- **A plan may impose a lower limit.** The statutory $24,500 is a ceiling, not a guarantee. The plan document, an employer's matching-contribution design, or the ADP test under §401(k)(3) can reduce how much a given highly compensated employee may actually defer. The IRS's own catch-up language acknowledges this by referring to "the limit of $24,500 in 2026 **or** the ADP test limit of section 401(k)(3) **or** the plan limit (if any)." Where a plan-level or testing limit is lower, the lower limit controls for that participant; the $24,500 remains the statutory maximum.
- **Payroll system configuration.** Set the §402(g) deferral cap for the 2026 plan year at $24,500 per participant, measured across all 401(k) plans of the employer, with catch-up contributions tracked in a separate bucket so they are not counted against this cap. Confirm the 2025 cap ($23,500) is retired at the plan-year boundary so no participant is capped at the prior-year figure.
- **Year of deferral, not year of deposit.** The limit is applied to the year in which the deferral is made (i.e., the year it is withheld from wages), not the year it is deposited to the trust, subject to the DOL deposit-timing rules.

## Scope caveat

This answer is the **U.S. federal statutory limit** for 401(k) elective deferrals for the 2026 calendar year. It does not address state-law requirements, non-U.S. plans, collectively bargained or governmental plan variations, or plan-specific limits, none of which are determined by §402(g) and none of which are covered by the sources above.

CURRENT U.S. NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5

ANSWER (primary, health-based standards)
- Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter)
- 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter)

Both are primary (health-based) standards. They are codified at 40 CFR §50.18 (National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5). The 9.0 µg/m³ annual level was established by EPA's 2024 final rule strengthening the PM NAAQS; the 35 µg/m³ 24-hour level was retained unchanged by that same rule.

1. SOURCE LANGUAGE (verbatim, EPA)
- Annual: "EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science." (EPA, NAAQS for PM / PM2.5 rulemaking materials; PM NAAQS overview, Feb 2024)
- 24-hour: "EPA is retaining the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard, with its level of 35 µg/m3." (EPA, PM NAAQS monitoring fact sheet, Feb 2024)
Sources of record for the current levels: https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/national-ambient-air-quality-standards-naaqs-pm ; https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-02/pm-naaqs-overview.pdf ; https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-02/pm-naaqs-monitoring-fact-sheet.pdf ; designations page: https://www.epa.gov/particle-pollution-designations/particle-pollution-designations-2024-revised-annual-pm25-naaqs

2. STATISTICAL FORM OF EACH STANDARD (the level alone is misread without this)
- Annual primary standard (9.0 µg/m³): the annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 consecutive years, evaluated at each monitoring site. A site meets the standard when the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³. Annual means are rounded to one decimal place (hence "9.0").
- 24-hour primary standard (35 µg/m³): the 98th percentile of 24-hour average concentrations, averaged over 3 consecutive years, evaluated at each monitoring site. A site meets the standard when the 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour values is ≤ 35 µg/m³. 24-hour values are rounded to the nearest 1 µg/m³ (hence "35"). 24-hour averages are computed from midnight-to-midnight sampling days.
- Designations and compliance determinations are made against these forms, not against single-day or single-year maxima.

3. "CURRENT" — PINNING THE VERSION
- As of the source set used here (pages fetched 2026-11-16), the operative levels are annual 9.0 µg/m³ and 24-hour 35 µg/m³, from the 2024 final rule (signed February 7, 2024; published in the Federal Register in March 2024; effective May 6, 2024).
- Caveat a practitioner should carry: PM2.5 NAAQS are periodically reviewed. Before relying on these numbers in a regulatory submittal, confirm no later final rule has revised them, by checking the current text of 40 CFR §50.18 and EPA's NAAQS table. Nothing in the grounding indicates a revision after the 2024 rule.

4. SUPERSEDED VALUES — DO NOT USE (common source of error)
- Annual: 15.0 µg/m³ (1997 and 2006 standards) — superseded; 12.0 µg/m³ (2012 standard) — superseded by the 2024 rule.
- 24-hour: 65 µg/m³ (1997 standard) — superseded by the 2006 rule, which set 35 µg/m³; 35 µg/m³ has been retained since 2006 through the 2012 and 2024 reviews.

5. UNITS AND SCOPE NOTES
- Units are µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter) for both standards. No ppm-equivalent form is part of the NAAQS; do not convert.
- The request asks for primary standards. For completeness only, and explicitly labeled as SECONDARY (welfare-based, not the answer to this request): the secondary PM2.5 standards are an annual standard of 15.0 µg/m³ (3-year average of annual means) and a 24-hour standard of 35 µg/m³ (3-year average of 98th percentiles), at 40 CFR §50.19. The secondary annual 15.0 µg/m³ figure must not be confused with the primary annual answer of 9.0 µg/m³.
- These are standard levels, not monitored ambient concentrations and not designations status; no monitoring data are implied.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Under US federal OSHA general industry standards, the trigger height is 4 feet (1.2 m).

An employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling. 4 feet (1.2 m) is the answer; anything below 4 feet does not trigger the 1910.28(b)(1) duty (though other duties, such as housekeeping or guarding holes, may still apply).

GOVERNING CITATION

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) - Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection (General industry, Subpart D, Walking-Working Surfaces).

Quoted text: "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

WHAT THE DUTY REQUIRES ONCE 4 FEET IS REACHED

At or above the 4-foot trigger, the employer must provide at least one of:
- Guardrail systems meeting 29 CFR 1910.29(b);
- Safety net systems meeting 29 CFR 1910.29(c); or
- Personal fall protection systems (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning) meeting 29 CFR 1910.140, with training under 29 CFR 1910.30.

HOW THE HEIGHT IS MEASURED

The measurement is the vertical distance from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level below - not the distance from the employee's body or center of gravity to the lower level. A surface 3 feet 11 inches above the floor below is not covered by the 4-foot trigger; a surface 4 feet above it is.

SCOPE NOTES

1. General industry vs. construction. The 4-foot figure is the general industry figure. Construction work covered by 29 CFR Part 1926 has a different trigger: 6 feet under 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) for unprotected sides and edges. Do not use 6 feet for general industry work; the requester correctly excluded construction.

2. "Except as provided elsewhere in this section." The 4-foot rule is the default and is the correct answer to the question as asked. Specific provisions inside 1910.28(b)(1) can change what must be provided, and a practitioner should screen for them before finalizing a compliance decision:
- Loading rack, loading dock, or teeming platform: where the employer can demonstrate that use of fall protection systems is not feasible on the working side of the platform, the work may be done without a fall protection system, provided the conditions of that provision are met. This relieves the method requirement; it does not change the 4-foot figure.
- Dockboards: each employee on a dockboard must be protected from falling 4 feet (1.2 m) or more to a lower level by a guardrail system or handrails. Guardrails/handrails are not required only when ALL THREE of the following are satisfied: (A) the dockboards are used solely for materials-handling operations using motorized equipment; (B) the employees engaged in those operations are not exposed to fall hazards greater than 10 feet (3 m); and (C) those employees have been trained in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.30. Note carefully that the 10-foot figure here is a ceiling on permitted fall-hazard exposure under a narrow relaxation of the guardrail requirement - it is NOT a fall-protection trigger height. The trigger for dockboards remains 4 feet.

3. Version of the rule. This reflects the current, in-force text of 1910.28, which has been the general industry walking-working-surfaces fall protection rule since the 2016 Walking-Working Surfaces final rule took effect on January 17, 2017 (81 FR 82494). The 4-foot threshold is consistent with the pre-2017 general industry guardrail requirement for open-sided floors, so the answer is stable across the rule change.

4. State-plan states. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard and in practice adopt the 4-foot trigger, but a State Plan may have stricter or additional requirements for specific industries. If the workplace is in a State Plan state, confirm against the state's adopted text.

5. Employer duty. The obligation runs to the employer ("the employer must ensure"), not to the employee.

HOW TO APPLY - QUICK PROCEDURE

Step 1. Identify each walking-working surface (any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location).
Step 2. For each, identify sides or edges that lack a guardrail system or other compliant protection.
Step 3. Measure the vertical distance from that surface to the lower level.
Step 4. If the distance is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more, the duty attaches: select and implement guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection, and train exposed employees under 1910.30.
Step 5. Screen for the 1910.28(b)(1) exceptions (loading dock/loading rack/teeming platform infeasibility; dockboard materials-handling conditions) before relying on any relaxation, and document the basis, including the training record and the measured fall-hazard exposure where the dockboard exception is used.

VERIFICATION POINT

Confirm the quoted text against the current eCFR at 29 CFR 1910.28 before adopting it in a written compliance program, and confirm the internal subparagraph designation used in your citation style; the 4-foot (1.2 m) trigger itself is directly supported by the quoted regulatory text.
Regulatory fuel reserve requirement for VFR flight

asks.quote: How much reserve fuel must a helicopter carry to begin a VFR flight in the US, beyond the fuel to reach the first point of intended landing?

findings.question: How much reserve fuel must a helicopter carry to begin a VFR flight in the US, beyond the fuel to reach the first point of intended landing?

quotes.question_text: How much reserve fuel must a helicopter carry to begin a VFR flight in the US, beyond the fuel to reach the first point of intended landing?
quotes.text: (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry fuel sufficient to fly to the first point of intended landing and then continue for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. The reserve beyond the first point of intended landing is therefore 20 minutes of fuel, not a fixed quantity of gallons or pounds.

GOVERNING STANDARD

14 CFR § 91.151(b), quoted verbatim from eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 a8a7e00944fb):

"(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

This is the rotorcraft-specific paragraph. It is the complete Part 91 VFR fuel-reserve requirement for helicopters; there is no additional Part 91 day/night, terrain, or overwater increment layered on top of it for rotorcraft.

SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY

1. Operation: Part 91 general operating rules, U.S.-registered rotorcraft, VFR. If the flight is conducted under Part 135, the parallel helicopter VFR rule is § 135.209(b) and is also 20 minutes; the Part 91 answer does not change for a Part 91 flight.
2. Rule structure: § 91.151 is a pre-flight prohibition — it bars *beginning* a flight without the required fuel. It is not a landing-fuel requirement and it does not by itself make an in-flight fuel state unlawful. (Independent exposure still exists under § 91.13, careless/reckless operation, and under § 91.3 responsibility of the pilot in command.)
3. No destination alternate credit: the rule names only "the first point of intended landing." Unlike the IFR reserve in § 91.167, no alternate-airport allowance is built into the VFR rotorcraft reserve, and none may be subtracted from the 20 minutes.
4. Conditions baked into the calculation: the rule requires the assessment to consider *wind and forecast weather conditions*. The 20 minutes is not a flat 20 minutes of still-air time; it must be evaluated against forecast winds and conditions on the route.
5. "Normal cruising speed": the verified text conditions the reserve on normal cruising speed (not on maximum range speed, and not on an economy cruise chosen to shrink the reserve). Practically, the planner converts the 20 minutes into fuel using the burn rate at the speed the aircraft will actually be flown at in normal cruise.
6. Airplanes are different: § 91.151(a) sets 30 minutes (day VFR) and 45 minutes (night VFR) for airplanes. Those figures do not apply to helicopters and must not be substituted for the 20-minute rotorcraft value.
7. IFR is different: § 91.167 sets a 45-minute reserve after the approach/alternate for IFR. Not applicable to a VFR flight.

CONVERSION TO A FUEL QUANTITY (PROCEDURE)

Step 1. Establish normal cruising speed and the corresponding fuel burn rate for the specific helicopter, from the flight manual / pilot's operating handbook, for the planned altitude and temperature.
Step 2. Reserve fuel = burn rate (unit/hour) × (20 / 60) = burn rate × 0.3333.
Step 3. Required fuel at brake release = trip fuel to first point of intended landing (adjusted for forecast wind) + reserve fuel from Step 2 + taxi/takeoff/climb allowance + any operator or PIC additive policy.
Step 4. Confirm the result is usable fuel (not total tank capacity) and that the resulting weight is within maximum gross weight and CG limits.

Worked illustrations (burn rates are round-number placeholders for arithmetic only — substitute POH values):
- 16 gal/h normal cruise → 16 × 0.3333 = 5.3 gal reserve.
- 30 gal/h normal cruise → 30 × 0.3333 = 10.0 gal reserve.
- 40 gal/h normal cruise → 40 × 0.3333 = 13.3 gal reserve.
Each of these is a representation of the same 20-minute requirement, not a separate or higher minimum.

WHAT THE 20 MINUTES DOES NOT COVER

- It is a regulatory floor, not a safe-planning target. Operators frequently impose a higher company reserve; a Part 135 certificate holder's operations specifications or manual may do so, and those higher figures govern that operation.
- It does not account for holding, airborne re-planning, or unforecast headwinds beyond what the required wind/forecast-weather consideration captures.
- It does not relieve the pilot of the § 91.3 in-flight responsibility to land when further flight is unwise, nor of weight-and-balance limits, since reserve fuel is carried weight at brake release.

PRECISION NOTE ON SOURCE WORDING

A paraphrased secondary description of the rule refers to "normal cruising fuel consumption." The verified regulatory text of § 91.151(b) reads "assuming normal cruising speed." The regulation's own wording governs: the reserve is expressed as 20 minutes of flight time at normal cruising speed, converted to fuel by the aircraft's burn rate. Either way, the stated reserve is 20 minutes.
Info request about which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0/1.1 and the status it assigned to the defining RFCs.

asks.quote: Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1,
what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?

findings.question: Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, and what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?

quotes.question_text: Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, and what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?
quotes.text: This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status.

verdict.summary:
# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1

## Answers

**1. Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1?**

**RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (IETF; published March 2021; authors K. Moriarty and S. Farrell).

**2. What status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?**

**Historic.** RFC 8996 moves **RFC 2246** (which defined TLS 1.0) and **RFC 4346** (which defined TLS 1.1) to Historic status.

## Primary-source text

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction), states verbatim:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html

## Document map

| Document | Role | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 2246 | Defined TLS 1.0 | **Historic** (moved by RFC 8996) |
| RFC 4346 | Defined TLS 1.1 | **Historic** (moved by RFC 8996) |
| RFC 5246 | Defined TLS 1.2 | Unchanged by RFC 8996 — not moved to Historic |
| RFC 8446 | Defines TLS 1.3 | Unaffected |
| RFC 8996 | Deprecates TLS 1.0 and 1.1 | The deprecating document |

## Precision notes (what the answer does and does not claim)

- **"Status" here means the RFC Editor / IETF document status category, not a verb in the prose.** RFC 8996 does not merely *say* the versions are deprecated; it causes the status field on RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 to read **Historic** in the RFC Editor's index. Both readings converge on the same label, which is why "Historic" is the correct answer under either interpretation.
- **"Moved to Historic" is not the same as "obsoleted by RFC 8996."** RFC 2246 was already obsoleted by RFC 4346, and RFC 4346 was already obsoleted by RFC 5246. RFC 8996's action is a status reclassification layered on top of that existing obsoletion chain, and it is the reclassification — not a new obsoletion — that produces the Historic label.
- **Scope is exactly two TLS documents.** RFC 8996 does not touch RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2). Anyone reading the answer as "all pre-1.3 TLS RFCs are Historic" would be over-reading it.
- **The same RFC also deprecates DTLS 1.0 (RFC 6347).** That is a separate protocol track bundled into the same document and is outside the scope of the question asked; it does not change either answer above.
- **Operative effect.** Beyond the status change, RFC 8996 directs that TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 not be used in protocols or implementations, and that fallback to these versions is prohibited.
- **Metadata caveat.** The deprecation sentence and the Historic status are quoted directly from the fetched RFC text. Header fields (exact publication date, BCP number, and the Updates/Obsoletes lists) should be read off the RFC's own header block or https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ if a citation requires them; they are not load-bearing for either answer.

## Verification procedure

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html and read Section 1 — confirm the quoted sentence naming RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 and the phrase "moved to Historic status."
2. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/ and https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346/ — confirm each shows **Status: Historic**.
3. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5246/ — confirm it is *not* Historic, which validates the scope note above.

## One-line citation

RFC 8996, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1*, March 2021 — deprecates TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) and moves both defining documents to Historic status.

verdict.summary:
# US Social Security contribution and benefit base for 2026

## Answer

**$184,500** — the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax in calendar year 2026, and simultaneously the maximum amount of earnings creditable for Social Security benefit-computation purposes.

This is the officially published figure, not a projection. SSA has already issued its 2026 automatic determinations, so the answer does not depend on estimating the national average wage index.

## Scope and definition

- The "contribution and benefit base" is defined by SSA as *the maximum amount of earnings taxable and creditable for benefit computation purposes*. It is the same figure used for the OASDI payroll tax and for the benefit formula — one number, not two.
- The base applies identically to FICA (employees/employers) and SECA (self-employed). No adjustment is needed between them.
- It applies to **OASDI only**. The Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) tax has **no wage cap** and is unaffected by this figure. SSA's 2026 table lists the two programs separately:

  | Program | 2026 taxable maximum |
  |---|---|
  | OASDI (Social Security) | $184,500 |
  | HI (Medicare) | No limit |

  Anyone who quotes a single "payroll tax cap" is quoting the OASDI figure; the 1.45% HI tax (plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above the statutory thresholds) continues on all wages above $184,500.

## Source and authority

- SSA, *Contribution and Benefit Base* determination page — "Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500."
- SSA, *Automatic Determinations* table — 2026 row shows the contribution and benefit base at 184,500.
- SSA, *Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026* — program table lists OASDI 184,500 / HI No limit.

Governing authority is the Social Security Act's automatic-adjustment mechanism, under which the base is derived from the national average wage index and rounded to the nearest $300 (note that $184,500 = 615 x $300, consistent with the statutory rounding).

## Derived figures (for payroll-system configuration)

| Item | Calculation | 2026 amount |
|---|---|---|
| OASDI taxable maximum | — | $184,500.00 |
| Employee OASDI rate | — | 6.2% |
| Employer OASDI rate | — | 6.2% |
| Maximum employee OASDI withholding | 184,500 x 0.062 | $11,439.00 |
| Maximum employer OASDI contribution | 184,500 x 0.062 | $11,439.00 |
| Combined maximum (employee + employer) | 184,500 x 0.124 | $22,878.00 |
| Maximum SECA OASDI liability (self-employed) | 184,500 x 0.124 | $22,878.00 |
| Medicare HI taxable maximum | — | No limit |

Withholding mechanics: once an employee's year-to-date OASDI wages reach $184,500, the 6.2% deduction stops for the remainder of the calendar year and resumes at zero on January 1, 2027 (at the then-current base). Excess OASDI withheld by an employer is refundable via the employee's Form 1040; a mid-year employer change can produce over-withholding that is likewise claimed on the return.

## Change from 2025

The 2025 base was $176,100. The 2026 base of $184,500 represents an increase of **$8,400** in the amount of earnings subject to OASDI tax. (The precise percentage growth is not asserted here because the base is a rounded function of the national average wage index, not a flat percentage uplift.)

## As-of note

Figure reflects SSA's published 2026 determinations as retrieved on 2026-11-16. Because the 2026 base has already been formally announced, no later SSA action will revise it; the next change takes effect for tax year 2027.
