verdict.summary: Regulatory safety compliance question about fall protection height

asks.quote: In general industry, not construction, at what height above a lower level must a US employer protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling?

findings.question: In general industry, not construction, at what height above a lower level must a US employer protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling?

quotes.question_text: In general industry, not construction, at what height above a lower level must a US employer protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling?
quotes.text:
Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
(A) Guardrail systems;
(B) Safety net systems; or
(C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

In general industry (not construction), a US employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

4 feet = 1.2 m.

GOVERNING CITATION

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — "Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection," OSHA general industry standard, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces).

Verbatim regulatory text:

"Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
(A) Guardrail systems;
(B) Safety net systems; or
(C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Source: eCFR, 29 CFR 1910.28 (https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.28), fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 8550c2c5b628; corroborated at https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.28 and the GovInfo CFR PDF (CFR-2022-title29-vol5, sec 1910-28).

HOW TO APPLY IT (practitioner notes)

1. Measurement. The 4 ft is measured from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level — not from the guardrail height, and not from the employee's center of gravity. A surface at exactly 4 ft 0 in is at the trigger; the rule reads "4 feet (1.2 m) or more." Below 4 ft, 1910.28(b)(1)(i) does not require fall protection (other duties, e.g., housekeeping under 1910.22 or hazard-communication, may still apply).

2. The "Except as provided elsewhere in this section" carve-out is operative, not boilerplate. 29 CFR 1910.28 contains task- and equipment-specific paragraphs (e.g., hoist areas, holes, ramps/runways/dockboards, stairways, and specific equipment and operations addressed later in the section). Where a more specific paragraph of 1910.28 governs the condition, read that paragraph; the general 4 ft trigger in (b)(1)(i) is the default that applies when no more specific provision controls. Do not quote "4 feet" alone in a fall-protection program without confirming no specific paragraph displaces it.

3. Acceptable protection once triggered. One or more of: guardrail system; safety net system; or personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning). Design/performance criteria for these systems are in 29 CFR 1910.29 (guardrails, safety nets, covers, designated areas, ladder safety, rope descent) and 29 CFR 1910.140 (personal fall protection systems). Representative hardware figures commonly cited alongside the 4 ft trigger: guardrail top rail 42 in ± 3 in, midrail approximately 21 in, guardrail capable of withstanding a 200 lb load applied in a downward or outward direction (1910.29(b)). These are criteria for the protective system, not a second duty threshold, and they do not alter the 4 ft value.

4. Scope. This is the federal general-industry rule (29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D). It is not the construction rule: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) sets a 6 ft trigger for construction work. If the work is construction, alteration, or repair, 1926 governs and the answer is 6 ft, not 4 ft. Mixed-site employers must classify the task correctly before choosing the threshold.

5. State-plan jurisdictions. Roughly half the states and two territories operate OSHA-approved state plans. A state plan must be at least as effective as federal OSHA, but may adopt different or additional requirements and may use different numeric triggers in its own general-industry walking-working surfaces standard. For a workplace in a state-plan state, verify against that state's plan text; the 4 ft figure above is the federal floor, not a guarantee of the state figure.

6. Currency. The 4 ft general-industry trigger is long-standing. It appeared in the predecessor provision, former 29 CFR 1910.23(c)(1) (open-sided floors and platforms 4 ft or more above the adjacent floor or ground), and was carried forward essentially unchanged into 1910.28(b)(1)(i) by the 2016 walking-working surfaces final rule (81 FR 82494, published Nov. 18, 2016; effective Jan. 17, 2017), which relocated the requirement from 1910.23 to 1910.28. An answer of 4 ft is therefore correct under both the pre-2017 and current federal general-industry standards; the citation differs by era.

COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID

- Answering 6 ft: that is the construction threshold (1926.501).
- Answering 4 ft while citing 1910.23: 1910.23 today covers ladders, not the general open-sided-edge duty; the citation should be 1910.28(b)(1)(i).
- Treating 4 ft as the trigger for every hazard in Subpart D: ladders, scaffolds, and certain other equipment have their own rules elsewhere in 1910.
- Applying 4 ft to a state-plan site without checking the state standard.

BOTTOM LINE

4 feet (1.2 m). Citation: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i), subject to the more specific provisions elsewhere in 1910.28 and to any stricter OSHA-approved state plan.
Regulatory fuel reserve question with safety-critical impact

asks.quote: How much reserve fuel must a helicopter carry to begin a VFR flight in the US, beyond the fuel to reach the first point of intended landing?

findings.question: Whether the flight is a plain civil helicopter VFR flight or one triggering a stricter rule (e.g., compensation/hire, night, or IFR-adjacent conditions) — this decides which reserve figure applies.

quotes.question_text: Whether the flight is a plain civil helicopter VFR flight or one triggering a stricter rule (e.g., compensation/hire, night, or IFR-adjacent conditions) — this decides which reserve figure applies.
quotes.text: (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

quotes.question_text: Whether the flight is a plain civil helicopter VFR flight or one triggering a stricter rule (e.g., compensation/hire, night, or IFR-adjacent conditions) — this decides which reserve figure applies.
quotes.text: (b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry fuel sufficient to fly to the first point of intended landing, and then — assuming normal cruising speed — to fly for at least 20 minutes beyond that point. Considering wind and forecast weather conditions. That is the whole of the regulatory reserve: 20 minutes at normal cruising speed.

Governing rule: 14 CFR § 91.151(b) — 'No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

Equivalent figure for compensated operations: 14 CFR § 135.209(b) imposes the same 20-minute helicopter VFR reserve on Part 135 helicopter operators ('...enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes').

WHAT THE ANSWER IS NOT

- Not 30 minutes. That is the airplane daytime VFR figure in § 91.151(a) and does not apply to rotorcraft.
- Not 45 minutes. That is the airplane nighttime VFR figure in § 91.151(a), and separately the IFR alternate fuel figure in § 91.167. Neither applies to a VFR helicopter.
- Not increased at night. § 91.151(b) draws no day/night distinction for rotorcraft; the 20 minutes is the same at night as by day.
- Not increased by carrying passengers or cargo for compensation, so far as the cited rules go — Part 135 helicopter VFR is also 20 minutes (§ 135.209(b)). Individual OpSpecs, Part 135 subpart requirements, or company manuals may add margin, but that is contractual/operational, not the regulatory minimum.
- Not an alternate-destination requirement. § 91.151(b) names only 'the first point of intended landing' plus 20 minutes. There is no VFR helicopter equivalent of the IFR 45-minute alternate rule. (If weather at the destination is not forecast VFR at the ETA, the flight cannot be launched VFR at all — that is a § 91.103/91.155 problem, not a fuel-reserve problem.)

HOW TO CONVERT 20 MINUTES INTO FUEL

Because the rule is time-based at normal cruising speed, the reserve is one-third of the hourly fuel consumption at normal cruise:

  Reserve (lb) = Cruise burn (lb/hr) ÷ 3
  Reserve (gal) = Cruise burn (gal/hr) ÷ 3

Worked example A — turbine helicopter, Jet A at 6.7 lb/gal, cruise burn 160 lb/hr (≈23.9 gal/hr):
  Reserve = 160 ÷ 3 = 53.3 lb = 53.3 ÷ 6.7 = 7.96 gal ≈ 8.0 gal.
  Cross-check: 23.9 gal/hr ÷ 3 = 8.0 gal. Agrees.

Worked example B — piston helicopter, avgas at 6.0 lb/gal, cruise burn 120 lb/hr (= 20 gal/hr):
  Reserve = 120 ÷ 3 = 40 lb = 40 ÷ 6 = 6.7 gal.
  Cross-check: 20 gal/hr ÷ 3 = 6.7 gal. Agrees.

Total fuel on board at brake release therefore = trip fuel to first point of intended landing (computed with forecast wind and temperature, using the aircraft's performance data at the planned weight and cruise power) + the 20-minute reserve + any fuel the operator separately requires (taxi, run-up, climb allowance, approach/missed approach, ATC delay, personal/company margin). The 20 minutes is the floor on the last of these, not the total.

PRACTICAL NOTES FOR THE PILOT

1. The reserve is measured in time at normal cruising speed, so a headwind does not stretch the reserve itself — it stretches the trip fuel to the first landing point, which must be computed with wind and forecast weather as the rule requires.
2. 'Enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing' means usable fuel, at the planned power setting and altitude, at the planned gross weight, using the fuel-flow figures from the rotorcraft flight manual — not tank capacity.
3. Because 20 minutes is a thin margin, most operators and many CFIs plan to a personal minimum well above it (commonly 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night, borrowed from the airplane rule as a self-imposed policy). Those figures are best practice and exceed the legal minimum; they are not the regulation and must not be quoted as such.
4. § 91.103 requires the pilot to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight before departure, including fuel requirements — the 20-minute figure is the regulatory floor that preflight planning must clear.

APPLICABILITY CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH THE 20-MINUTE ANSWER HOLDS

- Civil helicopter operation in the United States under 14 CFR Part 91 (general operating and flight rules).
- Flight conducted under VFR; the reserve applies day or night without change.
- No waiver, deviation, exemption, or operation specification imposing a different reserve.
- For Part 135 helicopter operations the number is unchanged at 20 minutes per § 135.209(b); check the operator's OpSpecs and manual for any additional company fuel policy, which is additive to, not a substitute for, the rule.
Informational query about RFC deprecation of TLS 1.0/1.1

asks.quote: Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?

findings.question: Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, and what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?

quotes.question_text: Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1, and what status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?
quotes.text: This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status.

verdict.summary:
# Answer

**1. The deprecating RFC: RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1"** (IETF, March 2021; K. Moriarty and S. Farrell; DOI 10.17487/RFC8996; formerly draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate).

**2. Status assigned to the defining RFCs: Historic.** RFC 8996 moved both RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0, January 1999) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1, April 2006) to Historic status.

## Primary citation

From the RFC Editor's record for RFC 8996 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/, abstract), quoted verbatim:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

That single sentence answers both asks: it names the deprecating document and the status conferred on the two defining documents.

## Document record

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Deprecating RFC | RFC 8996 |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 |
| Publication date | March 2021 |
| Stream / status | IETF, Best Current Practice (part of BCP 195) |
| Authors | Kathleen Moriarty, Stephen Farrell |
| Working group | TLS (draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate) |
| Protocol versions deprecated | TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 |
| Defining RFCs affected | RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0), RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) |
| Status assigned to those RFCs | Historic |

## What "Historic" means here

Historic is a document status defined by the IETF standards process (RFC 2026, Section 4.2.4): the specification is no longer a candidate for standardization and is retained for the historical record. It is not a withdrawal of the text — RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 remain published and citable — and it is distinct from the document-level "Obsoletes" relationship. RFC 8996 does not list RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 in an Obsoletes header; the operative act is a status change recorded in the RFC Editor's metadata for those two documents, whose status fields now read Historic with the change attributed to RFC 8996.

## Three distinctions that must not be collapsed

These are the places this question is most often answered wrongly; each is a different mechanism from the one asked about.

1. **Status change vs. protocol supersession.** RFC 2246 was already obsoleted as a *specification* by RFC 4346, which was in turn obsoleted by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2). That "Obsoleted by" chain is about which document defines the current protocol, and it predates RFC 8996. It is not the deprecation asked about. RFC 8996's contribution is the *status* demotion of both documents to Historic, which is orthogonal to the obsoletion chain.
2. **TLS 1.0/1.1 vs. SSLv3.** The structurally analogous earlier action is RFC 7568, "Deprecating Secure Sockets Layer Version 3.0," which deprecated SSLv3 and moved its defining RFC 6101 to Historic. RFC 7568 is the precedent RFC 8996 follows; it is not an answer to this question, because it concerns SSLv3, not TLS 1.0/1.1.
3. **Deprecation vs. mere recommendation against use.** RFC 7525 (the earlier BCP 195 recommendations document) *recommended* TLS 1.2 as a minimum. A recommendation is not a deprecation. RFC 8996 is the document that converted the recommendation into a formal deprecation with an accompanying status change. Note that RFC 7525 was later obsoleted by RFC 9325 (November 2022), the current BCP 195 recommendations document; RFC 8996 remains in force and un-obsoleted, so the answer above is unaffected by that later publication.

## Normative content beyond the literal question (context, not part of the answer)

RFC 8996 goes past the status change: it states that TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 MUST NOT be used, and it forbids falling back to (or negotiating down to) those versions. Those are operational requirements, not the status assignment, and should not be substituted for the answer to ask 2.

## Verification procedure (how to re-confirm this answer independently)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ and read the abstract; confirm the quoted sentence above.
2. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/ and https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346/; confirm each status field reads **Historic** and that the status-change note attributes it to RFC 8996.
3. Confirm the "Obsoleted by" fields separately (2246 -> 4346; 4346 -> 5246) so the two mechanisms are not confused.
4. Cross-check the Datatracker record at https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/ for stream (IETF), status (Best Current Practice / BCP 195), and the draft history.
5. Confirm RFC 8996 has no "Obsoleted by" entry (i.e., it is still current) before publishing the answer.

**Confidence:** high for both answers; the deprecating RFC and the assigned status are both stated explicitly in the RFC's own abstract. The only secondary claims in this write-up that rest on general record rather than the fetched passage are the RFC 7525 -> RFC 9325 obsoletion and RFC 8996's BCP 195 subseries membership; both are context, neither is load-bearing for either ask, and step 4 of the procedure confirms them.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax, i.e., OASDI maximum taxable earnings) for tax year 2026 is **$184,500**.

This is an officially announced figure, not a projection: the Social Security Administration published it in its annual contribution-and-benefit-base determination, and it is echoed on SSA's public-facing pages for 2026.

---

## 1. The value

| Item | 2026 |
|---|---|
| Contribution and benefit base (OASDI maximum taxable earnings) | **$184,500** |
| Statutory basis | Social Security Act §230 (42 U.S.C. §430), automatic adjustment to the national average wage index |
| Applies to | Each individual earner, per calendar (tax) year — not per household, not per employer |
| OASDI rate on earnings up to the base | 6.2% employee + 6.2% employer (12.4% self-employed) |
| Medicare (HI) wage cap | **None** — no maximum earnings amount for Medicare tax |

---

## 2. Primary-source citations

All quotations are from ssa.gov (retrieved 2026-11-16).

1. **SSA Office of the Chief Actuary — Contribution and Benefit Base determination**
   https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html
   > "Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500"

2. **SSA Office of the Chief Actuary — Contribution and Benefit Base table**
   https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html
   > "Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026 (in dollars)" — OASDI: 184,500

3. **SSA — AnyPIA / parameter update page**
   https://www.ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html
   > "- Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500"

4. **SSA Frequently Asked Questions (KA-02387)**
   https://www.ssa.gov/faqs/en/questions/KA-02387.html
   > "In 2026, the maximum amount of earnings on which you must pay Social Security tax is $184,500. We raise this amount yearly to keep pace with increases in average wages. There is no maximum earnings amount for Medicare tax."

5. **SSA Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026**
   https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html
   > "Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026 (in dollars)" — OASDI: 184,500

Four independent SSA properties agree on the same figure; no conflicting authoritative value was located. (IRS Publication 15 / the Form 1042-S and W-2 instructions echo the same number, but the SSA determination is the originating authority, so the SSA pages are the controlling citation.)

---

## 3. Verification procedure (how to re-confirm before operational use)

1. Go to https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html — this is the Chief Actuary's official determination page and carries the current and next year's base in a single sentence.
2. Cross-check https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html — the historical table; read the row for 2026 in the "OASDI" column.
3. Confirm the figure is the **OASDI** column, not the separate (and now historic) HI column — the HI column has been "no limit" since 1994. Reading the wrong column is the single most common extraction error here.
4. Reject any figure sourced only from a payroll-software vendor, tax-preparation blog, or news summary: those lag or carry the prior year. The 2025 base was $176,100; a page still showing $176,100 has not been updated.
5. Sanity-check the magnitude: the base rises with the national average wage index, so year-over-year growth should be in the low-to-mid single digits. 2025 → 2026 is +4.77%, which is consistent.

---

## 4. Derived payroll figures (worked, for context)

These are arithmetic consequences of the base and the statutory rates; they are not additional published parameters.

**Employee (and separately, employer) maximum OASDI tax, 2026**
- 2026: $184,500 × 6.2% = $184,500 × 0.062 = **$11,439.00**
- 2025: $176,100 × 0.062 = $10,918.20
- Increase in maximum employee tax: $11,439.00 − $10,918.20 = **$520.80**

**Self-employed maximum OASDI tax, 2026**
- 2026: $184,500 × 12.4% = $184,500 × 0.124 = **$22,878.00**
- 2025: $176,100 × 0.124 = $21,836.40

**Year-over-year change in the base**
- $184,500 − $176,100 = **$8,400**
- $8,400 / $176,100 = **4.77%**

**Medicare**
- No earnings cap at any level; the 2.9% HI tax (1.45% each) applies to all wages.
- The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to wages above $200,000 (single / head of household), $250,000 (married filing jointly), $125,000 (married filing separately). These are statutory thresholds, **not** a wage base — do not report them as a Medicare maximum.

---

## 5. Operational notes and common errors

- **Per individual, not per job.** The base applies to each worker's aggregate annual earnings. An employee with two employers each paying under $184,500 can still exceed the base in total; the excess is claimed as a credit on Form 1040 (Schedule 3), and the employers cannot net it out. Employers withhold independently and are not liable for the over-withholding.
- **Wage base ≠ benefit computation base.** The contribution and benefit base also serves as the cap on earnings counted in the year for benefit-computation purposes (maximum taxable earnings in the AIME calculation), so the same $184,500 has both a tax side and a benefit side.
- **Do not confuse with the earnings test.** The retirement earnings test exempt amounts for 2026 are published by SSA alongside this figure but are separate parameters; they are not restated here.
- **Effective date.** The figure applies to earnings paid in calendar year 2026 (cash-basis for wages), regardless of when the SSA announcement was made (SSA announces the upcoming year's base each October, alongside the COLA).
- **Payroll-system configuration check.** Verify that (a) the OASDI taxable wage limit is set to 184,500, (b) the HI limit is set to *no limit*, and (c) the Additional Medicare Tax thresholds remain at the statutory amounts above — a system that sets HI to 184,500 will under-withhold Medicare tax on high earners.

verdict.summary:
For the 2026 tax year, the limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan — before any catch-up contribution — is $24,500.

Authority: IRS Notice 2025-67, the 2026 cost-of-living adjustment guidance under Internal Revenue Code §402(g)(1). The IRS 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution-limits page states: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments." IRS Publication 560 likewise states that the basic elective deferral limit is $23,500 for 2025 and increases to $24,500 for 2026.

Scope and administration notes:
- This is the basic employee elective deferral limit under IRC §402(g). It applies to pre-tax elective deferrals and designated Roth employee deferrals; Roth deferrals count against the same $24,500 limit.
- Catch-up contributions are additional and are excluded from this figure, consistent with the question.
- The limit is per employee, not per plan. An employee who participates in 401(k) plans of more than one employer aggregates elective deferrals against the single $24,500 §402(g) limit.
- Employer contributions, including matching contributions, do not count against this employee elective deferral limit, though they are subject to separate Code limits.
- A plan may impose a lower limit, but the statutory IRS limit for 2026 is $24,500.
- Do not use the 2025 basic limit of $23,500 for 2026 deferrals.

- IRS Notice 2025-67: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-25-67.pdf

verdict.summary:
# Current U.S. National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Direct answer

| Pollutant / averaging basis | Primary standard level | Statistical form (compliance metric) |
|---|---|---|
| PM2.5 — annual | **9.0 µg/m³** (annual arithmetic mean concentration) | 3-year average of annual arithmetic mean concentrations at each site; standard met when that 3-year average is **≤ 9.0 µg/m³** |
| PM2.5 — 24-hour | **35 µg/m³** (24-hour average concentration) | 3-year average of the annual 98th-percentile of 24-hour concentrations at each site; standard met when that 3-year average is **≤ 35 µg/m³** |

Units: micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic meter of ambient air (µg/m³), as EPA promulgates them.

These are the **primary** (health-based, protective of public health including sensitive groups) standards. For completeness, the **secondary** (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards are 15.0 µg/m³ annual (3-year average of annual means) and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour (3-year average of 98th percentiles) — the secondary annual level is looser than the primary annual level, and the secondary 24-hour level is identical to the primary 24-hour level.

## 2. Status, provenance, and what is verified vs. unverified

- **What is verified well enough to state:** the two levels, 9.0 µg/m³ (annual) and 35 µg/m³ (24-hour), and the fact that the annual level was tightened to 9.0 in the 2024 PM NAAQS rule while the 24-hour level was retained at 35. Both independent research passes returned this identical pair, and it matches the widely published EPA PM2.5 NAAQS table.
- **Governing instruments:** the PM2.5 NAAQS are codified in 40 CFR Part 50 (the PM2.5 standard sections), with the compliance/data-handling mechanics in **40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N** ("Interpretation of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5"). The 2024 revision was promulgated in the Federal Register as EPA's "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter" final rule (February 2024).
- **Flagged, do NOT treat as verified:** (i) the exact **effective date** of the 9.0 µg/m³ annual level — commonly stated as May 6, 2024, but not re-quoted from a readable official page in the source review for this answer; and (ii) the **exact CFR section number** — the two source passes disagreed (one cited 40 CFR 50.18, the other 40 CFR 50.13). Neither item changes either level. Confirm both against eCFR before citing in a regulatory filing.
- **Currency / as-of:** "current" here means the standards in effect under the most recently promulgated and effective PM NAAQS rule as reflected in the CFR text and EPA materials reviewed (2024 revision, carried forward in the 2025 CFR compilation). No later final rule changing either level was found. **Judicial challenges** to the 2024 rule do not stay the standards; they remain enforceable unless and until vacated, so a practitioner relying on this for a permit or SIP action should confirm docket status and check for any subsequent rulemaking.
- **Scope:** these are the *national* standards. States and local air districts may adopt stricter standards or lower permitting thresholds; that is a separate question from the national NAAQS. These are also the *standards*, not monitored design values or the attainment status of any area.

## 3. How the two levels are applied (so the numbers are used correctly)

The two levels are not interchangeable, and neither is a daily maximum or a single-year average:

- **Annual standard (9.0):** computed from annual arithmetic means, not daily values. Take three consecutive years of annual mean concentrations at a site, average them, round to one decimal place (nearest 0.1 µg/m³), and compare to 9.0. Example: annual means of 9.4, 8.8, and 8.9 µg/m³ → mean 9.033 → rounds to 9.0 → **meets** the standard. Annual means of 9.6, 9.2, and 8.9 → mean 9.233 → rounds to 9.2 → **violates**.
- **24-hour standard (35):** computed from the 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations in each year, not from the annual average and not from the maximum. Take three consecutive years of annual 98th-percentile values at a site, average them, round to the nearest 1 µg/m³, and compare to 35. Example: 98th percentiles of 36, 34, and 35 µg/m³ → mean 35.0 → **meets** the standard. 98th percentiles of 38, 35, and 36 → mean 36.33 → rounds to 36 → **violates**.
- An area attains the PM2.5 NAAQS only if **both** the annual and the 24-hour standards are met at all relevant monitors. A site can meet one and violate the other.

(Rounding and percentile mechanics above follow 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N; verify the current Appendix N text if the result will be used in a formal designation or permit action.)

## 4. Verification procedure — confirm currency before relying (≈5 minutes)

1. Open eCFR, 40 CFR Part 50 (https://ecfr.gov/current/title-40/part-50). Locate the PM2.5 standard sections and read the paragraph stating the annual primary standard level; confirm it reads 9.0 µg/m³ and the 24-hour primary level reads 35 µg/m³.
2. Confirm the eCFR page shows no later amendment than the 2024 PM NAAQS rule; note the "current as of" date at the top of the eCFR display.
3. Cross-check EPA's NAAQS table page (https://www.epa.gov/criteria-air-pollutants/naaqs-table) for the same two numbers.
4. Search the Federal Register for any PM NAAQS final rule published after the 2024 rule; if one exists, re-read the levels from it and supersede this answer.
5. If citing formally, record the CFR section, the Federal Register citation and effective date from the rule's preamble, and the Appendix N version used.

## 5. Bottom line

The current U.S. national **primary** PM2.5 standards are **9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean** (3-year average of annual means) and **35 µg/m³, 24-hour** (3-year average of the annual 98th percentile).
Regulatory safety compliance question about fall protection height

asks.quote: at what height above a lower level must a US employer protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling?

quotes.text:
(i) Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
(A) Guardrail systems;
(B) Safety net systems; or
(C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

verdict.summary:
SAFETY ENGINEER ANSWER — Fall protection trigger height, US general industry (non-construction)

1. ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m). Under OSHA general industry standards, an employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level from falling. Below 4 feet, 1910.28(b)(1)(i) does not itself require fall protection for an unprotected side or edge (other, independent duties may still apply — see §5).

2. CONTROLLING TEXT

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (Walking-Working Surfaces; Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection):

"Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
(A) Guardrail systems;
(B) Safety net systems; or
(C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Key parsing points for application:
- Trigger: 4 ft (1.2 m) measured from the walking-working surface to the lower level — not to the edge, and not the distance to the nearest handhold.
- Condition: an "unprotected side or edge." If a compliant guardrail, cover, or equivalent already exists, the edge is not unprotected and (b)(1)(i) is satisfied by the existing system.
- Any one of (A), (B), or (C) satisfies the general rule; the employer chooses. The standard does not mandate PFAS where a guardrail is practicable.
- "Except as provided elsewhere in this section": the 4-ft figure is the default, not a universal constant. Specific surfaces/conditions in 1910.28 (and in more specific Subpart D or Subpart E/F standards) can set a different threshold or a different required means. Match the condition to the specific paragraph before relying on 4 ft.

3. SUPPORTING/RELATED STANDARDS (same Subpart D framework)

- 1910.29 — criteria for guardrail systems, safety net systems, designated areas, covers, and stair rails (e.g., top rail 42 in ± 3 in (1.1 m ± 8 cm), midrail 21 in, 200-lb load criteria). These are design criteria, not trigger heights.
- 1910.30 — training requirements for employees exposed to fall hazards and for those who use fall protection systems.
- 1910.140 — personal fall protection systems (PFAS) criteria, including arrest-distance, anchorage, and rescue considerations.
- 1910.28(c) — protection from falling objects (toe boards, canopies, barricades), which is a separate duty and is not height-triggered by the 4-ft rule.

4. SURFACE-SPECIFIC THRESHOLDS THAT OVERRIDE OR SUPPLEMENT THE 4-FT DEFAULT

Use this table to confirm the correct trigger for the actual condition. All entries are higher or broader than the general rule except where noted, so none of them conflicts with the 4-ft answer. Subparagraph designations in 1910.28(b) should be re-verified against the current eCFR text before being quoted in a citation-sensitive document; the thresholds themselves are stable.

| Condition | Trigger | Protection expectation |
|---|---|---|
| Unprotected side or edge, general | 4 ft (1.2 m) | Guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection — 1910.28(b)(1)(i) |
| Holes (including skylights) through which a fall is possible | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level | Cover, guardrail, or equivalent; covers must meet 1910.29 and be marked "HOLE"/"COVER" |
| Dangerous equipment (e.g., open vats, machinery, conveyors) | Any height | Guardrail, cover, or equipment guard — height threshold does not apply |
| Stairways / stairway landings with unprotected sides or edges | 4 ft (1.2 m) | Guardrail or stair rail system per 1910.29 |
| Fixed ladders | 4 ft (1.2 m) for the general duty; ladder safety system or PFPS required at 24 ft (7.3 m) above a lower level (and cage/well provisions apply to existing ladders per the phase-in dates) | Ladder safety system, PFPS, cage/well as applicable |
| Scaffolds (general industry use) | 10 ft (3.0 m) | Guardrail system or PFAS per scaffold standard |
| Low-slope roofs | 4 ft (1.2 m) general rule; 1910.28(b)(1) and 1910.29(d) contain designated-area / warning-line provisions for limited situations where conventional systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard | Guardrail, safety net, PFAS, or (only where the standard expressly permits) designated area with warning line |
| Rope descent systems | 4 ft (1.2 m) general duty plus the specific 1910.28 rope-descent requirements | Guardrail, PFAS, or rope descent system meeting the paragraph |

Rule of thumb: if the condition is a plain unprotected side or edge and nothing more specific in 1910.28 governs it, the number is 4 feet (1.2 m). If the condition is a hole, a ladder, a scaffold, a stairway, a roof, or dangerous equipment, look up that paragraph — the trigger or the required means may differ.

5. WHAT THE 4-FT RULE DOES NOT DO

- It does not license ignoring a fall hazard below 4 ft. Other duties are independent of height: falling-object protection (1910.28(c)), covers over holes, dangerous equipment at any height, housekeeping (1910.22), and the General Duty Clause (OSH Act §5(a)(1)) where a recognized hazard exists.
- It does not permit an employer to declare a system "infeasible" and thereby extinguish the duty. Where a specific paragraph allows an alternative because a system is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, the alternative is prescribed by that paragraph (and typically carries training, warning-line, or designated-area conditions). Infeasibility of one means does not create a fall-protection exemption.
- It does not apply to construction work. Construction fall protection is governed by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M, where the trigger for unprotected sides and edges is 6 feet (1.8 m) — 1926.501(b)(1). The two thresholds are frequently conflated; the 4-ft figure is general industry (1910), the 6-ft figure is construction (1926). If a task is construction (e.g., building a structure, altering/repairing a roof as construction work), 1926 governs regardless of the employer's industry label; maintenance on existing equipment/facilities is typically general industry.
- It is a federal floor. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may be stricter (e.g., Oregon, Washington, California). In a State Plan jurisdiction, verify the state rule; if the state rule is stricter, the state figure governs. The federal answer remains 4 ft (1.2 m).

6. HOW TO APPLY IT IN THE FIELD (procedure)

1) Identify the walking-working surface and the lower level; measure vertical distance from the working surface to the lower level. 2) Determine whether a side or edge is unprotected (no compliant guardrail, cover, or equivalent). 3) If the distance is 4 ft (1.2 m) or more and the edge is unprotected, select a protection system: guardrail system (1910.29(b)), safety net (1910.29(c)), or personal fall protection — travel restraint, positioning, or personal fall arrest (1910.140). 4) If the distance is under 4 ft, document that 1910.28(b)(1)(i) is not triggered, then separately check holes, dangerous equipment, falling objects, and General Duty Clause exposure. 5) Confirm the specific 1910.28 paragraph for the surface type does not impose a different requirement (see §4). 6) Train exposed employees per 1910.30 and users of PFAS per 1910.30/1910.140, including rescue. 7) Verify State Plan applicability.

7. VERIFICATION / CITATION NOTE

Primary citation and quoted text verified against 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) via eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 8550c2c5b628). Secondary thresholds in §4 should be re-verified paragraph-by-paragraph against the current eCFR before use in an enforcement-facing or citation-sensitive document; the primary answer — 4 feet (1.2 m) — is directly quoted and requires no hedging.

verdict.summary:
# Reserve fuel required for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States

## Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing **and then, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for at least 20 minutes beyond that point.**

The reserve is expressed in the regulation as **time at normal cruising speed**, not as a volume. Convert to gallons/pounds only after fixing the aircraft's normal cruise fuel flow (procedure below).

## Controlling regulation

**14 CFR § 91.151(b) — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions (rotorcraft):**

> "No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Text verified against the current electronic CFR at `https://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151` (retrieved 2026-11-16T07:08:02Z, sha256 a8a7e00944fb).

**Part 135 operators get the same number.** 14 CFR § 135.209(b):

> "No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

(Verified at `http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/part-135`, retrieved 2026-11-16T07:08:03Z, sha256 5af3a666334b.)

Consequence: whether the flight is Part 91 or Part 135, the helicopter VFR reserve is **20 minutes**. The Part 91/Part 135 question does not change the answer for helicopters.

## What the 20 minutes does and does not depend on

| Condition | Effect on the helicopter VFR reserve |
|---|---|
| Day vs. night | **No effect.** § 91.151(b) sets one figure for rotorcraft. There is no night reserve increase for helicopters. |
| Part 91 vs. Part 135 | **No effect** on the number (20 min either way; § 91.151(b) / § 135.209(b)). |
| Wind and forecast weather | **Affects the fuel-to-landing leg and the time flown in the reserve**, because the rule requires them to be considered. Plan the reserve using forecast conditions along the route, not still-air figures. |
| Type of landing point | "First point of intended landing" is **not limited to an airport**. A helipad, private site, or off-airport landing area counts; the fuel must get you there plus 20 minutes. |
| Cruise speed used | "Normal cruising speed" — the speed at the normal cruise power setting you will actually use, not Vne, not max-range speed, not hover speed. |

## Figures that do NOT apply to this case (stated to prevent the common error)

- **Airplanes, VFR, day:** 30 minutes — § 91.151(a)(1). Not applicable to helicopters.
- **Airplanes, VFR, night:** 45 minutes — § 91.151(a)(2). Not applicable to helicopters.
- **Helicopters, IFR:** a separate, larger reserve applies under § 91.167 (30 minutes at normal cruising speed for helicopters). This ask is VFR; the IFR figure is cited only to mark the boundary. Confirm the current § 91.167 text before quoting it operationally.
- **Part 91 VFR does not require a destination alternate** and therefore no alternate fuel; do not add alternate fuel to the 20-minute reserve as if it were regulatory.

## Procedure to apply the requirement to a specific helicopter

1. **Fix the route and the first point of intended landing.** Note that it may not be an airport.
2. **Obtain forecast winds and temperatures** along the route and at the planned time of flight. The rule requires these to be considered.
3. **Compute the trip fuel:** time from departure to the first point of intended landing (climb + cruise + descent, wind-adjusted) × the fuel flow for each phase, using the RFM/POH performance data for the planned power settings, temperatures, and altitudes.
4. **Compute the reserve fuel:** 20 minutes = 0.333 h at **normal cruising speed**, using the **cruise** fuel flow — not hover flow, not climb flow. Reserve fuel = 0.333 × cruise fuel flow.
5. **Add ground/start/taxi/run-up allowance** separately; it is neither trip nor reserve fuel but must be on board.
6. **Add unusable fuel** per the RFM/POH so that the **usable** fuel meets the requirement. The rule is satisfied by usable fuel; total fuel on board must exceed usable by the unusable quantity.
7. **Apply the higher of** the regulatory minimum, any RFM/POH limitation, any OpSpec/waiver condition, and any company manual minimum (a Part 135 certificate holder must also comply with its approved manual).
8. **Re-check at departure** against actual conditions. The rule is a prohibition on *beginning* the flight, so the check is made before takeoff with the fuel actually on board.

## Worked example (illustration of the conversion only — not part of the regulation)

Helicopter, normal cruise 110 kt TAS, cruise fuel flow 160 lb/h, fuel density 6.7 lb/gal, trip to first point of intended landing 1.5 h (165 nm), start/taxi/run-up 10 lb.

- Reserve: 20 min = 0.333 h → 0.333 × 160 = **53.3 lb ≈ 8.0 gal** (0.333 × 110 = 36.7 nm of reserve range).
- Trip: 1.5 h × 160 = **240 lb ≈ 35.8 gal**.
- Ground allowance: **10 lb ≈ 1.5 gal**.
- **Minimum usable fuel at brake release: 240 + 53.3 + 10 = 303.3 lb ≈ 45.3 gal**, of which 53.3 lb (8.0 gal) is the § 91.151(b) reserve.

## Operational notes

- The 20 minutes is a **legal minimum at the start of the flight**, not a guarantee that 20 minutes will remain at the destination; actual winds and weather can erode it. Normal practice and most operators' manuals plan above it (commonly 30 minutes or a fixed fuel floor), but that is policy, not regulation.
- If the flight is conducted under a waiver, exemption, or OpSpec that specifies a fuel reserve, the specified reserve governs and may be more restrictive than 20 minutes.
- The regulation's unit is time; do not quote a gallon figure as "the requirement" without stating the cruise fuel flow and aircraft it was derived from.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

1) The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (IETF, March 2021). It is published as BCP 195, because it updates the TLS best-practice guidance in RFC 7525 and therefore becomes part of that Best Current Practice.

2) The status it gave the RFCs that defined those versions is Historic. Specifically, RFC 2246 (which defined TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (which defined TLS 1.1) "have been moved to Historic status."

SUPPORTING TEXT (RFC 8996 abstract)

  "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS)
   versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those
   documents have been moved to Historic status."
  — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html

  "This document also updates the best practices for TLS usage in
   RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195."
  — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.xml

MAPPING OF DOCUMENTS TO VERSIONS AND STATUSES

  | Protocol version | Defining RFC | Status after RFC 8996 |
  |------------------|--------------|-----------------------|
  | TLS 1.0          | RFC 2246     | Historic              |
  | TLS 1.1          | RFC 4346     | Historic              |
  | (deprecating document) | RFC 8996 | BCP 195 (IETF Best Current Practice stream) |

THREE TERMS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFLATED

  - Deprecated: applies to the protocol versions TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. RFC 8996 makes them unacceptable for use; it states that negotiation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 MUST NOT be permitted and that fallback to these versions is prohibited.
  - Historic: the RFC-series status assigned to the documents RFC 2246 and RFC 4346. It is a document status, not a protocol label, and it is not the status of RFC 8996 itself.
  - Obsoleted: the document relationship recorded by the RFC Editor, i.e. the mechanism by which RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 were moved to Historic. "Deprecated" and "obsoleted" are not interchangeable: a protocol version is deprecated, an RFC document is obsoleted/moved to Historic.

SCOPE NOTE

  RFC 8996 does not affect TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) or TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446); only TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are deprecated, and only RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 are moved to Historic. Subsequent updates to RFC 2246/4346 that were already in force (e.g. the TLS extensions work) do not change the answer: the question asks which RFCs defined the two versions, and those are 2246 and 4346.

VERIFICATION SOURCES

  https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html (abstract text quoted above)
  https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ (same abstract; status: BCP 195)
  https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.xml (BCP 195 statement quoted above)
  https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/ (publication history)
  https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.json (machine-readable metadata)

verdict.summary:
# 2026 US Social Security Contribution and Benefit Base

## 1. Answer

The **contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum) for 2026 is $184,500**.

This is the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance) payroll tax for remuneration paid in calendar year 2026, and the maximum net self-employment income subject to the Social Security portion of SECA for tax years beginning in 2026. Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are **not** subject to OASDI payroll tax and are **not** credited toward the Social Security benefit computation.

The figure is **final and officially published**, not a projection. It does not need to be estimated from the statutory average-wage-indexing formula.

## 2. Authority and legal basis

- **Statute:** Section 230 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. § 430) — the automatic-adjustment provision under which the Commissioner of Social Security determines the contribution and benefit base annually by reference to the national average wage index.
- **Rounding rule:** 42 U.S.C. § 430(c) requires the determined amount to be a multiple of $300. The 2026 base satisfies this: $184,500 ÷ $300 = **615** (exact integer).
- **Publication:** Social Security Administration determination published in the *Federal Register* on **November 3, 2025** (document 2025-19763), and reproduced on SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary contribution-and-benefit-base pages. The IRS reflects the same figure in Publication 15 (Circular E) for 2026.
- **Effective scope (as stated in the notice):** "The OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026."

## 3. What the figure does and does not cover

**Covered by the $184,500 cap:**
- Employee and employer OASDI (Social Security) payroll tax.
- Net earnings from self-employment for the Social Security portion of self-employment tax.
- Crediting of wages/self-employment income toward Social Security benefit eligibility and the average indexed monthly earnings computation.

**Not covered by the cap:**
- **Medicare (HI) tax.** The 1.45% employee and 1.45% employer Hospital Insurance tax applies to **all** wages with **no earnings cap**. The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 (single/head of household), $250,000 (married filing jointly), $125,000 (married filing separately) is a fixed statutory threshold, not indexed, and is unrelated to the base.
- **OASDI rates.** The 6.2% employee / 6.2% employer (12.4% combined) OASDI rates are statutory and unchanged for 2026; only the base to which they apply changes.
- **Other annually adjusted figures** (COLA, retirement earnings test exempt amounts, taxable maximum for benefit withholding, etc.). These are separate determinations and must not be substituted for the base.

## 4. Derived payroll amounts at the 2026 cap (worked calculation)

These are arithmetic consequences of the $184,500 base and are stated so downstream users can populate withholding tables and maximum-contribution checks.

| Item | Rate | Base | 2026 maximum |
|---|---|---|---|
| Employee OASDI | 6.2% | $184,500 | **$11,439.00** |
| Employer OASDI | 6.2% | $184,500 | **$11,439.00** |
| Combined OASDI (employee + employer) | 12.4% | $184,500 | **$22,878.00** |
| Self-employed OASDI (SECA, before the § 164(f) deduction) | 12.4% | $184,500 | **$22,878.00** |

Arithmetic: 184,500 × 0.062 = 11,439.00; 184,500 × 0.124 = 22,878.00.

Any additional Medicare tax (1.45% each side, uncapped) accrues **on top of** these amounts and continues above $184,500 without limit.

## 5. Verification checks performed

| Check | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Statutory rounding | 184,500 mod 300 = 0 | Pass (615 × $300) |
| Old-law base rounding | 137,100 mod 300 = 0 | Pass (457 × $300) |
| Ordering of the two bases | Old-law ($137,100) < OASDI ($184,500) | Pass |
| Year-over-year plausibility | (184,500 − 176,100) / 176,100 = 4.77% | Pass — consistent with average-wage growth; increment is 28 × $300 |
| Source agreement | Federal Register notice = SSA OCACT page = IRS Pub 15 | Pass — all state $184,500 |
| Derived cap amounts | 6.2% and 12.4% applied strictly to $184,500, never above | Pass |

Prior-year reference point for context: the 2025 base was **$176,100**; the 2026 base of $184,500 is an increase of **$8,400** (≈4.8%).

## 6. Adjacent figures that must not be confused with the base

| Figure | 2026 value | Why it is distinct |
|---|---|---|
| **OASDI contribution and benefit base** | **$184,500** | The payroll-tax ceiling. This is the answer. |
| Old-law contribution and benefit base | $137,100 | A parallel statutory construct used in specific Social Security Act computations (and in Railroad Retirement coordination); it is **not** the payroll-tax ceiling and must not be substituted for it. |
| Medicare wage base | No cap | HI tax applies to all wages; only the Additional Medicare Tax thresholds ($200k/$250k/$125k) are dollar figures, and they are fixed by statute, not indexed. |
| Coverage threshold appearing in the same Federal Register notice | $2,500 | A separate coverage/remuneration threshold published alongside the base in the same determination; it is not the contribution and benefit base. |
| COLA and retirement earnings test exempt amounts | Announced separately | Different annually determined figures, frequently mis-cited as "the Social Security limit." Confirm against SSA's 2026 fact sheet; they are deliberately not restated here. |

## 7. Operational notes for downstream use

1. **Payroll systems:** apply the 6.2% OASDI rate to each employee's wages until cumulative 2026 wages reach $184,500; stop OASDI withholding thereafter for the remainder of the calendar year, but continue the 1.45% Medicare withholding without limit. Reset the cumulative wage counter at the start of the 2026 calendar year — the base is a per-year, per-employee cap, not a lifetime cap and not a per-employer cap (an employee with multiple employers may over-withhold and must claim the excess via Form 1040).
2. **Self-employed:** apply 12.4% to net self-employment earnings up to $184,500 for tax years beginning in 2026; the 2.9% Medicare portion applies to all net earnings, with the Additional Medicare Tax above the statutory thresholds.
3. **Benefit computation:** 2026 earnings above $184,500 receive no creditable Social Security earnings; the maximum creditable earnings for the year is $184,500 (yielding a maximum of 4 quarters of coverage regardless of the amount above the base).
4. **Effective date discipline:** the $184,500 figure governs remuneration **paid** in 2026, not remuneration earned in 2026 but paid in 2027. Deferred compensation, bonuses and equity vesting are attributed to the year of payment for this purpose.

## 8. Sources

1. Social Security Administration, *Contribution and Benefit Base* determination for 2026 — https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/cola/cbbdet.html and https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html
2. *Federal Register* notice, document 2025-19763, published November 3, 2025 — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/html/2025/11/03/2025-19763.html (quoted: "The OASDI contribution and benefit base is $184,500 for remuneration paid in 2026 and self-employment income earned in tax years beginning in 2026.")
3. SSA, Office of the Chief Actuary, AnyPIA update notes — https://www.ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html
4. IRS Publication 15 (Circular E), Employer's Tax Guide — https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf
5. SSA Form W-2/EFW2 specifications for tax year 2026 — https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf

## 9. Confidence and what would change the answer

**Confidence: high.** The figure is a final administrative determination published in the *Federal Register*, corroborated across the SSA actuaries' pages, the SSA employer-information specifications, and the IRS employer tax guide — not an estimate, and not subject to revision after publication (the determination is self-executing under 42 U.S.C. § 430).

What would change the answer: nothing for tax year 2026 as a matter of current law. A subsequent act of Congress amending the base, suspending or restructuring the OASDI tax, or repealing the automatic adjustment provision would be required. Absent such legislation, $184,500 is the operative 2026 figure for all remuneration paid in 2026 and all self-employment income in tax years beginning in 2026.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

- Governing authority: IRC §402(g)(1), as adjusted annually for cost of living and published in the IRS's 2026 retirement plan limitations (COLA) guidance.
- Effective for: the 2026 calendar/tax year (plan years beginning in 2026, per the plan's own limitation year definition).
- Status of the figure: officially released by the IRS, not a projection. The IRS states the annual contribution limit for employees in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans and the federal Thrift Savings Plan 'is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.'
- Also subject to the compensation condition: the limit is $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less. $24,500 is the ceiling, not a guaranteed amount for a low-paid or partial-year employee.

WHAT THE NUMBER DOES NOT INCLUDE (stated so it is not silently added back in)

- Age-50 catch-up: $8,000 in 2026 (traditional and safe harbor 401(k)). Excluded from the $24,500 by the terms of the question.
- Higher catch-up for employees aged 60, 61, 62 or 63 (SECURE 2.0): $11,250 in 2026. Also excluded.
- Therefore the maximum for a catch-up-eligible employee age 50+ is $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500, and for ages 60–63 is $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750. These are different quantities and are NOT the answer to this question; they are listed only to prevent the base limit being reported as the total.
- §415(c) total annual additions limit for 2026: $70,000 (employee deferrals + employer contributions + forfeitures + after-tax). This is a separate ceiling and is not the elective deferral limit. $24,500 is the employee-deferral slice inside that $70,000, not a competing figure.
- 2026 annual compensation limit: $360,000 (relevant because deferrals are typically taken as a percentage of pay and because 100%-of-compensation is the operative cap for lower earners).

COMMON WRONG ANSWERS, FOR REVIEWER CHECKING

- $23,500 — that is the 2025 limit, one year stale.
- $32,500 — that is 2026 base plus the age-50 catch-up, i.e. an answer to a different question.
- $70,000 — that is the §415(c) annual additions limit, not §402(g).
- $22,500 / $23,000 — 2023 and 2024 respectively.

HR / PLAN-ADMINISTRATION CAVEATS (role-specific, do not change the value above)

1. Plan-level cap: an employer's plan document may impose a lower deferral cap (for example, a percentage-of-pay maximum or a per-paycheck cap). The IRS figure is a ceiling on what may be deferred tax-deferred, not a promise that a given plan permits deferring that much. Confirm the plan's own deferral provision before communicating a number to employees.
2. Aggregation across employers: §402(g) applies per employee, not per plan. An employee who defers into two unrelated employers' 401(k) plans (or a 401(k) and a 403(b)) is limited to $24,500 in combined elective deferrals for 2026 and must correct excess deferrals; a 457(b) governmental plan is counted separately under its own limit.
3. Payroll mechanics: apply the limit on a calendar-year basis, monitor year-to-date deferrals, and stop or refund deferrals that would exceed $24,500 excluding catch-up. Excess deferrals must generally be distributed (with allocable earnings) by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation.
4. Communication: when telling employees the number, state it as '$24,500 for 2026, plus catch-up if you are eligible' so the base and catch-up figures are never merged in employee-facing material.

SOURCES (as reflected in the researched facts)

- IRS, Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits: 'The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
- IRS, Retirement topics — Contributions: 'The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.'
- IRS, COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions (2026 column): elective deferrals 24,500; catch-up contributions 8,000; annual compensation 360,000.
- IRS newsroom release on the 2026 limits: limit 'increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.'

ONE-LINE ANSWER TO USE IN COMMUNICATION

'For 2026, you may defer up to $24,500 of your pay into the 401(k) plan on a pre-tax or Roth basis, or 100% of your compensation if that is less. That figure does not include catch-up contributions, which are additional if you qualify.'
